Title: The "almost" perfect trial conversion
Creator: Growth.Design
Bottom line: Show the user's most urgent, personal result before the paywall and let them take the core action once, so paying feels like a no-brainer.
What they did: The author uses Mine, an app that finds companies holding your personal data. Mine builds momentum with easy yes screens, a guessing quiz and a pre-validated action, but surprises the user with a request to read his emails and puts a paywall right before his first data reclaim. Only after paying does he learn 60 companies hold his financial data, which Growth.Design argues should have been shown before the paywall.
Takeaways: Easy yeses build momentum for a later ask; Show the path before a big permission; Long warnings get skipped; Confirm the action before users take it; Show the scariest personal insight before the paywall
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: before showing plans, show the user's own weak-subject result from their first practice set (e.g. "You scored 40% in Pharmacology"). Onboarding: show a short numbered list of what comes next (choose exam, take a 10-question check, see your plan) before asking for sign-in. Practice: let free users finish one full set and see the analysis before gating

Key points.title: Easy yeses build momentum for a later ask
Key points.detail: Mine opens with screens the user agrees with right away, then a short story the user says yes to. This "Yes" Ladder: "People are more likely to agree to a large task after saying 'yes' to a smaller one." It primes users for the later sign-in and paywall.

Key points.title: Show the path before a big permission
Key points.detail: Sign-in asked to view the user's messages, which felt alarming even though it is how Mine scans for companies. The redesign shows a clear step-by-step plan so "we know exactly what's coming and why." When a step is critical for funnel conversion, remove barriers upfront.

Key points.title: Long warnings get skipped
Key points.detail: Mine had warned about email access earlier, but the user missed it. "Our brains block complex or lengthy information to save us from overloading." Short, well-timed explanations work better than an early block of text.

Key points.title: Confirm the action before users take it
Key points.detail: Before reclaiming data from Headspace, Mine shows feedback confirming the action. "People seek validation to feel secure in their decisions - especially when it's the first time they take action." The tip: whenever you can validate someone's thoughts before they act, do it.

Key points.title: Show the scariest personal insight before the paywall
Key points.detail: The paywall hit just before the first reclaim, and the user nearly left. After paying, he saw that "60 companies have my financial data" and says they "should have told me from the get go." Growth.Design calls this a Journey Reorder: surfacing that risk earlier would make the paywall a no-brainer. The author also asks if users should get one free reclaim first. Mine scored a B.

Title: Zeigarnik Effect: Why it's hard to leave things incomplete
Creator: Growth.Design
Bottom line: Unfinished tasks pull people back, so show real progress and the remaining steps, but don't turn it into a loop that trains people to come back compulsively.
What they did: The piece explains the Zeigarnik Effect with a TV cliffhanger, then shows LinkedIn's profile-completion widget, which starts users with steps already done. It shows a Turo booking flow where the author churned and argues a progress bar with remaining steps would have helped. It ends with Clash of Clans as an example of overuse, where timers bring players back many times a day.
Results: Cited data, not a test: "Almost 70% of all checkout sessions are abandoned." "20% of those churned sessions were due to a long and complicated checkout process" (Baymard Institute, 2021).
Takeaways: Unfinished tasks create tension people want to resolve; Start users with real progress already made; Show the remaining steps to cut drop-off; Don't hold users' time hostage
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: show a setup checklist with steps already completed (exam chosen, account created) and the 2-3 left. Today's plan: show "3 of 5 done" with the remaining items named, so an unfinished plan pulls users back. Progress & streaks: avoid timers or partial rewards that push users to reopen the app many times a day

Key points.title: Unfinished tasks create tension people want to resolve
Key points.detail: "People hate the tension created by incomplete tasks. That's why we remember them better or take action to complete them." A cliffhanger makes you watch one more episode. Any digital product can use this, for example by leaving a visible, unfinished goal.

Key points.title: Start users with real progress already made
Key points.detail: LinkedIn added a profile-completion widget to fix empty profiles, and it shows two steps already completed. This is the Endowed Progress Effect: early progress raises motivation to finish. But "if you 'fake' the start, it can backfire"; LinkedIn's progress is real because the user already did those steps.

Key points.title: Show the remaining steps to cut drop-off
Key points.detail: After hours of research the author churned in Turo's booking flow. A clear view of the remaining steps and a progress bar could have closed the deal. Baymard data: almost 70% of checkout sessions are abandoned, and 20% of those due to long, complicated checkouts.

Key points.title: Don't hold users' time hostage
Key points.detail: Clash of Clans is built on waiting for buildings to complete and brings players back "every minute or so during onboarding." When people come back "100+ times a day" to start and finish tasks, "We're no longer helping people complete complex tasks. We're training them to get addicted." OnCourse should use open loops to help finish a plan, not to farm opens.

Title: Labor Perception Bias: Why faster isn't always better
Creator: Growth.Design
Bottom line: When users expect heavy work, show the work happening; an instant result can feel broken, while an honest progress animation builds trust and perceived value.
What they did: The piece compares a restaurant serving a complex dish in 15 seconds with HubSpot importing 287,539 contacts in 0.01 seconds, both of which feel suspicious. It shows Wise's animation of money being processed as a good example. It then uses the New York Times 2016 election needle, which jittered 10 times a second though data came every 15 seconds, as an unethical use.
Results: Cited research, not a test: "A well-designed effect can increase your app's perceived value by up to 15%" (Harvard, 2011). The NYT needle: data fed "every 15 seconds" while the needle jittered "10 times per second".
Takeaways: Instant results on big tasks feel suspicious; Show the work after a key action; Labor screens can lift perceived value up to 15%; Reassure, don't manipulate
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: when building the first study plan, show a short labor screen listing what is being considered (exam date, subjects, daily time) before revealing the plan. Practice: after a mock test, show a brief analysis step ("Comparing with 12,000 aspirants... finding weak topics") that reflects real work, not a fake delay

Key points.title: Instant results on big tasks feel suspicious
Key points.detail: HubSpot imports 287,539 contacts "in just 0.01 seconds" and the user wonders "Did it work?" Like a complex dish arriving in 15 seconds, speed can create doubt. When expectations are high (money, migration, analysis, reporting), users get skeptical if the wait is too short.

Key points.title: Show the work after a key action
Key points.detail: "People trust and value things more when they see the underlying work." Wise doesn't drop you into an activity log after a transfer; it shows a reassuring animation of your money being processed. For OnCourse, a plan or test analysis screen can show what the app is doing for the aspirant.

Key points.title: Labor screens can lift perceived value up to 15%
Key points.detail: "A well-designed effect can increase your app's perceived value by up to 15%." The net lift on activation, retention and revenue depends on context (waiting duration, audience, product), so it's worth testing. The concept applies to almost every product.

Key points.title: Reassure, don't manipulate
Key points.detail: The NYT election needle got new data every 15 seconds but jittered 10 times a second, amplifying uncertainty to maximize engagement and page views. "You should use Labor Perception to reassure users, not to manipulate them." Fake waits ("benevolent deceptions") need clear ethical rules.

Title: One simple way Apple could improve your sleep habits
Creator: Growth.Design
Bottom line: A habit reminder that looks like every other notification gets ignored; make it stand out, state the benefit, ask for a tiny commitment, then show progress and reward completion.
What they did: The author ignores Apple's bedtime reminder while watching YouTube. Growth.Design redesigns it step by step: a harder-to-ignore format, a test of added friction (rejected because people would turn it off), a reminder of the wind-down benefit, a swipe to commit, a progress view, a loss-aversion message if you keep scrolling, and positive reinforcement at the end.
Takeaways: Same-format reminders fall into banner blindness; More friction can make users turn reminders off; State the benefit of the habit; A tiny action creates commitment; Use only real losses, then reward completion
Ideas for OnCourse: Notifications: vary the format and content of the daily study reminder so it doesn't become wallpaper, and lead with the benefit ("20 questions now keeps Pharmacology fresh"). Today's plan: when opened from a reminder, ask for a one-tap "I'm starting" commitment, then show progress through the plan. Progress & streaks: celebrate completion with a clear positive end screen

Key points.title: Same-format reminders fall into banner blindness
Key points.detail: "We tune out things we get repeatedly exposed to." Notifications always share the same format, so when attention is already captured, they get ignored. Design for novelty when you want a new behavior.

Key points.title: More friction can make users turn reminders off
Key points.detail: The redesign first made the reminder harder to dismiss with added friction, then rejected it: "more friction isn't better because people will probably just turn it off." Friction is good only when it is positive, and you need to understand how users think to balance it.

Key points.title: State the benefit of the habit
Key points.detail: The improved reminder recalls why a wind-down period matters: "Just like a Tesla, your body needs to be pre-conditioned for optimal 'charging.'" A reminder that explains its benefit gives a reason to act, not just a nudge.

Key points.title: A tiny action creates commitment
Key points.detail: A simple swipe confirms the user is starting the wind-down. This is the Spark Effect: "We are more likely to take action when the effort is small." After committing, the user sees progress toward optimal sleep.

Key points.title: Use only real losses, then reward completion
Key points.detail: If the user opens one more reel, they see a reminder that they'll lose their "relaxed" state (loss aversion). It "needs to be a real loss" or people will reject and ignore it (reactance). When the wind-down ends, the user gets positive reinforcement.

Title: Strava: When good UX intentions fail without psychology
Creator: Growth.Design
Bottom line: A free gift that looks like a paywall gets read as an upsell; give it a clear title, a CTA that matches the offer and no decline option.
What they did: Returning to Strava after months away, the author sees a screen offering a free 30-day subscription preview but assumes it is an upsell. Growth.Design lists the cues that caused this: an "Upgrade" label, a 25% Off banner in the background, the word "Subscription", and a classic paywall layout with clever copy, a feature list and a decline option. It proposes a redesign with a clear title and a CTA aligned with the offer.
Takeaways: Users judge screens by pattern, not by reading; Context around a prompt changes its meaning; Words like Subscription and Upgrade signal payment; Be clear, not clever, with gifts
Ideas for OnCourse: Renewal: when giving a lapsed aspirant free premium days, use a gift layout ("7 days of Premium, on us") with one "Start" button and no plan list, price or "No thanks". Notifications: make sure win-back screens don't share the paywall's header, banners or layout

Key points.title: Users judge screens by pattern, not by reading
Key points.detail: Strava was giving a free 30-day subscription, yet the author's brain read it as "It's been a while, but—let's upsell you anyway." This is System 1 thinking: "We make rapid judgment calls based on previous patterns and experiences." The overall paywall look (clever copy, feature list, decline option) screamed upsell.

Key points.title: Context around a prompt changes its meaning
Key points.detail: An "Upgrade" label at the top and a 25% Off banner in the background framed the gift as a sale. "Always design something with consideration for its larger context. A chair in a room, a room in a house... A prompt in an app."

Key points.title: Words like Subscription and Upgrade signal payment
Key points.detail: The copy "Subscription" sounded like something to pay for, even though the screen said preview. For OnCourse, gift and trial screens should avoid paywall vocabulary.

Key points.title: Be clear, not clever, with gifts
Key points.detail: The redesign uses a clear title and "A CTA aligned with the offer and without 'decline' options." "It's always better to be clear than clever." A gift should look and read like a gift.

Chapters.summary: The Upgrade label and 25% Off banner behind the gift.

Title: Why Granola's Lack of Onboarding Backfires When You Test It
Creator: Built for Mars (Peter Ramsey)
Bottom line: A new user's first session is usually a test, so design a one-time test mode that makes that test feel great, rather than fighting it.
What they did: Peter Ramsey tried Granola, an AI note-taking app, on iOS. He argues that a new user's first recording is "probably isn't a real meeting, it's a test", and Granola has no onboarding for that moment. The iOS app hides the live transcript (the desktop app shows it), so a tester can't tell if it is working. He proposes leaning into the test behaviour with a one-time "try me" mode, like Whereby's QR code to join your own meeting from your phone.
Takeaways: Cater to instinctive behaviour instead of fighting it; New users want reassurance, not the everyday experience; A one-time test mode is worth building; The first session decides how the product feels
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: let a new user try 3 sample MCQs before sign-up, with instant answers and explanations, so their natural 'let me test this' moment is a good one. Practice: in a user's first set only, show the explanation and the topic tag right after each answer, then switch to the normal layout from the second session. Design process: when a feature only shows once (first-session screens), judge it by its effect on first-week retention, not by how often it is seen.

Key points.title: Cater to instinctive behaviour instead of fighting it
Key points.detail: Ramsey's rule of thumb is that "it's more effective to cater to people's instinctive behaviour, rather than to try and outright change it." In Google Earth, people first search for their own house. The product could steer them to a landmark, or just make finding your old bedroom easier. For OnCourse, find what a new aspirant does first (for example, trying a hard question from a subject they fear) and make that path smooth.

Key points.title: Whereby lets new users test both sides first
Key points.detail: Whereby knows that after creating a meeting, new users want to test it. So it shows a QR code that lets you join the meeting from your phone. You see the experience from both sides before you invite anyone. The test is built into the flow, not left to chance.

Key points.title: New users want reassurance, not the everyday experience
Key points.detail: Granola's desktop app shows a live transcript, but the iOS app leaves it out. That is a fair trade-off for daily use, because a live transcript in the middle of a table would be distracting. But a new user is "seeking reassurance". So the first-use experience can differ from the everyday one.

Key points.title: A one-time 'try me' mode bridges the gap
Key points.detail: Ramsey compares this to toy pull tabs, like on an Elmo toy. They hold the toy in a "try me" mode so children can hear it without going through every function. An app can show a lite version just to satisfy the first-use behaviour. The quiz in the case study gives the reason: it "lowers the cost of getting things wrong".

Key points.title: The first session shapes how the whole product feels
Key points.detail: Teams find it hard to fund a feature only seen once. But "the first session in an app is disproportionately influential" in how it feels, especially with many competitors. Granola also grows by word of mouth, since meetings have several people. Someone "fumbling around awkwardly, making noises into the microphone" and getting a meaningless summary hurts that growth.

Title: Twitch Celebrates the Wrong Thing (and Misses the Aha Moment)
Creator: Built for Mars (Peter Ramsey)
Bottom line: An aha moment is not praise; it is the moment a user sees what they could get next, so show a route to the next level instead of celebrating a small number.
What they did: Peter Ramsey streamed on Twitch himself (and, in the UX Planet write-up, paid a bot farm to boost his streams). After his first stream, Twitch showed a badge-like card: "Good job! Your last stream hit a record 7 unique viewers." He argues this is a celebration, not an aha moment, because it does not change what the user expects to get in the future. He also shows how unlabelled controls and costly mistakes stop new users from exploring features.
Results: No test results. Observed: after a 1h 4m first stream, Twitch said "Your last stream hit a record 7 unique viewers". The analytics compared the debut to a previous stream that did not exist ("+0s from last stream", "+0 from last stream"). The Quick Actions grid has "eleven controls"; each chat message has "five moderation icons" that are unlabelled, and he deleted his own messages by mistake.
Takeaways: An aha moment changes what users expect next; Celebrating a small number is a vanity metric; Users muddle and stop at the first workaround; Lower the cost of failure to get people exploring; Explain locked features in the moment
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: after a user's first set, replace generic praise with a forward-looking line like 'You got 6/10 in Anatomy. Users who practise 20 Anatomy MCQs a day reach 75% in 3 weeks,' with a button to start that plan. Progress & streaks: never compare a new user to a previous session that does not exist; show a first-time state instead of '+0 from last time'. Practice: let users try features like bookmarking or 'mark for review' in a safe sample question so a mistake costs nothing.

Key points.title: An aha moment changes what users expect next
Key points.detail: Ramsey defines the aha moment as "suddenly rewriting the future expected value of a product", the moment someone thinks "if I do this, I will get that". Badges and praise are celebrations, not aha moments. A badge only raises expected value "if the user believes that it will happen again". OnCourse's post-practice screen should show what the user can reach next, not only a score.

Key points.title: Celebrating a small number misses the point
Key points.detail: After his first stream Twitch said: "Good job! Your last stream hit a record 7 unique viewers." Most first streams are poor, so this gives no evidence that 70 or 100 viewers is possible. The real aha would be "that was a start, but here's how we can help you get to 100 viewers". Twitch "celebrates the wrong thing, and so the future expected value doesn't change."

Key points.title: Comparing a first session to nothing wastes the ending
Key points.detail: In the UX Planet write-up, the analytics after the debut read "+0s from last stream" and "+0 from last stream". Every card compares the first stream to one that does not exist. Under the Peak-End Rule, the last moment shapes how the whole experience is remembered. A first-time summary needs its own design.

Key points.title: Users muddle and stop at the first workaround
Key points.detail: Citing Steve Krug, Ramsey says people "muddle through" products: they find a way that works and stop looking. Workarounds "feel the same as mastery", so better features stay unused. Twitch assumes users will learn advanced features by trial and error. "They won't, especially if they find a workaround first."

Key points.title: Lower the cost of failure to get exploration
Key points.detail: Ramsey deleted his own messages in his first livestream because the moderation icons are tiny and unlabelled. One deletes a message and another blocks a person for 10 minutes. When a mistake can't be undone, people stop exploring. He suggests a sandbox that simulates a busy stream, or empty states that explain a feature (like a raid) in the moment, instead of just saying you can't use it.

Title: Why Confetti Celebrations Backfire (and How to Make Them Work)
Creator: Built for Mars (Peter Ramsey)
Bottom line: Celebrate the user's real milestone at the moment the goal is actually reached, not the company's milestone, and add useful next-step value rather than just confetti.
What they did: A short summary of Built for Mars' Chase Bank teardown. Ramsey looks at celebrations that fire on account creation or sign-up, when the user has not yet got what they came for. He explains why early celebrations feel cheap and gives four rules for celebrations that work, especially in "serious" products.
Takeaways: Celebrate the user's milestone, not yours; Celebrating too early breaks expectations; Close the loop on what you promise; Add useful context instead of balloons; Tone matters more for serious products
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: drop any celebration on account creation; save it for the first finished practice set. Today's plan: when the plan is complete, pair a small celebration with real value, such as accuracy by subject and what tomorrow's plan covers. Progress & streaks: keep celebration tone calm and exam-focused for medical students, using micro-celebrations on top of real progress rather than full-screen confetti.

Key points.title: Celebrate the user's milestone, not the company's
Key points.detail: "Celebrations only work when they align with what the user wanted to do." If you buy a printer, you want to print, but you are forced to make an account and then get a little celebration. That celebrates the company's milestone, not yours. For OnCourse, signing up is not the user's goal; answering questions and improving is.

Key points.title: Celebrating too early breaks the user's expectations
Key points.detail: People crave completion, and a clear outcome gives a sense of closure. That is the point where a celebration amplifies the feeling. If you celebrate too early, users think the flow is finished when it is not. "The result? Frustration, not delight."

Key points.title: Celebrate first use, not sign-up
Key points.detail: Ramsey's first rule: "Don't celebrate account creation; celebrate the moment the account is usable. Don't celebrate sign-up; celebrate first use." His second rule: close the loop. If you promise motivation such as "unlock everything", follow through with something meaningful.

Key points.title: Add useful context instead of balloons
Key points.detail: Instead of balloons, Chase could have reassured users that their card was on the way, or prompted them to deposit funds. "Confetti works best when layered on top of real progress — not as a substitute for it." OnCourse's completion screens can carry the useful next step.

Key points.title: Tone matters more in serious products
Key points.detail: "Nobody wants their bank to behave like Duolingo." In banking, healthcare and B2B, a misplaced celebration "risks looking childish or out of touch". Serious products should still celebrate, but only when it adds real value. Medical exam prep sits closer to the serious end, so OnCourse should keep celebrations meaningful and restrained.

Title: The 3 boring secrets to writing great UX copy (that converts)
Creator: Built for Mars (Peter Ramsey)
Bottom line: Good UX copy is predictable, specific and short: use one title pattern across steps, write buttons that say what happens next, and cut until it stops making sense.
What they did: A short summary of Built for Mars' UX copy cheatsheet. Ramsey shows a multi-step onboarding flow with mixed title styles and a checkout with generic vs specific buttons. He lists what users care about in copy and what they ignore.
Takeaways: Use a predictable title pattern across steps; Make CTA labels say what happens next; Users care about the next action, benefit and impact; Cut copy, then cut again
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: give every step the same title pattern (for example 'Choose your exam', 'Choose your exam date', 'Choose your daily goal') so users can scan. Paywall: replace 'Continue' with a specific label such as 'Start 7-day free trial' or 'Pay ₹X for 12 months'. Notifications: cut 'We're excited to announce' style openers and lead with the action and benefit.

Key points.title: Use one predictable title pattern across steps
Key points.detail: In a multi-step onboarding flow with mixed title styles, users must read each title carefully because there is no pattern. A standard format like "Enter your ____" makes scanning effortless and removes cognitive load. Design systems keep fonts and spacing consistent but often forget title structure. "When in doubt, go for clarity over creativity."

Key points.title: Make buttons say exactly what happens next
Key points.detail: Generic buttons like "Continue" or "Submit" leave users unsure. In a checkout example, the most specific button label is "the safest bet" because it confirms what you are doing and removes second-guessing. On OnCourse's paywall, the button should name the plan or trial being started.

Key points.title: Users care about action, benefit and impact
Key points.detail: Users care about what action they can take next, what benefit they get, and how it affects their experience. They don't care about "Overly enthusiastic company messaging" like "we're so excited", generic claims about a "new" feature ("new doesn't mean good"), or unnecessary explanations.

Key points.title: Write, then cut as much as you can
Key points.detail: Too much text and users tune out; too little and they get confused. Ramsey's trick: write the copy, cut as much as you can, and if it still makes sense, keep trimming. "The best copy goes unnoticed because it feels natural."

Chapters.summary: Use a consistent title format across multi-step flows.

Title: The 10 Best Moments of UX (2024)
Creator: Built for Mars (Peter Ramsey)
Bottom line: Ten small, copyable UX moments from Built for Mars' 2024 UX Bites, several of which map directly to trial reminders, value framing, cancellation and gamified focus in a learning app.
What they did: Ramsey picked the most popular UX Bite from each of 10 categories in 2024, from Built for Mars' library of short real-world examples (posted daily and emailed to "38,000 product teams"). Each is one screen or interaction, with a one-line explanation of why it works.
Takeaways: Let users feel the value during onboarding; Offer a trial-end reminder at sign-up; Show subscribers when they've saved more than they pay; Turn focus time into visible progress; Remind cancelling users what they'd lose; Make the final CTA specific
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: add a 'Remind me before my trial ends' toggle on the trial screen, like Rise, to reduce the fear of being charged. Renewal: show a moment like 'You've solved 2,140 MCQs and 38 mock tests this year with Pro' before renewal, framing value against the price, as Uber One does. Renewal: on the cancel screen, list the features the user actually used (for example saved flashcards and mock test history) that they would lose, as Canva does.

Key points.title: Let users feel the value during onboarding
Key points.detail: Arc's onboarding (Best Onboarding Idea) asks you to toggle adverts on a web page on and off. You see the difference and the value Arc adds for yourself. It shows rather than tells. OnCourse could let users feel its value in onboarding, for example by showing one question with and without a high-yield explanation.

Key points.title: A trial-end reminder toggle at sign-up
Key points.detail: Rise (Best Conversion Trick) lets users opt in during sign-up to be reminded before the trial ends, "reassuring them that they won't forget." This removes a common reason not to start a trial. It fits directly on OnCourse's trial paywall.

Key points.title: Frame the subscription's value against its price
Key points.detail: Uber (Best use of Framing) celebrates when you've saved more money through Uber One than the monthly cost of the subscription. It makes the value concrete just before people think about whether to keep paying. OnCourse can frame Pro value in exam terms ahead of renewal.

Key points.title: Turn focus time into visible progress
Key points.detail: Focus Traveller (Gamification) has a hero who hikes a trail: the longer you focus, the further they walk. When paused, they rest by a bonfire, and longer focus unlocks "gear". It's a calm, non-competitive way to show effort, which suits long study sessions.

Key points.title: Use loss aversion on the cancellation screen
Key points.detail: Canva (Avoiding Churn) frames how good your current deal is when you try to cancel. It also lists the features your team uses but would lose. The list is personal, not a generic feature list.

Key points.title: Specific, live details make CTAs stronger
Key points.detail: Etsy's final checkout CTA shows where you are sending the item. Too Good To Go shows exactly when a surprise bag sold out, which motivates users to come earlier. Air New Zealand lets you hold a fare price for a small fee, a lower-commitment way to go ahead.

Title: 12 simple UX changes Audible should make to sell more stuff
Creator: Built for Mars (Peter Ramsey)
Bottom line: Small fixes add up: keep recommendations fresh, mark things done automatically, state time in days not dates, and make badges clear with visible progress.
What they did: A summary of Built for Mars' Audible case study (which is 93 slides long). Ramsey lists 12 changes to nudge repeat purchases, from refreshing "for you" carousels to auto-finishing books with only credits left. Several are about making progress and badges clear.
Takeaways: Keep recommendation carousels fresh; Mark items finished automatically; Show time as 'days until', not a date; Make price per unit obvious; Badges must say how to unlock them; Show progress towards each badge
Ideas for OnCourse: Progress & streaks: replace any vague badge with a clear rule ('Solve 500 Pharmacology MCQs') and a progress bar showing how close the user is. Renewal: show '7 days until your plan renews' instead of a date. Lessons: mark a lesson complete automatically when only the summary or closing seconds are left, so the library doesn't fill with 'almost done' items.

Key points.title: Keep recommendations fresh on every visit
Key points.detail: Audible's "for you" carousels and featured book stay the same. Ramsey wants them to refresh and reorder, to fetch more results at the end of a carousel "like Amazon do", and to show new featured books on refresh. "I'm sick of looking at the same one all day." OnCourse's Home suggestions should change as the user progresses.

Key points.title: Mark items finished automatically
Key points.detail: When a listener reaches the final chapter (acknowledgments), Audible should mark the book "finished". His library is "full of books with seconds or minutes left." Lessons and videos in OnCourse can do the same to avoid fake 'in progress' items.

Key points.title: Say 'in 7 days', not a date
Key points.detail: Show "days until your next credit" in days, not as a date. "'7 days until your next credit' is more useful than printing a date." The same rule applies to trial ends, renewals and exam countdowns.

Key points.title: Make the real price obvious
Key points.detail: Audible says "3 credits for £28.99" and makes users work out the price per credit. Ramsey wants the price per credit shown, and the cheapest purchase option marked when a deal beats credits. OnCourse's paywall should show the per-month or per-day price clearly.

Key points.title: Badges need clear rules and visible progress
Key points.detail: Audible's "riddle" badges "are nonsense, just tell me what I need to do to unlock them." Then let users track progress with a bar: "I've got no idea how close I am." He also says the listening-time bar charts are broken. Clear goals with progress are what make badges motivating.

Title: How Khan Academy Is Building a Better AI Tutor: Our Most Recent Learnings
Creator: Khan Academy Blog
Bottom line: An AI tutor teaches better when it knows the student's recent answers and weak prerequisites, and every change should be judged on whether the student gets the next question right alone.
What they did: Over six months (October 2025 to April 2026) Khan Academy ran about 20 A/B tests on Khanmigo across more than 15 million tutoring threads. They tracked three core metrics: response latency, next-item correctness (does the student answer the next problem on the same skill correctly without help) and cognitive engagement quality. They shipped a change only if its "chance to win" was above 0.95 with no harm to guardrails such as giving the answer away or math errors.
Results: Giving Khanmigo a summary of the student's recent problem history "improved next-item correctness by +3.4% across 608,000 tutoring threads." Surfacing unmastered prerequisite skills with a brief review "improved next-item correctness by 2.7% across 1.36 million tutoring threads," for "a 6.1 percent improvement in next-item correctness" in total. Asking the math agent for more concise output "reduced mean response time by three seconds across 352,000 tutoring threads"; limiting it to the student's own work cut latency by another 400 ms and "reduced giving away the answer by 50%." Passing 24 hours of conversation as plain text instead of JSON gave "a 5.09% increase in cognitive engagement." Adding example problems to the prompt "showed no effect."
Takeaways: Measure the next question answered alone, not help used; Feed the tutor the student's recent history; Offer a prerequisite review before the hard question; Speed is part of the teaching; Raw data does not help until it is readable; Ship only what wins, and publish what failed
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: after a wrong answer, track whether the student gets the next MCQ on the same topic right without help, and use that as the main success metric for explanations and any AI help. Practice: when a student misses a hard question, offer a short review of the underlying basic concept (for example, a related flashcard set) before the next hard one. Design process: set guardrail metrics (time to load an explanation, answer give-aways) for every Practice experiment, not just one goal metric

Key points.title: Measure the next question answered alone, not help used
Key points.detail: Khan's main learning metric is next-item correctness: did the student answer the very next problem on the same skill, in the same session, without help from Khanmigo. They call it "a direct measure of independent learning transfer, not just of performance with AI assistance." It is paired with latency and a passive/active/constructive engagement rating. For OnCourse, this is a cleaner success metric for explanations than time spent or taps on 'explain'.

Key points.title: Feed the tutor the student's recent history
Key points.detail: Before the tests, Khanmigo saw the current problem but not how the student had been doing. Adding a summary of how many problems they attempted recently and which they got right or wrong lifted next-item correctness by 3.4% across 608,000 threads, with a 97.5% chance of being better. All guardrails held. Context about the learner beat clever prompting.

Key points.title: Offer a prerequisite review before the hard question
Key points.detail: Surfacing prerequisite skills the student has not mastered, and offering a brief review before the harder problem, improved next-item correctness by 2.7% across 1.36 million threads. Together with the history summary that makes 6.1%. For OnCourse, a wrong answer on a high-yield clinical MCQ could link back to the basic concept it depends on.

Key points.title: Speed is part of the teaching
Key points.detail: Khan treats wait time as a learning issue: "Faster responses keep students focused." A faster model saved 0.3 seconds over 1.35 million threads, concise outputs saved 3 seconds, and a pre-check that skips unneeded math verification saved about 0.3 seconds, all with math accuracy steady. Focusing the math agent only on the student's own work also cut answer give-aways by 50%.

Key points.title: Raw data does not help until it is readable
Key points.detail: Passing the full in-session conversation log as JSON did not help at first. When they switched to plain text and included all threads on that skill from the previous 24 hours, cognitive engagement rose 5.09%. Adding example problems to the prompt showed no effect, and better follow-up links did not move correctness but shipped because they did no harm and were slightly faster.

Key points.title: Ship only what wins, and publish what failed
Key points.detail: Each test ran against the current product, and a change shipped only if the platform's "chance to win" was above 0.95 with no guardrail harm. The post reports neutral results alongside wins. "No single improvement on its own produced a dramatic leap forward," but small wins added up across millions of daily sessions.

Title: Four Things to Look for in Edtech, and How Khan Academy Measures Up
Creator: Khan Academy Blog
Bottom line: Learning gains come from a steady weekly dose of practice, so the product's job is to set a concrete weekly target and protect the time to hit it.
What they did: Khan Academy summarises four independent randomized trials of its math product and a 2026 PNAS study of more than 200,000 students. From these it sets a concrete practice target: about two skills to Proficient or Mastered each week, roughly 60 a year. It also explains a product change from classroom testing: Khanmigo used to never give the answer, and now it can become more direct after an incorrect attempt.
Results: "Three RCTs found gains": 0.06 SD over two years in Hamilton County, 0.12 SD in Arlington ISD grades 3 to 6, and 0.09 to 0.11 SD in El Salvador; "In grades 7 and 8, where practice averaged about 4 minutes a week, there was no effect." The PNAS study found "about 0.0031 SD per Khan Academy skill brought to Proficient, or roughly 0.18 SD for 60 skills." In Uttar Pradesh, schools with facilitators practiced "about 47 minutes a week and scored 0.44 to 0.47 SD higher in math after seven months." With implementation support, "more than 20% of learners reach our recommended goals, compared with about 10% overall." Benchmark: the median education RCT effect is 0.10 SD.
Takeaways: Too little practice has no effect at all; Give a concrete weekly practice target; Protected time and support drive results; A never-give-the-answer rule was too rigid; Be explicit about what the product can't do
Ideas for OnCourse: Today's plan: express the plan as a weekly target in concrete units (for example, topics brought to a set accuracy) and show progress toward it, not only a daily streak. Home: warn gently when weekly practice drops toward a very low level, since a few minutes a week showed no effect. Practice: let explanations get more direct after a wrong attempt rather than always holding back the answer

Key points.title: Too little practice has no effect at all
Key points.detail: In the Arlington ISD trial, grades 3 to 6 gained 0.12 SD. But in grades 7 and 8, where practice averaged about 4 minutes a week, there was no effect. Access to the product is not the same as learning. For OnCourse, a user who opens the app but practices a few minutes a week is not really being served.

Key points.title: Give a concrete weekly practice target
Key points.detail: Khan recommends about two skills reaching Proficient or Mastered each week, roughly 60 skills a year. A 2026 PNAS study of more than 200,000 students found about 0.0031 SD per skill brought to Proficient, or about 0.18 SD for 60 skills. A target in countable units turns 'study more' into something a learner can track.

Key points.title: Protected time and support drive results
Key points.detail: The three trials with gains shared "strong implementation," with protected practice time and support. In Uttar Pradesh, 24 of 74 schools got facilitators who visited twice a week; those students practiced about 47 minutes a week and scored 0.44 to 0.47 SD higher after seven months. With support, more than 20% of learners reach the goals, versus about 10% overall.

Key points.title: A never-give-the-answer rule was too rigid
Key points.detail: Khanmigo was first built never to give students the answer. Testing with about 5,100 students across five districts showed the rule was too rigid. Now it still asks students to try first, but after an incorrect attempt it can become more direct and explain what went wrong.

Key points.title: Be explicit about what the product can't do
Key points.detail: The post says making the product available is not enough, and that AI can be wrong, misleading or inappropriate. Khan links to its own write-ups of past math accuracy problems. Honest limits build trust with people choosing a study tool.

Title: Hand-crafted, machine-made: How we make learning games with AI
Creator: Brilliant (Brilliant Staff)
Bottom line: Brilliant skipped AI chatbot tutors and instead uses AI to build many interactive problem variants fast, while human designers own the learning goal, the difficulty curve and the final review.
What they did: Brilliant decided against an AI tutoring chatbot after internal testing, because text explanations are not how they want people to learn. Instead they built prompt chains and LLM-friendly game APIs so designers can describe a problem and get a playable puzzle and solution in seconds, plus a second tool that makes practice variants with the same learning objective. Every generated problem gets multiple rounds of human review.
Results: A pre-algebra course has "50+ core concepts" and needs "20+ problems per concept," so "a course like this requires 1,000+ individual problems." For gear train puzzles, "we went from a 0% to 93% success rate in generating creative and correct puzzles" in 48 hours by making game representations more LLM-friendly, not by changing models. Asset setup "that took hours per lesson now happens in minutes."
Takeaways: Learn by doing, not by reading explanations; Each concept needs 20+ problems on a difficulty ramp; Make your content format easy for AI to read; Humans own the aha moment, AI owns the busywork; One wrong question can damage trust
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: plan each high-yield topic as a ramp of 20+ MCQs from easy to edge cases, not a flat list. Design process: store questions in a clean structured format so AI can draft variants, with a doctor reviewing every one before it ships. Lessons: prefer a question or interactive step over another paragraph of explanation

Key points.title: Learn by doing, not by reading explanations
Key points.detail: Brilliant compares learning to Super Mario: you don't get a text box saying you jumped too early, you fall into the pit and try again. After ChatGPT launched they chose not to build a tutoring chatbot, because "Text explanations, no matter how perfect, just aren't our goal." They want learners to build intuition through interaction.

Key points.title: Each concept needs 20+ problems on a difficulty ramp
Key points.detail: You can't explain a concept once and move on. Learners need variations, a difficulty ramp and edge cases that test understanding, which means 20+ problems per concept. A pre-algebra course with 50+ concepts therefore needs 1,000+ problems. This is the real cost of good practice content.

Key points.title: Make your content format easy for AI to read
Key points.detail: Early GPT-3.5 outputs were "janky" and often unsolvable. For gear train puzzles, success went from 0% to 93% in 48 hours, and "The breakthrough didn't come from upgrading to r1 or o3; it came from making the representations in our game engine more LLM-friendly." The structure of your content matters more than the model.

Key points.title: Humans own the aha moment, AI owns the busywork
Key points.detail: Course authors stay responsible for the learning objective, the progression and the aha moment. AI handles technical setup, which took hours per lesson and now takes minutes. A second tool generates more practice sets like a level the team already likes, so learners can master an idea before moving on.

Key points.title: One wrong question can damage trust
Key points.detail: Every generated problem goes through multiple rounds of human review for design and correctness. "A single wrong problem can shake a learner's confidence or reinforce misconceptions." For a medical exam app, this bar is even more important.

Title: Spaced Repetition for All: Cognitive Science Meets Big Data in a Procrastinating World
Creator: Quizlet Engineering (Shane Mooney)
Bottom line: Most students cram, so Quizlet stopped scheduling cards by calendar and instead always shows the cards a student is most likely to get wrong right now, which works for one night or many weeks.
What they did: Quizlet found classic spaced repetition did not fit how students actually study, since most study a set over only a few days. They built a model from about 1.5 million answers that predicts recall probability from four features: answer history, time since the last answer, time between previous answers and study direction. The new Learn always asks about the terms with the lowest predicted recall.
Results: After getting a term right on the first try, "there's only about an 87% chance they'll get it right" the next time, and if it took a few tries, "below 70%." "95% study a set over four days at most," too few for classic spaced repetition. The logistic regression model had an "AUROC was 0.815." (Note added later by Quizlet: Long-Term Learning was replaced by Memory Score and Scheduled Review.)
Takeaways: Design for the cramming students actually do; One correct answer does not mean learned; Order by what the student is closest to forgetting; Recent answers matter more than old ones; Test both directions of a fact; A simple model can run offline
Ideas for OnCourse: Flashcards: order each session by predicted weakest cards (recent wrong answers, longest gap) rather than a fixed due-date queue, so a pre-exam cram still targets weak spots. Flashcards: show a card again later in the session even after one correct answer if it took several tries. Practice: for drug and disease pairs, test both directions (drug to indication and indication to drug)

Key points.title: Design for the cramming students actually do
Key points.detail: Quizlet's earlier Long-Term Learning used a standard schedule (1 day, 3, 7, 16, reset on a miss). It works without a deadline, but 95% of users study a set over four days at most. "Cramming is a reality for many students," so the algorithm had to work for any time scale. OnCourse users near NEET-PG are in the same spot.

Key points.title: One correct answer does not mean learned
Key points.detail: The old Learn repeated wrong questions until each was correct once, then stopped. But after one correct first try, the chance of getting it right next time was only about 87%, and below 70% if it took a few tries. Students who restarted spent time on terms they already knew.

Key points.title: Order by what the student is closest to forgetting
Key points.detail: Classic spaced repetition waits until recall is about 80%, but Quizlet did not want students walking into a test at 81%. So it prioritises the terms with the lowest predicted chance of a correct answer. Every question is then on one of the few terms that need the most work, whatever the deadline.

Key points.title: Recent answers matter more than old ones
Key points.detail: The strongest predictor of the next answer is whether the most recent one was correct, but older answers count too, with less weight. "Two wrong answers followed by a correct answer is very different from a correct answer followed by two wrong answers." Time since last seen (forgetting curve) and gaps between reviews (spacing effect) are also features.

Key points.title: Test both directions of a fact
Key points.detail: Knowing the English meaning of a Spanish word does not mean you can produce the Spanish word. Quizlet treats each direction as a separate but related fact and asks the side the student has gotten right less often. The same applies to medical facts learned only one way round.

Key points.title: A simple model can run offline
Key points.detail: They chose logistic regression over fancier models because it is easy to interpret and portable. It becomes a simple equation in a JavaScript module that runs on web, iOS and Android offline, for students with poor networks. This matters for OnCourse users on patchy hostel or hospital Wi-Fi.

Title: Selecting Question Formats to Maximize the Testing Effect
Creator: Quizlet Engineering (Shane Mooney)
Bottom line: Start unfamiliar material with multiple choice and move to recall as the learner improves, and drop formats like true/false and 'none of the above' that are easy to guess and make people quit.
What they did: Quizlet's Learn used five question formats: typed response, self-graded flashcards, true/false, multiple choice, and multiple choice with 'none of the above'. They compared them on guessability, difficulty, learning benefit, time and fun, and ran a test where each recognition format was used alone versus a random mix, measuring how far students got before finishing or quitting. They removed true/false and 'none of the above', and set a fixed path from multiple choice to typed recall (with self-graded flashcards as fallback).
Results: Chance of guessing: multiple choice "1 in 4," with none of the above "1 in 5," true/false "1 in 2." "Even the hardest question format is answered correctly on the first try over 60% of the time." 'None of the above' helped later recall, but when used more, "students were more likely to stop studying early." True/false "lead to higher study abandonment rates." (Charts in the post give the exact per-format numbers.)
Takeaways: Recall beats recognition, but only if answered correctly; Guessable formats give weak learning and weak signal; Measure fun as how far people get before quitting; True/false and none-of-the-above cost more than they give; Optimise learning per minute, not per question
Ideas for OnCourse: Flashcards: for a new card, start with a recognition step and move to self-graded recall once the student gets it right, rather than one fixed format. Practice: avoid true/false and 'none of the above' style items in OnCourse-written practice sets unless they mirror the real exam format. Design process: when testing a new Practice format, measure the share of a set completed before quitting as the engagement metric

Key points.title: Recall beats recognition, but only if answered correctly
Key points.detail: The testing effect says active retrieval is better than re-reading, and harder questions help more, but only if they can still be answered. Correct recalls teach more than failed ones. So Quizlet starts with easier formats on new material and moves to harder ones as the student learns, a technique called guidance fading.

Key points.title: Guessable formats give weak learning and weak signal
Key points.detail: Multiple choice can be guessed 1 in 4, with none of the above 1 in 5, and true/false 1 in 2. A lucky guess skips the benefit of recall, and also hides which terms the student really knows. Process of elimination lets students pick the right option without knowing the answer.

Key points.title: Measure fun as how far people get before quitting
Key points.detail: To estimate enjoyment, Quizlet compared a random mix of recognition formats against variants that used only one format each. They measured how much of the set students answered before completing or abandoning. Formats that led to more of the set completed were read as more fun and motivating.

Key points.title: True/false and none-of-the-above cost more than they give
Key points.detail: 'None of the above' made questions harder and improved later recall, but took longer and led more students to stop early. True/false was fast but highly guessable, hard to give clear feedback on when the answer is false, and led to higher abandonment. Both were removed in favour of standard multiple choice.

Key points.title: Optimise learning per minute, not per question
Key points.detail: Students have limited time, so the goal is learning per minute. "It might be better to ask two fast questions than one slower but more effective question." Typed answers are the main recall format, but Learn falls back to self-graded flashcards when the answer is too long to type or is an image.

Title: Spaced Repetition Systems Have Gotten Way Better
Creator: Domenic Denicola
Bottom line: A modern scheduler (FSRS) that predicts each card's recall and lets you choose a target retention gives far lighter daily reviews than fixed interval ladders, and missing a card no longer sends you back to day 1.
What they did: The author explains how the old SuperMemo-2 rule (1 day, 6 days, then multiply by 2.5, reset on a miss) works and why it is arbitrary. He describes FSRS, which fits difficulty, stability and retrievability per card from your own review history and schedules each card for when recall drops to a chosen target. He compares simulations of 90% and 70% target retention on his own Japanese deck and criticises the fixed ladders used by WaniKani and Bunpro.
Results: With spaced repetition you can "learn 10 new second-language words a day (3,650 per year!) with only 20 minutes of daily review time." The SuperMemo-2 rule "was developed by a college student in 1987 based on his personal experiments." Simulating 365 days with 10 new cards a day, the 70% target retention FSRS suggested gave "dramatically fewer reviews per day, in less time, while ending with many more cards memorized" than the 90% default.
Takeaways: Old schedules are arbitrary and punish a single miss; Predict recall per card instead of using a fixed ladder; Let users trade retention for workload; Fixed ladders make review feel like daily failure; Algorithm quality beats a pretty UI
Ideas for OnCourse: Flashcards: when a user misses a mature card, shorten its interval rather than resetting it to tomorrow, so missed cards don't pile up. Flashcards: offer a simple 'review load' setting (lighter vs. stronger memory) and show the estimated daily minutes for each choice. Progress & streaks: report cards retained, not only cards due, so review feels like progress rather than debt

Key points.title: Old schedules are arbitrary and punish a single miss
Key points.detail: SuperMemo-2 shows a card after 1 day, then 6 days, then multiplies by an ease factor of 2.5. A miss resets the card to day 1, so cards "ping-pong" between long and short intervals. The rule came from one college student's experiments in 1987.

Key points.title: Predict recall per card instead of using a fixed ladder
Key points.detail: FSRS turns 'review just before you forget' into a prediction problem: when does recall probability drop to the target? It fits three things per card: difficulty (1 to 10), stability and retrievability, using 21 parameters tuned on your own review history. Anki has supported it since version 23.10, but it is not on by default.

Key points.title: Let users trade retention for workload
Key points.detail: FSRS lets you pick a desired retention, default 90%, and can simulate your workload for any value. For the author's Japanese deck, the suggested 70% gave far fewer reviews and less time per day, and more cards memorised after a year, because he never hit the 200-review cap that blocks new cards. A visible trade-off gives users control over burnout.

Key points.title: Fixed ladders make review feel like daily failure
Key points.detail: WaniKani and Bunpro use fixed intervals that never adapt to the user or card, and stop showing cards after the last step. A miss drops a card one or two steps. The author says this "transforms these sites into a daily ritual of feeling bad about what you've forgotten, instead of feeling good about what you've retained," and he quit Bunpro for Anki.

Key points.title: Algorithm quality beats a pretty UI
Key points.detail: The author admits Anki's UI is "created by developers instead of designers." Still, with FSRS "The review load is much lighter" and "The feeling of despair when missing a card is significantly minimized." For OnCourse Flashcards, the schedule itself is part of the experience design.

Title: Re-designing busuu. One year as a Product Designer
Creator: Caylee Farndon Taylor (busuu)
Bottom line: Cutting steps between opening the app and starting a lesson, and simplifying sign-up, moved Busuu's numbers more than any visual polish.
What they did: Busuu's first in-house designers redesigned web and mobile after five years of work by four agencies. They cut the palette and fonts, built a style guide, replaced photos with icons for activities, removed the activity menu screen so lesson parts start straight from the dashboard, added a friends leaderboard and cut form fields from sign-up.
Results: Removing the activity menu screen "saw an immediate 27% rise in learning unit completion rates." "Our recent redesign of the sign up flow resulted in a 70% increase in sign ups." The switch to a lighter, brighter blue (#3190d0 to #61bcf9) was "one of the most successful design changes that we did in the last year; increasing conversion." No test setup or time window is given for these numbers.
Takeaways: Remove the menu between Home and the lesson; Fewer sign-up fields brought many more sign-ups; A lighter palette lifted conversion; Icons travel across languages better than words; Don't reskin bad flows; Build a style guide from day one
Ideas for OnCourse: Home: let each Today's plan item start the MCQ set directly from its card, with no in-between selection screen. Onboarding: count the fields before the first question and cut every one that isn't needed to personalise the first session. Design process: fix flow and navigation problems before or with a visual refresh, not after

Key points.title: Remove the menu between Home and the lesson
Key points.detail: Busuu removed the activity menu screen that sat between the user and a learning unit. That "saw an immediate 27% rise in learning unit completion rates." They split units into smaller sections reachable straight from the dashboard, since some users prefer speaking and others writing. OnCourse should check every screen between Home and the first question.

Key points.title: Fewer sign-up fields brought many more sign-ups
Key points.detail: Under the principle "Less steps good, more steps bad," the team cut the forms users had to fill, mainly in sign-up. The sign-up redesign "resulted in a 70% increase in sign ups." The post gives no test details, so treat it as a strong signal rather than a clean A/B result.

Key points.title: A lighter palette lifted conversion
Key points.detail: Changing the main blue from #3190d0 to #61bcf9 was hard to justify internally, but was one of the year's most successful changes, "increasing conversion and massively improving busuu's appearance of being fun and accessible." Colour can change how approachable a study app feels.

Key points.title: Icons travel across languages better than words
Key points.detail: Busuu supports many interface languages with very different text lengths (English vs Russian). They replaced activity photos with consistent icons to support or replace text. This is useful for OnCourse if it adds Hindi or Hinglish labels.

Key points.title: Don't reskin bad flows
Key points.detail: "Don't ignore obvious navigation, user flow and UX issues in favour of a re-skin unless you are going to be able to complete that re-skin VERY quickly; otherwise you'll end up re-building bad designs with a new colour scheme." Break a big redesign into parts.

Key points.title: Build a style guide from day one
Key points.detail: The author's main regret was not pushing for a style guide from the start. Style guides let developers reuse code, keep the product consistent without hours of design QA, and make live design changes faster and safer.

Title: Unacademy Rewrites the Book
Creator: The Hard Copy (Unacademy design team)
Bottom line: Unacademy rebuilt its exam-prep app around what learners do (plan the day, study on their own, check progress) instead of around features, and a calendar planner that showed free time nudged more self-study.
What they did: After research showed users struggled to find content and educators, Unacademy built a new app from scratch between January and April 2021. They cut five tabs (Schedule, Syllabus, Tests, Updates, Profile) to three (Planner, Self study, Profile), removed the hamburger menu, turned the schedule list into a calendar that shows free time, set up content during onboarding, added Groups with leaderboards and built a new design system.
Results: No numbers. The app had "600,000+ paying subscribers, who typically spend 2-3 hours a day on it." The team says the calendar Planner "nudged them to increase their learning productivity by undertaking practice tests and other self-study activity in the open gaps during their day," and that with Groups learners became "more competitive and study more to collect points and climb the leaderboard." A reader comment notes Play Store complaints about finding older recordings after the change.
Takeaways: Organise the app by learner needs, not features; Three tabs: Planner, Self study, Profile; Show free time, not just scheduled time; Set up the library during onboarding; Groups and leaderboards raised effort; A rebuild is a reset for the design system
Ideas for OnCourse: Today's plan: show the day as a timeline that includes free gaps and suggests a short MCQ set or flashcard review to fill them. Onboarding: right after subscribing, ask the target exam and attempt year and set up the plan, with a skip for self-directed users. Navigation: check whether OnCourse tabs follow learner jobs (today, self-study, progress) rather than content types

Key points.title: Organise the app by learner needs, not features
Key points.detail: Unacademy's structure had grown complex and users struggled to discover content and educators. Instead of patching it, the team built a new information architecture "based on a user-based view, rather than a feature-based one." Needs fell into three buckets: daily tasks, self-study and tracking progress.

Key points.title: Three tabs: Planner, Self study, Profile
Key points.detail: Navigation went from Schedule, Syllabus, Tests, Updates and Profile to Planner, Self study and Profile. They also removed the hamburger menu, since users can't see what it holds. The personas ranged from learners who need hand-holding to independent learners; the app gives the first smart defaults and "gets out of the way" of the second.

Key points.title: Show free time, not just scheduled time
Key points.detail: The schedule moved from a list to a calendar that also shows the learner's free time. The team says this nudged learners to take practice tests and other self-study in the open gaps of their day, which drove more use of the Self study tab. A small layout change reframed how learners saw their day.

Key points.title: Set up the library during onboarding
Key points.detail: The team pictured a first day at college, when your schedule and directions are handed to you. Before, the user had to start content discovery alone. Now onboarding learns their goals right after they subscribe and sets up their content library, with an option to skip for self-motivated users.

Key points.title: Groups and leaderboards raised effort
Key points.detail: Groups let learners see other members' activity and progress. The VP of Design says learners became more competitive and studied more to collect points and climb the leaderboard. This was early reception, not a measured result.

Key points.title: A rebuild is a reset for the design system
Key points.detail: Starting fresh made it easier to set up a design system than to clean up the old one, reducing time-to-design and time-to-build. Post-launch fixes were mostly UI and labels, plus several rounds on the popular dark mode. Hardik Pandya's advice: no amount of prior data prepares you, so work closely with users throughout.

Title: Testing, testing — how we created an assessment tool for Babbel users
Creator: Babbel Design (Carina de Magalhães)
Bottom line: Babbel shipped a minimal, low-stakes level test, then fixed what eight user tests showed: a clear results screen and an easy way to review every answer at the end.
What they did: Babbel built a CEFR-based assessment as a low-stakes test, not an official certificate. The MVP tested only grammar and vocabulary, with an intro screen giving the duration and skills, a look distinct from lessons, and no instant right/wrong feedback. Eight unmoderated tests found a confusing results screen and a wish to check answers, so they added a list view of all answers and later a listening section.
Results: "~ 1900 users completing the Assessment in the first 2 weeks (organic)", "~ Average completion rate 80%", and "~90% of the users check their answers in the end of the test." Research was "eight unmoderated tests with non-Babbel users."
Takeaways: Learners want tests that do not feel like school; Set expectations before the test starts; Turn off instant feedback in test mode; Let people review all answers in one list; Ship the smallest version, then add
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: in mock test mode, hide per-question feedback, then end with a results screen that lists every question with the user's answer and the correct one in a single scrollable list. Practice: open each mock test with a short screen stating duration, number of questions and subjects covered. Progress & streaks: frame periodic tests as low-stakes check-ins on readiness, not grades

Key points.title: Learners want tests that do not feel like school
Key points.detail: User research kept showing that learners want to be tested and challenged, and that this motivates them. But Babbel's adult users are not in school, so the team was careful not to make them feel they were. They chose a low-stakes test that gives a CEFR level, not an official certificate.

Key points.title: Set expectations before the test starts
Key points.detail: The first prototype began with an onboarding screen for the test that stated its duration and which skills would be tested. The content design lead worked on the copy and content structure. The test also got a look different from regular lessons, still within Babbel's style.

Key points.title: Turn off instant feedback in test mode
Key points.detail: In lessons, users get immediate right/wrong feedback. In the assessment, the team changed this behaviour because it is a test. That makes the results screen carry all the feedback, so it has to be clear.

Key points.title: Let people review all answers in one list
Key points.detail: Eight unmoderated tests found the results screen confusing (grammar and vocabulary were hard to tell apart), the intro info felt irrelevant, and people wanted to see correct and incorrect answers. The team added a way to check answers in a list rather than one by one. After launch, about 90% of users checked their answers at the end.

Key points.title: Ship the smallest version, then add
Key points.detail: The MVP tested only grammar and vocabulary. Once data showed users wanted assessments (about 1,900 organic completions in two weeks, 80% completion), the team invested in listening questions. Next they planned placement tests and small recaps between lessons.

Title: Mobile Tutorials: Wasted Effort or Efficiency Boost?
Creator: Nielsen Norman Group (Alita Kendrick)
Bottom line: In a 70-person test, people who read a deck-of-cards tutorial were no more successful and no faster than people who skipped it, and they rated the app as harder to use.
What they did: NN/g ran a remote, unmoderated quantitative test with 70 iPhone users on 4 little-known apps that had swipe-through tutorials. Half the users always read the tutorial and half always skipped it. Each then did a task the tutorial had taught, such as "Set a target of 6500 steps" in Movesum. They measured task success, a 1–7 ease rating (SEQ) and task time.
Results: Task success was "91% for the those who read the tutorial (n=35) and 94% for those who skipped the tutorial (n=35)", not significant (p=0.443). Ease rating was 4.92 for tutorial readers vs. 5.49 for skippers, significant (p=0.047); "Half a point is a fairly substantial difference on a 1–7 rating scale." Mean task time was 93.49 seconds with the tutorial vs. 85.17 seconds without (p > 0.1), and that excludes the time spent reading the tutorial.
Takeaways: Tutorials did not raise task success; Tutorials made tasks feel harder; Tutorials did not make people faster; Spend the effort on the UI instead; Prefer contextual help to a manual
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: cut any swipe-through feature tour and drop new users straight into a short first MCQ set. Practice: teach controls like bookmark or report-question with a one-time tip the first time the user reaches them, not upfront. Design process: before adding an onboarding tour, test the flow without it and only add one if people fail

Key points.title: Tutorials did not raise task success
Key points.detail: Readers succeeded 91% of the time and skippers 94%, a gap that was not statistically significant (p=0.443). The tasks were simple, and one reader said "I didn't even have to watch the tutorial." A tour adds a step without making people more able to use the app.

Key points.title: Tutorials made tasks feel harder
Key points.detail: People who read the tutorial rated the task 4.92 out of 7 for ease, against 5.49 for people who skipped it (p=0.047). NN/g thinks a tutorial signals that the app is complicated, and they saw the same effect with coach marks and overlays. For OnCourse, a tour at install could make a simple practice flow seem heavy.

Key points.title: Tutorials did not make people faster
Key points.detail: Mean task time was 93.49 seconds for readers and 85.17 seconds for skippers, with no significant difference. That number leaves out the time spent reading the tutorial itself, so total effort was clearly higher for readers.

Key points.title: Spend the effort on the UI instead
Key points.detail: The conclusion is to "think twice about creating a tutorial for simple applications." Design and build time is better spent making the interface easy enough that no tutorial is needed. Many users skip tutorials anyway.

Key points.title: Prefer contextual help to a manual
Key points.detail: If some onboarding is needed, NN/g suggests interactive methods such as contextual help rather than "a polished manual". The study only covered 4 iOS apps, which the authors list as a limitation.

Title: Mobile-App Onboarding: An Analysis of Components and Techniques
Creator: Nielsen Norman Group (Alita Kendrick)
Bottom line: Skip onboarding when you can; keep only short content customization that the app truly needs, and teach by doing rather than by slides.
What they did: NN/g splits mobile onboarding into three parts: feature promotion, customization and instructions. It reviews real apps for each part and says which are worth keeping. It builds on their own tutorial study, which found tutorials "didn't improve task performance", and lists the few cases where onboarding helps.
Takeaways: Skip onboarding whenever possible; Onboarding earns its place in only three cases; Feature promotion belongs on the store page; Ask only content questions you can explain; Teach by doing, not by slides
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: keep only the questions that shape the plan (exam, exam date, daily time), say why each one is asked, show a progress bar and allow Skip. Onboarding: move theme or appearance choices out of onboarding and into Settings. Home: introduce features like stats only when they become useful, for example after 7 days of practice data

Key points.title: Skip onboarding whenever possible
Key points.detail: Onboarding adds interaction cost even when skipped, strains memory, and may not help: NN/g's own tutorial study found no performance gain. Their advice is to avoid app onboarding "whenever possible" and spend the resources making the UI more usable. Test the app with no onboarding first, and add a flow only if a prototype of it actually helps.

Key points.title: Onboarding earns its place in only three cases
Key points.detail: It helps when you need user information to start, when the app is "highly tailored to the user's context and preferences", or when a key feature is new and unfamiliar. An exam-prep app fits the second case: the exam and date really change the plan.

Key points.title: Feature promotion belongs on the store page
Key points.detail: Promo screens at first launch feel like marketing and are usually skipped, because people already chose to download the app. Show features in the App Store preview, or in context when they become useful. For example, a habit app could highlight its statistics after 7 days of data. Feature tours are fine for existing users when something is truly new, like Chase's short, skippable intro to its budgeting feature.

Key points.title: Ask only content questions you can explain
Key points.detail: Visual customization like picking a colour scheme (as Reflectly forced) does not belong in onboarding, because people can't judge it before using the app and usually stick with defaults. Content customization can belong there. Fitplan's short survey explained why it needed each answer, showed a progress indicator and offered Skip. If you can't explain why you need data at launch, ask later.

Key points.title: Teach by doing, not by slides
Key points.detail: Deck-of-cards tutorials make simple apps look complicated, and overlays like NOAA Weather's that highlight every control overwhelm people. Interactive walkthroughs, such as Temple Run 2's practice level or MindNode's guided first mind map, work when the interaction is truly new. They should be short and skippable. For OnCourse, a first practice question works as the tutorial.

Title: Progress Indicators Make a Slow System Less Insufferable
Creator: Nielsen Norman Group (Katie Sherwin)
Bottom line: Show feedback right away, use a spinner only for 2–10 second waits and a percent-done bar for longer ones; people with a moving indicator waited about 3 times longer.
What they did: The article explains why progress feedback matters and gives timing rules for each type of indicator. It cites a University of Nebraska-Lincoln study where one group saw an animated progress bar while a page loaded and a control group saw nothing. It also covers how to pace a percent-done bar and which indicators to avoid.
Results: People who saw the moving feedback bar "experienced higher satisfaction and were willing to wait on average 3 times longer than those who did not see any progress indicators" (Nah, 2004). Timing rules: immediate feedback on every tap, an indicator for anything over "about 1.0 second", looped animation for "2-10 seconds", percent-done for "10 seconds or more".
Takeaways: Moving feedback makes people wait 3 times longer; Give feedback on every tap immediately; Spinners only for 2–10 second waits; Use percent-done bars for long waits; Start slow and finish fast; Never use static or threatening messages
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: when an answer is submitted, change the option state instantly before the server replies, so no one taps twice. Today's plan: while a personalised plan or test is generated, show a percent-done bar or step count ("Building your plan, step 2 of 3"), not an endless spinner. Lessons: for video or PDF downloads, show a percent-done bar with a rough time estimate and a Cancel option

Key points.title: Moving feedback makes people wait 3 times longer
Key points.detail: In a University of Nebraska-Lincoln study, people who saw a looping progress bar while a page loaded were more satisfied and waited "on average 3 times longer" than people who saw nothing. Indicators reassure, give people something to look at, give a reason to wait and shrink perceived time.

Key points.title: Give feedback on every tap immediately
Key points.detail: The wait starts the moment the user taps. The button should look pressed or the screen should start to change right away. Without a visible change, "most users will assume the action was not registered and they will try again."

Key points.title: Spinners only for 2–10 second waits
Key points.detail: Under 1 second, a flashing spinner is distracting. Over 10 seconds, a spinner makes people unsure if the app is stuck, and they may abandon the task. Add text like "Loading comments…" to say why they are waiting, and remember network delays can turn 2 seconds into 15.

Key points.title: Use percent-done bars for long waits
Key points.detail: For waits of 10 seconds or more, show how much is done and how much is left, a rough estimate like "About 3 minutes remaining", or a step count such as "Updating address 3 of 50." Give a way to stop long processes. Lower the cutoff when your time estimates vary a lot.

Key points.title: Start slow and finish fast
Key points.detail: A bar that races ahead and then hangs at the end wipes out the benefit. Start slower and speed up near the end, so you beat expectations. NN/g notes that for surveys the opposite holds: indicators that start fast and end slow reduce drop-off. That matters for OnCourse's onboarding questions.

Key points.title: Never use static or threatening messages
Key points.detail: A static "Loading…" or "Please wait" can't show if the system is stuck. Warnings like "clicking again may create an extra order" threaten users and go unread. The fix is to show that the first tap was accepted.
