Title: Five Mistakes in Designing Mobile Push Notifications
Creator: Nielsen Norman Group (Alita Kendrick)
Bottom line: Ask for notification permission only after the user has felt value, say what you'll send, bundle bursts, stay relevant, and let people turn notifications off inside the app.
What they did: NN/g lists five common push-notification mistakes, with a do and a don't app example for each. It draws on what they saw in their own studies, where people often tap Don't Allow straight away, and on a Telefonica Research study of notification volume.
Results: "In 2016, the average mobile phone user received 56 notifications per day" (Pielot 2018). On first-launch permission prompts: "In many of our studies, the immediate response is to click Don't Allow." Rule of thumb: "If you have more than five notifications that you need to send at once, combine them into a single message."
Takeaways: Ask for permission after the first win; Say what the notifications will contain; Bundle notifications instead of sending bursts; Only send what concerns this user; Let users turn them off inside the app
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: remove the notification prompt from first launch and ask right after the first completed practice set, with a pre-prompt that names what you'll send (daily plan reminder, streak at risk, exam countdown). Notifications: combine same-day items like new test, plan reminder and streak into one message. Notifications: add an in-app settings page with a toggle for each notification type

Key points.title: Ask for permission after the first win
Key points.detail: New users don't yet know what the app is worth, and in NN/g's studies the usual response to a first-launch prompt is Don't Allow. FreePrints asked before users could even read the Getting Started page. The Conquest game asked only after the player's first level-up. Use reciprocity: give value first.

Key points.title: Say what the notifications will contain
Key points.detail: The default iOS text says what the company wants, not what the user gets. Night Sky explains its notifications (stargazing conditions, object rise times) before asking, while Tasty gives no reason. Being specific helps people decide and makes the app seem more trustworthy.

Key points.title: Bundle notifications instead of sending bursts
Key points.detail: Many notifications in a short time feel like someone ringing the doorbell over and over, and push people to turn them off or delete the app. Wunderlist sent one per due task. Instagram combines many likes into one message with two names and a count. Don't rely on iOS grouping to do this for you.

Key points.title: Only send what concerns this user
Key points.detail: Venmo notified people about friends' transactions that had nothing to do with them. Reddit sends trending posts only from subreddits the user follows. "They can turn them off in settings" is no excuse, because most users never change defaults.

Key points.title: Let users turn them off inside the app
Key points.detail: The Economic Times had a Notifications Hub and a Settings page, and neither let users change notifications. Elevate, a brain-training app, has a Push Notifications page in Settings with a toggle per type. Hiding the off switch is deceptive and gives people a reason to delete the app.

Title: Hamburger Menus and Hidden Navigation Hurt UX Metrics
Creator: Nielsen Norman Group (Kara Pernice, Raluca Budiu)
Bottom line: Navigation hidden behind a menu icon gets used less and later, and makes tasks slower and feel harder, so keep the main destinations visible when there are 4 or fewer.
What they did: NN/g and WhatUsersDo ran a quantitative study with 179 participants on 6 live websites, on phones and desktops. They compared hidden navigation (hamburger), visible navigation, and combo navigation (some visible, some hidden). They measured navigation use, time to first use, content discoverability, rated difficulty and task time. Fully visible navigation was not tested on phones.
Results: On mobile, people "used the hidden navigation in 57% of the cases, and the combo navigation in 86% of the cases — 1.5 times more." Content discoverability showed "a more than 20% drop" with hidden navigation. Difficulty ratings rose 21% vs. visible and 11% vs. combo. "On mobile people were 15% slower when the navigation was hidden (compared with the combo condition)"; on desktop at least 39% slower. Mobile users took about 2 seconds longer to first use hidden navigation.
Takeaways: Visible navigation gets used far more; Hidden navigation cuts discoverability by over 20%; Hiding navigation makes tasks slower and harder; Low salience, low scent and extra taps explain it; Show 4 or fewer items as visible links
Ideas for OnCourse: Navigation: keep Home, Practice, Lessons and Flashcards as a visible bottom tab bar and avoid tucking a main destination under a More or hamburger menu. Home: add direct links to features that live outside the tab bar, such as Streaks or Notifications, from cards on Home. Design process: when adding a fifth tab, test whether discoverability of the other tabs drops

Key points.title: Visible navigation gets used far more
Key points.detail: On phones, people used hidden navigation in 57% of tasks and combo navigation in 86%, 1.5 times more. On desktop the gap was larger: 27% for hidden vs. 48% visible and 50% combo. When options are on screen, people notice them and act on them.

Key points.title: Hidden navigation cuts discoverability by over 20%
Key points.detail: Content discoverability measured whether people found content through navigation when it wasn't linked from the homepage. It dropped by more than 20% with hidden navigation, on both mobile and desktop. Content that is only reachable through the menu suffers most.

Key points.title: Hiding navigation makes tasks slower and harder
Key points.detail: Rated difficulty rose 21% compared with visible navigation and 11% compared with combo. On mobile, tasks took 15% longer with hidden navigation than with combo, and people reached for the menu about 2 seconds later. A few seconds can start frustration and self-doubt.

Key points.title: Low salience, low scent and extra taps explain it
Key points.detail: A small icon is easy to miss, it doesn't say what is inside, and people must open it to find out. Patterns also vary across apps. NN/g expects only familiarity to improve over time; the other problems are built into hiding.

Key points.title: Show 4 or fewer items as visible links
Key points.detail: For phones, NN/g recommends visible links when there are 4 or fewer top-level items. With more, hide some, since a menu still beats the alternatives on mobile. Back up any hidden menu with in-page links to important content.

Title: The Peak–End Rule: How Impressions Become Memories
Creator: Nielsen Norman Group (Lexie Kane)
Bottom line: People judge an experience by its most intense moment and its ending, so design the high points and the last screen with care, and handle errors so they don't become the memory.
What they did: The article explains the peak–end rule using Kahneman and Fredrickson's 1993 cold-water study. It then applies it to UX: positive peaks (Duolingo's encouragement), negative peaks (a frustrating Maytag menu seen in an NN/g usability session), endings (TurboTax's relief screen vs. exit pop-ups), and edge cases like Spotify's outage error.
Results: In the cold-water study, Round 2 added 30 seconds at a slightly warmer 15°C after 60 seconds at 14°C. "80% of the study participants preferred Round 2 and chose to repeat that condition," even though it meant more total discomfort. HCI research also shows that "if a progress indicator speeds up towards the end, the process is judged to have been faster."
Takeaways: A better ending changes the whole memory; Amplify the moments that already reward; Frustrating moments become peaks too; End on a high note, not a pop-up; Plan for errors and outages
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: end every MCQ set on a win, for example close with an easier question or a summary that leads with what improved before what went wrong. Today's plan: give plan completion a clear celebratory end screen with no upsell on it. Renewal: avoid "please don't go" pop-ups when a user cancels; make the cancel flow calm and respectful so the last memory is good

Key points.title: A better ending changes the whole memory
Key points.detail: Participants held a hand in 14°C water for 60 seconds, and in another round for 60 seconds plus 30 more at 15°C. 80% chose to repeat the longer round, because it ended slightly better. People remember snapshots, weighted toward peaks and endings, not the total.

Key points.title: Amplify the moments that already reward
Key points.detail: Duolingo's mascot congratulates users after 10 correct answers, adding to the pleasure of learning. NN/g suggests finding the moments where the product is most helpful or valuable and making them better with colour, an icon or an illustration. For OnCourse, that is a correct streak of answers or a finished plan.

Key points.title: Frustrating moments become peaks too
Key points.detail: In an NN/g usability session, a participant fought a Maytag menu that closed whenever the cursor moved off it. At the end she still talked about that menu and said she might look at other brands. People remember negative moments more vividly than positive ones.

Key points.title: End on a high note, not a pop-up
Key points.detail: TurboTax ends tax filing with an illustration of relief and no upsell. In contrast, "please-don't-go" exit pop-ups, like Ann Taylor's surprise discount, irritate users and leave a bad last impression. Let the experience end when the user's task ends.

Key points.title: Plan for errors and outages
Key points.detail: During an outage, Spotify showed a red box saying "This feature is currently unavailable," with no explanation and no action. Sudden dead ends make strong memories. Explain the problem, estimate when it will be fixed, and never blame the user.

Title: Reading Content on Mobile Devices
Creator: Nielsen Norman Group (Kate Moran)
Bottom line: People understand easy text just as well on a phone as on a computer, but they slow down on hard text on mobile, so keep dense content short and well-structured.
What they did: NN/g asked 276 people across four studies to read easy and hard articles on a phone and on a computer, then answer multiple-choice comprehension questions. Easy articles averaged 404 words at an 8th-grade level; hard ones averaged 988 words at a 12th-grade level. In the in-person study they also timed reading speed. The analysis covered 1,629 article-plus-quiz cases.
Results: "Comprehension on mobile was about 3 percentage points higher than on a computer, with a 95% confidence interval of 1% to 5%", not practically significant. For hard passages, participants "spent about 30 milliseconds more on each word when reading on mobile" (device by difficulty interaction p=0.01). A marginal interaction (p=.10) hints that very difficult content may lower comprehension on mobile.
Takeaways: Comprehension on mobile matched the computer; Hard text is slower on mobile; Mobile readers trade speed for understanding; Medical content needs its own testing; Brevity still matters on mobile
Ideas for OnCourse: Lessons: break dense topics into short chunks with clear headings, since medical text is the hard content that slows mobile reading. Practice: keep MCQ explanations short up front, lead with the key fact, and put the long discussion behind "Read more". Design process: test a hard lesson with real NEET-PG students on a phone and time how long they take

Key points.title: Comprehension on mobile matched the computer
Key points.detail: A 2010 study had found worse comprehension on small screens. Across 276 participants and 1,629 reading cases, NN/g found mobile scores were about 3 points higher, which they call not practically significant. Bigger, sharper screens and easy thumb scrolling likely closed the gap.

Key points.title: Hard text is slower on mobile
Key points.detail: Easy passages were read at the same speed on both devices. Hard passages took about 30 milliseconds more per word on a phone (p=0.01). Hard articles were long (988 words) and written at a 12th-grade level.

Key points.title: Mobile readers trade speed for understanding
Key points.detail: To reach the same comprehension, people slowed down, read more carefully or re-read passages. That is a speed–accuracy tradeoff caused by higher working-memory load on a small screen. With very complex text, NN/g expects comprehension may drop on mobile too.

Key points.title: Medical content needs its own testing
Key points.detail: NN/g names medical and scientific sites as cases with "extremely challenging content" and recommends running your own usability studies on mobile. OnCourse's lessons and explanations are exactly this kind of content.

Key points.title: Brevity still matters on mobile
Key points.detail: Short, easy passages were faster to read on any device. Most mobile reading also happens on the go with fragmented attention. NN/g's rule stands: prioritise and keep mobile content brief.

Title: Autonomy, Relatedness, and Competence in UX Design
Creator: Nielsen Norman Group (Tanner Kohler)
Bottom line: People stay motivated by products that give them choice, make them feel understood, and help them feel capable, so good gamification lets learners choose their path and pace.
What they did: The article applies Ryan and Deci's self-determination theory to UX. It explains each of the three needs (autonomy, relatedness, competence) with good and bad product examples. It also covers when the needs conflict, as in TurboTax's wizard, and shows how Minecraft and Figma meet all three.
Takeaways: Motivation comes from three basic needs; Good gamification gives a choice of path and pace; Well-timed, relevant messages build relatedness; Build competence with help pulled at the right moment; The needs can conflict, so test
Ideas for OnCourse: Lessons: let students pick the subject order and pace within the plan, as Duolingo and Mimo do, instead of a single forced path. Notifications: send fewer, better-timed messages that show you understand the student's day, like an evening nudge sized to what they can still finish. Practice: show a tip for a feature the first time the student opens it (a pull tip), not in an upfront tour

Key points.title: Motivation comes from three basic needs
Key points.detail: Self-determination theory says people are driven by autonomy, relatedness and competence, and are happier when these are met. NN/g's framing is that users "aren't lazy, they're efficient" and only do what they are motivated to do. Products that meet these needs are used because people want to, not because they have to.

Key points.title: Good gamification gives a choice of path and pace
Key points.detail: "Properly designed gamification offers users varying degrees of freedom in choosing their path through the experience." Duolingo and Mimo let learners pick the order, pace and mastery level. Justanswer.com is the counter-example: it forces every user into a chat box with no categories or FAQ.

Key points.title: Well-timed, relevant messages build relatedness
Key points.detail: An Apple Watch nudge in the early evening uses an encouraging tone and a goal the user can still reach, so it feels understood. Peel sent four texts in one week trying to sell more phone cases right after a purchase. One tone-deaf message, like calling someone by the wrong name, is hard to recover from.

Key points.title: Build competence with help pulled at the right moment
Key points.detail: Otter's first-launch tutorial is "good", a single later tip is "better", and showing calendar help only when the user first opens My Agenda is "best". If testing shows orientation makes no difference, improve the design rather than writing instructions.

Key points.title: The needs can conflict, so test
Key points.detail: Wizards like TurboTax's raise competence by taking away autonomy. NN/g says to test with users to see which need matters more for the task. Minecraft and Figma show it is possible to meet all three at once.

Title: Designing Empty States in Complex Applications: 3 Guidelines
Creator: Nielsen Norman Group (Kate Kaplan)
Bottom line: Never leave an empty screen blank: say what state the system is in, explain what will appear there, and give a direct button to fill it.
What they did: NN/g gives three guidelines for screens and panels that have no content yet, drawn from complex enterprise apps. Empty states should communicate system status, teach the feature in context, and link straight to the task that fills them. Each guideline has bad and good examples.
Takeaways: Blank screens make users doubt the system; A false "no records" is worse than nothing; Use the empty state to teach the feature; Link directly to the first action
Ideas for OnCourse: Flashcards: when a student has no saved cards, explain how cards get added and offer a "Make cards from my mistakes" button. Practice: when a filter gives no questions, say so in plain words and offer to clear filters, instead of showing a blank list. Home: never show "No progress yet" while data is still loading; show a loading state until the real answer is known

Key points.title: Blank screens make users doubt the system
Key points.detail: When a panel is simply empty, people wonder if it is still loading, if an error occurred or if they set the wrong filters. They may refresh several times. A short message like "There are no records to display for the selected date range" fixes this.

Key points.title: A false "no records" is worse than nothing
Key points.detail: Some apps show "No records" while still loading, then replace it with content a few seconds later. At best users learn to distrust the app; at worst "trigger-happy users (that is, most users)" leave and never see the content. Show a progress indicator while loading and the empty message only when truly empty.

Key points.title: Use the empty state to teach the feature
Key points.detail: Empty states are a natural place for pull revelations, help that appears only when the user reaches that spot. DataDog's empty favourites panel says "Star your favorites to list them here." This in-context help is usually more memorable than a forced tutorial.

Key points.title: Link directly to the first action
Key points.detail: "Send a request to view details" tells users what to do but not how or where. Better empty states include a Create button and a Learn more link. Loggly offers two paths: add real data or load demo data to explore safely.

Title: Error-Message Guidelines
Creator: Nielsen Norman Group (Tim Neusesser, Evan Sunwall)
Bottom line: Make errors visible next to the problem, explain them in plain, blame-free words with a fix, and protect the user's input and effort.
What they did: NN/g expands usability heuristic #9 into guidelines in three groups: visibility, communication and efficiency. Each guideline has good and bad examples from real products. A final guideline covers total outages, where a bit of novelty can soften the failure.
Takeaways: Put the error next to its cause; Match the error's weight to its impact; Don't show errors too early; Say what happened and how to fix it, without blame; Keep the user's input and suggest the fix; Use novelty only for total failures
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: when a payment fails, explain why in plain words, keep the chosen plan selected and offer another payment method (UPI, card) in one tap. Onboarding: validate the phone number or OTP inline only after the user finishes typing, not while they are still typing. Practice: if a test fails to submit offline, keep all answers saved locally and say they'll sync, instead of a generic "Something went wrong"

Key points.title: Put the error next to its cause
Key points.detail: Show the error message beside the field or element that caused it. Instagram's URL error was subtle and far from the field. Amazon uses a border highlight, an icon and red text together. Never rely on colour or animation alone, because about 350 million people have a colour-vision deficiency.

Key points.title: Match the error's weight to its impact
Key points.detail: Warnings that don't block progress can be a label, toast or banner, like Kohl's neutral shipping-delay note. Save modal dialogs for severe errors that must be resolved before continuing.

Key points.title: Don't show errors too early
Key points.detail: Showing an error before the user has finished is "like grading a test before the student has had a chance to answer." A Texas form flagged an empty email field just because focus moved away. Use real-time inline checks only for error-prone inputs, such as CLEAR's password rules.

Key points.title: Say what happened and how to fix it, without blame
Key points.detail: Use plain language, not codes or jargon, and avoid generic text like "An error occurred." Offer a remedy, such as a restock alert for an out-of-stock item. Avoid words like invalid, illegal or incorrect, and avoid humour that goes stale with repetition. Target frames a shipping threshold around the goal, not the user's mistake.

Key points.title: Keep the user's input and suggest the fix
Key points.detail: Let people edit what they typed instead of starting over. Instagram offers to save a story draft when you back out. Where possible, guess the fix and offer it as a button, like choosing the city that matches the ZIP code entered.

Key points.title: Use novelty only for total failures
Key points.detail: When the whole system is down and users can only wait, an apology plus something surprising can soften a moment they'll remember because of negativity bias and the peak–end rule. Twitter's Fail Whale is the classic example. This is for rare outages, not everyday errors.

Chapters.summary: Placement, redundant indicators, severity and timing.

Chapters.title: Communication
Chapters.summary: Plain language, precise description, constructive advice, no blame.

Chapters.title: Efficiency
Chapters.summary: Prevent likely mistakes, preserve input, suggest fixes, explain briefly.

Chapters.anchor: Mitigate Failure with Novelty in Dire Situations

Chapters.summary: When an apology plus novelty can help.

Title: 7 Practical Animation Tips
Creator: Emil Kowalski
Bottom line: Small, exact motion rules (a 0.97 press scale, starting from 0.9+ not 0, ease-out, under 300ms, scaling from the trigger) make an interface feel faster and more responsive.
What they did: Emil lists seven tricks you can apply without any special talent for animation. Each comes with exact values: scale buttons to 0.97 when pressed, never animate from scale(0), skip the delay on tooltips after the first one, and use ease-out for things entering or leaving. He also says popovers should grow out of the button that opened them, animations should stay fast, and a 2px blur can hide a rough crossfade.
Results: These are rules of thumb from practice, not test results. "A scale of 0.97 on the :active pseudo-class should do the job." Start from "a higher initial scale instead (0.9+)"; his demo uses 0.93. Two dropdowns both last "300ms", but "the ease-in one feels slower." "A 180ms select animation feels more responsive than a 400ms one." "UI animations should generally stay under 300ms." The blur trick adds "2px of blur" to a crossfade.
Takeaways: Scale buttons down to 0.97 on press; Never animate in from scale(0); Ease-out for anything entering or leaving; Grow popovers from their trigger; Keep UI motion under 300ms; Blur hides a clumsy crossfade
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: scale each MCQ option to 0.97 while it is pressed, so a tap feels heard before the answer is checked. Practice: show the correct/wrong state with an ease-out transition under 300ms, never ease-in. Home: any menu or sheet opened from a button should scale in from that button (from about 0.93), not from the screen centre

Key points.title: Scale buttons down to 0.97 on press
Key points.detail: The interface should feel like it is listening, so give feedback on every action as soon as possible. The cheapest way is a subtle scale down when a button is pressed: "A scale of 0.97 on the :active pseudo-class should do the job." For OnCourse, MCQ options, the Start button and flashcard buttons should all shrink slightly while the finger is down.

Key points.title: Never animate in from scale(0)
Key points.detail: Things that grow from scale(0) look like they come out of nowhere. Start from 0.9 or higher (his demo uses 0.93), like a balloon that still has a shape when deflated. The motion then feels gentler and more natural.

Key points.title: Ease-out for anything entering or leaving
Key points.detail: Easing is "the most important part of any animation." Two dropdowns both run for 300ms, but the ease-in one feels slower because it starts slow; ease-out starts fast and feels responsive. Built-in CSS curves are often too weak, so he uses stronger custom ease-out curves (he recommends easings.co).

Key points.title: Grow popovers from their trigger
Key points.detail: A popover should scale in from the button that opened it, not from its own centre (the default transform-origin). Radix and Base UI expose a CSS variable that sets this origin for you. Users may not consciously notice it, but "in the aggregate, unseen details become visible, they compound."

Key points.title: Keep UI motion under 300ms
Key points.detail: A faster-spinning spinner makes loading feel quicker even when the load time is the same. A 180ms select feels more responsive than a 400ms one, and UI animations should generally stay under 300ms. Things people see tens or hundreds of times a day should often have no animation at all.

Key points.title: Blur hides a clumsy crossfade
Key points.detail: If easing and duration are tuned and a state change still feels off, add a little filter: blur(), about 2px. Blur bridges the gap between old and new states, so the eye sees one object changing instead of two objects swapping. It is a good fix for a button label changing from "Submit" to a result.

Chapters.summary: Scale buttons to 0.97 when pressed so the interface feels like it is listening.

Chapters.summary: Start entering elements at 0.9+ so they do not appear from nowhere.

Chapters.title: Tooltip timing
Chapters.summary: Delay the first tooltip, then open its neighbours instantly with no animation.

Chapters.title: Easing
Chapters.summary: Ease-out for entering and exiting; the same 300ms feels slower with ease-in.

Chapters.title: Origin
Chapters.summary: Popovers should scale from the trigger, not the centre.

Chapters.title: Speed
Chapters.summary: 180ms beats 400ms; keep UI motion under 300ms and drop it for very frequent actions.

Chapters.summary: A 2px blur blends two states into one smooth change.

Title: Great Animations
Creator: Emil Kowalski
Bottom line: Great animations feel natural, are fast, have a purpose, run smoothly, can be interrupted, respect reduced motion, and match the feel of the product.
What they did: Emil lists the principles he thinks make animations great, each with a live demo. He covers springs for natural motion, ease-out and under-300ms timing, never animating keyboard actions, animating only transform and opacity for smoothness, using interruptible transitions, and swapping movement for a fade when the user prefers reduced motion. He ends by saying easing and duration must fit the product's personality, and that you should review motion again the next day.
Results: Rules of thumb, not test results. Animations "should also usually be shorter than 300ms." "If our animations won't run at 60 frames per second, everything else we've talked about becomes useless." On Raycast: he "can't imagine how frustrating it would be if every time I opened it, I was greeted with a 500ms enter animation."
Takeaways: Natural motion comes from springs; Fast ease-out motion feels responsive; Animate only where it adds meaning; Animate transform and opacity only; Let users interrupt any animation; Reduced motion means fade, not move; Easing must match the product's personality
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: animate answer feedback, sheets and cards with transform and opacity only, so they hold 60fps on low-end Android phones. Flashcards: make flips and swipes interruptible, so a fast user can tap through mid-animation without waiting. Design process: for every custom animation, define a reduced-motion version that fades instead of moving

Key points.title: Natural motion comes from springs
Key points.detail: The Dynamic Island feels "almost like a living organism", and this natural motion is a major reason mobile apps feel better than web apps. Nothing in the real world appears or disappears instantly. He suggests trying spring animations, tuned by stiffness, damping and mass.

Key points.title: Fast ease-out motion feels responsive
Key points.detail: A spinner that spins faster looks like it is working harder, even with the same load time. Ease-out starts fast and slows at the end, so it feels like a quick response. Keep animations shorter than 300ms; he points to Family's iOS app as a model of a snappy interface.

Key points.title: Animate only where it adds meaning
Key points.detail: Too many animations overwhelm users and lose impact. Good uses explain something (his v0 animation for Vercel) or show a change of state (App Store cards, a modal entering). Never animate keyboard actions, which can repeat hundreds of times a day; Raycast has no animation and "it feels right."

Key points.title: Animate transform and opacity only
Key points.detail: If animations don't run at 60fps, nothing else matters. Transform and opacity only trigger the compositing step, while padding or margin trigger layout, paint and composite. At Vercel the active-tab animation dropped frames while the new page loaded, and moving it to CSS fixed it.

Key points.title: Let users interrupt any animation
Key points.detail: Users should be able to change their mind mid-animation and get a smooth change to the new state. CSS keyframes cannot be retargeted, but transitions can, so toasts added quickly still slide smoothly. For OnCourse, a sheet or card closed halfway through opening should reverse smoothly, not finish first.

Key points.title: Easing must match the product's personality
Key points.detail: Sonner's toast is a bit slower than usual and uses ease rather than ease-out, to feel more elegant and match its design and name. Getting Family's drawer right was trial and error. He reviews his work the next day with fresh eyes to spot flaws.

Chapters.summary: Use a fade-only version when the user prefers reduced motion.

Title: Building a drawer component
Creator: Emil Kowalski
Bottom line: A bottom sheet feels native only when it copies iOS's hidden rules: flick to dismiss, damped over-drag, scroll-then-drag, snap points, the iOS curve and 500ms.
What they did: Emil built Vaul, an open-source drawer (bottom sheet) for the web, to match how Apple's Sheet feels on iOS. He describes each detail he had to get right: momentum-based flick to close, damping when you drag past the top, only letting the sheet drag when its content is scrolled to the top, ignoring a second finger, snap points, and the background scaling into a card. He also shares the exact easing curve and duration copied from iOS.
Results: Implementation values, not test results. Dragging got laggy once content "got bigger than ~20 list items" because a CSS variable forced style recalculation on all children. After reaching the top of scrolled content, "a timeout of 100ms" blocks dragging so fast scrolls don't close the sheet. "Dragging the drawer down by 40% will change the border radius to 60% of its max value." Motion: "transition: transform 0.5s cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1)", with a "Duration of 500ms" to mimic iOS's Sheet.
Takeaways: Use a drawer, not a modal, on mobile; A flick should close it, not just distance; Over-dragging should slow down, not stop; Only drag when content is scrolled to top; Copy iOS's sheet curve and 500ms; Snap points should respect momentum
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: open the explanation and "report question" panels as bottom sheets that close on a quick downward flick, with the iOS curve cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1) at 500ms. Lessons: for a long sheet with scrolling content, only let it drag closed when the content is scrolled to the top. Flashcards: give the deck options sheet snap points (half and full) that a hard flick can skip past

Key points.title: A flick should close it, not just distance
Key points.detail: Vaul uses momentum-based dragging: you don't need to drag past a set point, a quick flick is enough. Snap points work the same way, so a hard flick can skip points or close the sheet entirely. This matches what iPhone users already expect from system sheets.

Key points.title: Over-dragging should slow down, not stop
Key points.detail: Dragging up past the top is damped: the more you drag, the less the sheet moves. Things in real life slow down before they stop, so this feels natural. A hard stop would feel broken.

Key points.title: Only drag when content is scrolled to top
Key points.detail: A sheet that both scrolls and drags is tricky, so dragging is only allowed once the content is at the top, like iOS. Because people scroll fast, they can fly past the top and close the sheet by accident; a 100ms pause before dragging is allowed fixes this. Long explanation sheets in OnCourse need the same rule.

Key points.title: Copy iOS's sheet curve and 500ms
Key points.detail: The curve closely matches iOS and comes from the Ionic Framework: cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1). The 500ms duration mimics iOS's Sheet. "Using the right easing and duration makes a big difference in terms of how this, and any other component, feels."

Key points.title: Invisible details meet unspoken expectations
Key points.detail: If you drag with one finger and add a second, the sheet would jump, so Vaul ignores extra touches until release. The background can scale and round its corners as the sheet opens, tracking drag progress (40% down gives 60% of the max radius). These details are "invisible" because they match what people already expect.

Key points.title: Test motion on a real phone
Key points.detail: You can't test a drawer by shrinking a desktop window. Emil tested on his phone connected by cable to Safari dev tools, visiting his local server by IP on the same Wi-Fi. The Xcode Simulator is an alternative.

Title: Building a toast component
Creator: Emil Kowalski
Bottom line: Sonner stood out in a crowded market because of a satisfying stacking animation and many small details, like velocity-based swipe, pausing when hidden and gap-free hover.
What they did: Emil explains how he built Sonner, a toast library. Toasts stack with a fixed offset and shrink by 5% per step, all toasts take the height of the front one, and the stack fans out on hover. He switched from keyframes to transitions so toasts can be interrupted, made swipe-to-dismiss work on speed as well as distance, and added small details like pausing the timer when the tab is hidden.
Results: Sonner "is now downloaded over 40,000,000 times per week from npm and used by companies like Cursor, X, and OpenAI." Stacked toasts scale down by "0.05 * index" (e.g. "Y(-14px) scale(0.95)", "Y(-28px) scale(0.9)"). A swipe dismisses if past the threshold or if "velocity is higher than in this case 0.11" (found "through trial and error"). Toasts disappear "after 4 seconds unless you hover over it."
Takeaways: The stacking animation is what people fell for; Use interruptible transitions, not keyframes; Stack with offset and 5% shrink for depth; Dismiss on swipe speed as well as distance; Pause timers when the user can't see them; Unseen details add up to 'feels right'
Ideas for OnCourse: Flashcards: when a card is saved or bookmarked, confirm with a small toast that can be flicked away and stacks neatly if several fire in a row. Practice: pause any auto-dismissing feedback (like "streak saved") while the app is in the background, so the student actually sees it. Design process: when specifying a swipe, define both a distance threshold and a speed threshold

Key points.title: The stacking animation is what people fell for
Key points.detail: The toast market was already crowded in 2023. Emil believes Sonner took off because of its stacking animation, which some companies had done but never open-sourced. He built the launch video around that one motion. Sonner now gets over 40,000,000 npm downloads a week.

Key points.title: Use interruptible transitions, not keyframes
Key points.detail: With CSS keyframes, older toasts jumped into place when new ones arrived quickly, because keyframes can't change their end point mid-run. Transitions can be retargeted, so he switched. Any OnCourse animation that can be triggered again before it finishes needs the same property.

Key points.title: Stack with offset and 5% shrink for depth
Key points.detail: Each toast behind the front one moves up by a fixed gap times its index and shrinks by 0.05 times its index (1, 0.95, 0.9). Toasts of different heights didn't stick out evenly, so in the stack every toast takes the height of the front one. On hover the stack expands to show all toasts.

Key points.title: Dismiss on swipe speed as well as distance
Key points.detail: Swipe-down-to-dismiss works if the toast passes a distance threshold or if the swipe is fast enough. Velocity is drag distance divided by time; above 0.11 it dismisses, a number found by trial and error. Dragging the wrong way is allowed but slows with friction instead of stopping dead.

Key points.title: Pause timers when the user can't see them
Key points.detail: Toasts vanish after 4 seconds unless hovered. If the tab is hidden, the timer pauses, so the message isn't missed. A pseudo-element fills gaps between toasts so hover doesn't flicker, and pointer capture keeps a drag going even when the finger leaves the toast.

Title: Invisible Details of Interaction Design
Creator: Rauno Freiberg
Bottom line: Interactions feel right when they borrow real-world physics and metaphors, respond during the gesture, keep spatial logic consistent, and skip animation for frequent actions.
What they did: Rauno replays iOS and macOS interactions in slow motion and explains why each one feels right. He covers when a swipe should fire (during the gesture for light actions, only on release for destructive ones), why gestures should respond right away before any threshold, how motion shows where things come from, and why frequent actions should not animate. He backs this with his own prototypes, like removing motion from his bookmarking tool after it began to feel slow.
Takeaways: Reuse metaphors so one gesture teaches many; Light actions fire mid-swipe, destructive ones on release; Respond to the gesture immediately, before thresholds; Motion should show where things come from; High-frequency, low-novelty actions shouldn't animate; Show what's under the finger
Ideas for OnCourse: Flashcards: let the card follow the finger from the first pixel of a swipe, and only commit "Again"/"Good" when the finger lifts. Practice: animate the answer reveal once per question but drop motion from things tapped all session, like next-question and bookmark. Lessons: open a lesson from the card that was tapped, so the motion shows where it came from and where Back will return

Key points.title: Reuse metaphors so one gesture teaches many
Key points.detail: iOS only explicitly teaches swiping up to open, which tells you the interface is stacked layers like a deck of cards. That one lesson unlocks swiping down for controls and swiping up to dismiss an app. Horizontal swipes navigate because that is how we have turned book pages for thousands of years.

Key points.title: Light actions fire mid-swipe, destructive ones on release
Key points.detail: Lightweight actions like showing an overlay feel right when they trigger during the swipe, once elements reach their final position. Destructive actions wait: the iOS App Switcher never dismisses an app before the gesture ends, whatever the distance, so you can change your mind. For OnCourse, a flashcard rating should commit only on release.

Key points.title: Respond to the gesture immediately, before thresholds
Key points.detail: A naive pinch that only zooms after a threshold gives no sign the card is pinchable. It feels better to apply the scale change immediately and then animate past the threshold. He notes iOS Settings feels less responsive than the App Switcher because a mistaken tap can't be interrupted by swiping back.

Key points.title: Motion should show where things come from
Key points.detail: When the Dynamic Island is expanded, Spotify opens from its app icon so it is clear which app is playing; otherwise it slides in from the right, its place in the App Switcher. The Clock app always opens from the Island, because only one app can own that timer. Spatial consistency tells users where things live.

Key points.title: High-frequency, low-novelty actions shouldn't animate
Key points.detail: On his bookmarking tool (bmrks.com) he animated the active indicator and list changes, but after a few days they felt sluggish even when made snappier. Removing motion from core interactions made him feel faster. macOS context menus appear with no motion, yet the chosen item blinks and the menu fades out to confirm the choice.

Key points.title: Show what's under the finger
Key points.detail: Fingers hide content, so iOS shows a loupe above the text caret and an enlarged key when typing. For small sliders, the drag should not cancel when the thumb drifts off the track. Where a finger covers key content, show it somewhere visible.

Title: Quality Wednesdays: How we trained our team to see what doesn’t work
Creator: Linear (Tuomas Artman)
Bottom line: Make polish a weekly habit: everyone fixes one small flaw (30 minutes or less) and shows it at a standup, and over time the team learns to see flaws before they ship.
What they did: At a 2023 offsite, Linear's CTO showed engineers a screen recording of three hover buttons, and nobody could spot the flaw. A group review then found that each person noticed different small flaws. So Linear made every Wednesday standup a show-and-tell where each engineer presents a small polish fix, not a bug fix, tracked with a "quality" label.
Results: "Over the last two years we've completed more than 1,000 small acts of polish." "Many of these quality fixes take 30 minutes or less. None should take more than an hour or so." The flaw nobody saw: one button "darkened instantly when the mouse moved away, rather than fading out over 150 milliseconds as it should have." An engineer: "you start noticing patterns and common pitfalls while building stuff, so fewer of these papercuts ship."
Takeaways: People can't see flaws in what they built; Quality is a team sport; Make polish a small, weekly habit; Cap each fix at about an hour; Polish fixes are not bug fixes; Training the eye prevents future papercuts
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: run a weekly 'quality' slot where each designer and engineer shows one small OnCourse fix under an hour, tagged in the tracker. Design process: run a group review of one screen (say Practice) where each person lists everything slightly off, and compare lists. Practice: audit that every pressed and released state uses the same duration, since an inconsistent timing was the flaw no one could see

Key points.title: People can't see flaws in what they built
Key points.detail: Tuomas showed the team a short recording of three buttons lighting up on hover; after several viewings nobody could see what was wrong. The flaw was that one button went dark instantly instead of fading out over 150ms like the others. Inconsistent motion timing is easy to ship and hard to notice.

Key points.title: Quality is a team sport
Key points.detail: In a group review of parts like display options and issue lists, each person noticed different small flaws that were invisible to everyone else. It is hard to see subtle problems in a UI you built yourself. Reviewing as a group gives a much fuller picture.

Key points.title: Make polish a small, weekly habit
Key points.detail: Quality should be like brushing your teeth: nobody says they have no time for it. One of three weekly standups became a show-and-tell of quality fixes. Miss a week and the joke is "just bring two next week."

Key points.title: Polish fixes are not bug fixes
Key points.detail: The ask was to fix small imperfections that "degrade the overall experience", not "bugs per se." Examples include making adjacent button sizes match and stopping the issue composer from changing height when you add a line. Some engineers keep a running note of things that feel off; others work by theme, like menus, keyboard navigation or accessibility.

Key points.title: Training the eye prevents future papercuts
Key points.detail: Over two years the team shipped more than 1,000 small fixes. The bigger effect is that engineers now spot common pitfalls while building, so fewer papercuts ship at all. For OnCourse, a weekly polish ritual would train designers and engineers to catch issues in review.

Title: A Linear spin on Liquid Glass
Creator: Linear (Robb Böhnke)
Bottom line: Linear rebuilt Liquid Glass itself so it could own its tab bar, keep the tactile details (touch lift, edge stretch, edge blur, Increase Contrast outlines), and drop refraction for readability.
What they did: For a mobile redesign that needed more flexible navigation, Linear chose not to use Apple's Liquid Glass APIs and built its own material in SwiftUI. It has a blur layer, a gradient, and a shader-made highlight lit by a light source that moves as you scroll and tap. They built a custom tab bar that can hold more than five items. They also added tactile details and matched Apple's accessibility behaviour, but left out refraction to keep dense screens readable.
Results: No metrics. Team size: "just two engineers" on iOS. Doing it themselves let them ship the new navigation "to all of our users, including those on iOS 18." On tab bars: "Five items is a sensible limit for apps for a general audience, but Linear users often need more."
Takeaways: Own the material if you need to own the navigation; Take the aesthetic with a ProKit discipline; Touch lift and edge stretch give tactile feedback; Variable blur at scroll edges; Match system accessibility settings exactly; Skip effects that hurt readability
Ideas for OnCourse: Home: on press, lift tappable cards slightly with a quick pulse, and let lists stretch a little past their edge instead of stopping hard. Practice: keep glass or blur effects off the question and options; reserve them for chrome like the tab bar, so dense text stays readable. Design process: for any custom material or colour treatment, define how it looks with Increase Contrast turned on

Key points.title: Own the material if you need to own the navigation
Key points.detail: The redesign's real goal was navigation that adapts to different roles, like managers needing an overview. Apple's stock iOS 26 tab bar can't meaningfully change shape or behaviour, so Linear rebuilt the glass and its own tab bar. It can grow past the usual five items, similar to how an iPad tab bar becomes a sidebar.

Key points.title: Take the aesthetic with a ProKit discipline
Key points.detail: Apple once had Aqua for consumer apps and ProKit, flatter and sharper, for pro tools like Final Cut. Linear treated Liquid Glass as the new Aqua and applied its translucency, depth and physicality with a ProKit attitude: focused and disciplined. An exam-prep app used for long focused sessions sits closer to ProKit too.

Key points.title: Touch lift and edge stretch give tactile feedback
Key points.detail: When you touch an element it lifts slightly, giving "a quick pulse of feedback." Dragging past the edge of a view distorts it a little, which releases the physical tension. The highlight shifts as you scroll and tap because it is lit by a light source modelled in real time on the GPU.

Key points.title: Variable blur at scroll edges
Key points.detail: At the top and bottom of scroll views, a blur gets stronger as content nears the screen edge, with a subtle colour mask to match Apple's soft edge. Apple uses this internally but doesn't offer it through public APIs, so Linear recreated it. It helps a custom app feel at home on iOS.

Key points.title: Skip effects that hurt readability
Key points.detail: When Increase Contrast is on, iOS draws solid outlines around glass, and Linear's material copies this exactly. They chose not to copy refraction: it needs pixel data third parties can't access, and it "can make dense professional interfaces harder to read." Precise blur, masking and lighting give depth without losing clarity.

Title: Playing haptics
Creator: Apple Human Interface Guidelines
Bottom line: Use haptics sparingly and consistently: one pattern per meaning, matched to the animation's intensity, short for discrete events, and always optional.
What they did: Apple's guidelines explain when and how to play haptics. They say to use system patterns only for their documented meaning, keep each haptic tied to one cause, match haptic sharpness and intensity to the animation, avoid overuse, prefer short haptics, and let people turn them off. On iOS there are three families of feedback: notification (outcome of a task), impact (something snaps or collides) and selection (a value changing). Custom haptics are built from short transient taps and continuous vibrations, tuned by sharpness and intensity.
Takeaways: Use system patterns only for their documented meaning; One haptic, one cause; Match haptic to the animation it accompanies; Less is more, the best haptic goes unnoticed; Prefer short haptics for discrete events; Haptics must be optional
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: play a notification-success haptic on a correct answer and a different notification-error haptic on a wrong one, and never swap their meanings anywhere else in the app. Flashcards: use a light impact haptic when a card snaps into place, and selection haptics while scrolling a picker such as the daily goal. Design process: add a haptics toggle in settings, and make sure every haptic has a matching visual cue

Key points.title: One haptic, one cause
Key points.detail: Build a clear cause-and-effect link between each haptic and the action that causes it, so people learn what it means. If a pattern plays when a mission fails, using it again for a level completion will confuse people. Use system patterns only for their documented meaning; otherwise use a generic or custom one.

Key points.title: Match haptic to the animation it accompanies
Key points.detail: Visual, audio and touch feedback should agree, as they do in the physical world. Match the haptic's intensity and sharpness to the intensity and sharpness of its animation. A soft card settle should feel soft; a crisp snap should feel crisp.

Key points.title: Less is more, the best haptic goes unnoticed
Key points.detail: A haptic can feel right occasionally but tiring when frequent. User testing helps find the balance. "Often, the best haptic experience is one that people may not be conscious of, but miss when it's turned off." In most apps, prefer short haptics for discrete events, since long ones dilute meaning.

Key points.title: Three iOS families: notification, impact, selection
Key points.detail: Notification haptics report the outcome of a task, like depositing a check. Impact haptics give a physical metaphor, like a tap when a view snaps into place. Selection haptics play while a control's value changes, and standard toggles, sliders and pickers already play them.

Key points.title: Custom haptics: transient vs continuous, sharpness and intensity
Key points.detail: Transient events are brief taps, like the Flashlight button. Continuous events are sustained vibrations. Sharpness sets the feel, from soft and organic to crisp and mechanical, and intensity sets strength.

Key points.title: Haptics must be optional
Key points.detail: Let people turn haptics off and make sure the app still works without them. Haptics also shouldn't disturb the camera, gyroscope or microphone. The related Feedback page adds that feedback should use colour, text, sound and haptics together so it reaches everyone.

Chapters.title: Best practices
Chapters.summary: Consistency, matching animation, avoiding overuse, short haptics, optional.

Title: Web Interface Guidelines
Creator: Vercel
Bottom line: A checklist of hundreds of small interface decisions, with exact numbers for hit targets, loading-state timing, optimistic updates, motion rules and error copy.
What they did: Vercel keeps a living checklist of interface details, grouped into Interactions, Animations, Layout, Content, Forms, Performance, Design and Copywriting. Most rules are one line with a concrete value. Examples: 44px touch targets on mobile, a delay and a minimum display time for spinners to avoid flicker, optimistic updates with undo, and error messages that say how to fix the problem. It also offers an AGENTS.md file so AI coding agents follow the rules.
Results: Guidelines, not results. Hit targets: "if the visual target is < 24px, expand its hit target to ≥ 24px. On mobile, the minimum size is 44px." Loading: "add a short show-delay (~150–300 ms) & a minimum visible time (~300–500 ms) to avoid flicker on fast responses." Inputs: font size "≥ 16px on mobile to prevent iOS Safari auto-zoom." Performance: "POST/PATCH/DELETE complete in <500ms."
Takeaways: Make hit targets 44px on mobile; Delay spinners and hold them on screen; Update optimistically, offer Undo; Only animate to clarify cause and effect; Skeletons must mirror final content; Error messages should guide the exit
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: when submitting an answer, update the UI at once and reconcile with the server, and only show a spinner if the request takes more than about 150–300ms, then hold it for at least 300–500ms. Home: make skeletons for Today's plan match the final card layout exactly, so nothing jumps when content loads. Paywall: rewrite payment errors to say what to do next, not only what went wrong

Key points.title: Make hit targets 44px on mobile
Key points.detail: Visual and hit targets should match, but if a visual target is under 24px, expand its hit area to at least 24px; on mobile the minimum is 44px. Checkboxes and their labels share one generous target with no dead zones. If part of a control looks tappable, it should be tappable.

Key points.title: Delay spinners and hold them on screen
Key points.detail: To avoid flicker on fast responses, wait about 150–300ms before showing a spinner or skeleton, then keep it visible for at least 300–500ms. Loading buttons keep their label and add an indicator. Skeletons mirror the final content exactly, so there is no layout shift.

Key points.title: Update optimistically, offer Undo
Key points.detail: When success is likely, update the UI immediately and reconcile when the server responds. On failure, show an error and roll back, or offer Undo. Destructive actions need a confirmation or an Undo window.

Key points.title: Only animate to clarify cause and effect
Key points.detail: Animate only when it clarifies cause and effect or adds deliberate delight. Animations must respect reduced motion, be interruptible by user input, use transform and opacity, and start from where the motion "physically" begins. Never use transition: all.

Key points.title: Error messages should guide the exit
Key points.detail: Don't just say what went wrong; say how to fix it. Instead of "Invalid API key", say the key is wrong or expired and where to make a new one. Buttons should be specific: "Save API Key" rather than "Continue". Every screen offers a next step, and empty, sparse, dense and error states are all designed.

Key points.title: Gestures need tap alternatives
Key points.detail: Every drag, swipe or pinch also works with a tap and keyboard, unless the gesture is essential. Rarely autofocus on mobile, because the keyboard opening shifts the layout. Use overscroll-behavior: contain in modals and drawers so scrolling doesn't leak to the page behind.

Title: Principles in motion
Creator: Figma (Anja Laubscher with Chad Colby, Ben Hill, Gilles Desmadrille)
Bottom line: Learn the shared words for motion (anticipation, overshoot, settle, 'floaty', 'too linear') and look to real-world physics and film, so you can give and get precise motion feedback.
What they did: Figma's three brand motion designers explain how they think about motion. They describe looking to physics, nature and film for reference, and how they use transitions and cuts to keep momentum. The piece includes two short glossaries: core principles, and the shorthand the team uses in critique. They also explain how AI motion prompting changes the craft.
Takeaways: Motion is designing with time; Real-world physics is the reference; Name the principles: anticipation, overshoot, follow-through, hold, settle; Use shared shorthand in critique; Sound effects sell a motion idea; AI makes good motion easy, great motion still needs principles
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: add the core and shorthand glossaries to OnCourse's critique template, so feedback on motion says "feels floaty" or "needs a hold" instead of "feels off". Progress & streaks: when a streak milestone animates, use anticipation, a small overshoot and a short hold so the moment registers before the screen moves on

Key points.title: Motion is designing with time
Key points.detail: Graphic design communicates through frozen moments; motion adds rhythm, pacing, transformation and character. Instead of cramming everything into one image, you break it up: first this, then that. The main question is how easing and timing create a feeling.

Key points.title: Real-world physics is the reference
Key points.detail: A bouncing ball starts fast, slows near the top, falls again, and each bounce is lower. People recognise good motion even if they can't say why, because of its link to the real world. If you only copy other motion work, you fall into trends ("bouncy balls and rectangles only go so far").

Key points.title: Name the principles: anticipation, overshoot, settle
Key points.detail: The core glossary: ease in/ease out (acceleration over time), anticipation (a preparatory move), overshoot (going slightly past and settling back), follow-through (secondary motion after the main move), hold (a pause so the viewer can register), and settle (the final subtle motion at rest).

Key points.title: Use shared shorthand in critique
Key points.detail: The team's shorthand includes "Zippy", "Make it dreamy", "Chunky", "Make it snappier" (quicker timing, sharper easing), "Feels floaty" (lacks weight), "Too linear" (constant speed, mechanical) and "Dead on arrival" (no energy or intent). Shared words make motion feedback faster and more precise. They also use sound effects to sell an idea: it doesn't click until someone says "It'll go, 'Whoop!'"

Key points.title: Great motion still needs the principles
Key points.detail: Motion prompting lets you sketch slow, fast or bouncy ideas without scripting expressions. But "It's going to be very easy to create good motion, but if you don't understand the basic motion principles, it's going to be hard to create great motion." Skill, intention and restraint will set work apart.

Chapters.summary: Ease, anticipation, overshoot, follow-through, hold, settle; plus physics and match cuts.

Title: New data shows losing 80% of mobile users is normal, and why the best apps do better
Creator: Andrew Chen
Bottom line: Most users decide to drop an app in the first 3 to 7 days, so the best way to lift retention is a stronger first session and first week, not more reminder messages.
What they did: Andrew Chen worked with Quettra, which had usage data from over 125M Android phones, to plot day-by-day retention curves for Google Play apps (January to May 2015, apps with over 10,000 installs). He compared the average app with the top 10, next 50, next 100 and next 5000 apps by ranking. He then argued that the curve is bent through activation in the first days, not through notification volume.
Results: "the average app loses 77% of its DAUs within the first 3 days after the install. Within 30 days, it's lost 90% of DAUs. Within 90 days, it's over 95%." From the tabular data, Day-1 active users: Top 10 apps 74.67%, Next 50 64.85%, Next 100 48.72%, Next 5000 34.31%, Average 29.17%. Day-30: Top 10 59.80%, Next 5000 13.62%, Average 9.55%. Day-90: Top 10 50.87%, Average 3.97%.
Takeaways: Users decide in the first 3 to 7 days; Top apps win on day 1, not on the slope; Bend the curve with activation, not reminders; A lost daily user is not always a lost user; Long-term numbers are hard to move later
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: end the first session with a finished mini-set (for example 10 MCQs with explanations) so every new aspirant gets a real result on day 1, before any setup screens. Today's plan: design a fixed first-7-days plan with one short, clear task per day, because this window decides who stays. Notifications: drop generic "We miss you" pushes and spend that effort on day 1 to day 7 nudges tied to the user's next plan task.

Key points.title: Users decide to quit within 3 to 7 days
Key points.detail: Quettra's founder Ankit Jain says users try many apps but decide which ones to "stop using" within the first 3 to 7 days. For decent apps, most users still active at day 7 stay much longer. So the first week is the window that matters most. For OnCourse, the first seven days of Today's plan deserve more design attention than any later screen.

Key points.title: Average apps lose 77% of daily users in 3 days
Key points.detail: On average, only 29.17% of installers are active on day 1, 23.42% on day 3 and 9.55% on day 30. By day 90 it is 3.97%. Chen says this is why, of over 1.5 million Play Store apps, only a few thousand keep meaningful traffic. A steep early drop is normal, so OnCourse should compare itself with these curves before panicking.

Key points.title: Top apps win on day 1, then decay the same
Key points.detail: The top 10 apps keep 74.67% of users on day 1 and 59.80% on day 30, far above average. But Chen notes the fall from D1 to D30 is about the same speed as for other apps. The gap is created by being useful immediately and being used repeatedly in week one. The lesson is to raise the starting point, not to hope to flatten the slope later.

Key points.title: Bend the curve with activation, not notification spam
Key points.detail: Chen says most leverage is in how the product is described, the onboarding flow and the triggers set up in the first days. Long-term numbers are "hard to budge, no matter how many reminder emails you send." He gives examples of activation goals, like a blogger picking a theme and writing a first post. Spammy "We Miss You" emails are "unlikely to bend the curve significantly."

Key points.title: A lost daily user is not always lost
Key points.detail: Losing a daily active user can mean the person now uses the app weekly or monthly, not that they left. But daily and monthly use correlate, so you cannot keep monthly users without daily ones. For a daily-study app like OnCourse, daily activity is the right number to watch.

Title: New data on push notifications show up to 40% CTRs, the best perform 4X better than the worst (Guest post)
Creator: Andrew Chen (guest post by Alli Brian, Kahuna)
Bottom line: Push works best when it supports something the user already does as a routine, sent at that user's own best time and about their own content.
What they did: Kahuna shared push engagement rates by app category and explained why utility and finance apps do so much better than retail and social. It then gave three fixes for weaker apps: find a cadence per user, personalize to the person (not the device), and time each send to when that user is most likely to engage. Each fix is shown with real notification examples and user reactions.
Results: "push engagement rates for utility and financial services notifications (40%) are nearly four times higher than for e-commerce & retail notifications (12%)." Well-timed utility notifications can reach engagement "as high as 80%." "Kahuna data reveals that customizing delivery time based on user preference results in an average conversion uplift of 384%." Chen's intro also cites earlier Kahuna data that "up to 60% of users opt-out of push notifications."
Takeaways: Push works best for routine, high-frequency apps; Find each user's cadence and know when not to send; Personalize to the person's own context; A wrongly personalized push is worse than none; Send at each user's own best time
Ideas for OnCourse: Notifications: send the daily study reminder at the time each aspirant usually studies (learned from their recent sessions) instead of one fixed time for everyone. Notifications: write reminders about the user's own work, such as "18 Pharmacology cards due from yesterday", not generic motivation. Onboarding: ask "When do you usually study?" and use it as the starting send time.

Key points.title: Routine apps get four times the push engagement
Key points.detail: Utility and financial services pushes see 40% engagement, against 12% for e-commerce and retail. The winners are apps people already use daily or weekly, like directions, budgets and taxis. Push nudges a routine that already exists. A daily-study app is in the routine group, so OnCourse should tie pushes to the study routine itself.

Key points.title: Find each user's cadence, and know when to stop
Key points.detail: Tolerance for notifications differs by app type and by user, and engaged users tolerate far more than new or dormant users. The post says not every app should send daily, and "the elegance is in knowing when not to send a message." Netflix sends one push about the exact show you watch instead of one per new episode of any show. Automation that caps and prioritizes pushes per user is the recommended way to manage this.

Key points.title: Personal context makes the same push welcome
Key points.detail: Two sports apps got opposite reactions: a FIFA World Cup push felt like spam to users not interested in that match, while a SportsCenter push about the user's own fantasy league felt delightful. The difference was relevance to that person. For OnCourse, a push naming the subject or deck the user is working on should beat a generic "Time to study!".

Key points.title: Wrong personalization is worse than none
Key points.detail: Tracking devices instead of people sends the wrong content when someone else uses the phone. The post calls the mis-personalized push the worst case of all. Use a stable user ID so even anonymous users get accurate messages. OnCourse should make sure reminders follow the logged-in account and its real progress.

Key points.title: Send at each user's own best time
Key points.detail: Non-urgent pushes should arrive when each user is most likely to engage, since everyone keeps a different schedule. Kahuna reports an average conversion uplift of 384% from customizing delivery time to user preference. Mis-timed pushes, such as one that wakes someone up, draw angry reactions. Students preparing for NEET-PG keep very different hours, so per-user timing matters a lot.

Title: RRF: A Framework for Building Impactful Notifications
Creator: Phiture (Andy Carvell)
Bottom line: Rank notification ideas by Reach x Relevance x Frequency, and build the ones that can reach every user often (including new users) before niche ones.
What they did: Andy Carvell, who built SoundCloud's activity notification service, proposes scoring each notification idea on how many users it can reach, how relevant it is, and how often its trigger happens. He sorts notifications into four types (Stars, Northern Lights, Full Moons, Eclipses) and shows how to move one type into another, for example by Facebook treating a like or comment as implicit permission to notify. He insists on measuring against a control group that gets no notifications, including opt-outs and uninstalls.
Results: A worked example, not a measured result: a daily alert "sent to the entire user base of 10m active users, with 0.5% CTR" drives "50,000 clicks (re-engagements with the app) every single day." A one-to-one message with 100% CTR "would need to be generated at least 50,000 times per day" to match it.
Takeaways: Impact = Reach x Relevance x Frequency; Build full-reach notifications first; Scheduled daily notifications are the frequency you control; Use a portfolio of Stars, Northern Lights, Full Moons and Eclipses; Measure against a no-notification control
Ideas for OnCourse: Notifications: build one daily "Your plan for today is ready" push that every user qualifies for, including day-1 users, before building niche alerts for power users. Design process: score each proposed notification on reach, relevance and frequency in the spec before design starts. Notifications: keep a holdout group that gets no growth notifications and track opt-outs and uninstalls, not just taps.

Key points.title: Impact equals reach times relevance times frequency
Key points.detail: Reach is the share of users who can qualify for a notification. Relevance is how interesting it is, proxied by click rate once live. Frequency is how often the trigger event happens. A notification weak on any one of the three has little total impact, however good it is on the others.

Key points.title: Build full-reach notifications before power-user ones
Key points.detail: Notifications that only fire after deep engagement ("Northern Lights") never reach the users who churned early. The highest-impact ones can reach the whole base, "ideally including new users, who are particularly prone to churn." Carvell says to build these first even if their open rates are much lower. For OnCourse, a reminder every new user gets beats a clever alert only streak-holders see.

Key points.title: Daily scheduled pushes are the frequency you control
Key points.detail: Most trigger events depend on the outside world or other users, so teams can't make them happen more often. Scheduled "CronJob" events like daily recommendations or weekly summaries are the exception. Carvell says they "should be enthusiastically tested once relevance is established." A daily plan or due-cards reminder is exactly this kind of lever for OnCourse.

Key points.title: Relevance raises tolerance for more notifications
Key points.detail: Users' tolerance for frequency is "directly proportional to the relevancy of the notifications," and the reverse also holds. Personalized and timely content is more relevant, as is sending when the user is awake or usually active. Before building, you can fake a programmatic notification by sending it manually to a test segment and checking click rate, watching for novelty inflating the result.

Key points.title: Use a mix of the four notification types
Key points.detail: Stars are high reach and high frequency (Medium's personalized new-post pushes). Full Moons are high reach but rare, Northern Lights are frequent but only for power users, and Eclipses are rare and narrow but very relevant (a flight time change). Too many Stars cause fatigue, so mix in occasional Eclipses and reward engaged users with Northern Lights. Facebook turned a narrow notification into a Star by treating a past like or comment as permission to notify on new replies.

Key points.title: Measure against a group that gets nothing
Key points.detail: The fear that users hate notifications is a hypothesis, not a fact. Carvell says to measure click rates, longer-term engagement and retention, plus push opt-outs, email unsubscribes and uninstalls, all against a control group that receives no notifications. This settles the "too spammy" debate with data.

Title: Increasing Retention with Push, In-App and Email Part 3: Implementing the Strategy
Creator: Phiture (Andy Carvell)
Bottom line: Win push permission early with a pre-permission screen, nudge new users back to the exact step they dropped, use reminders to protect streaks and goals, and personalize win-back messages with what the user liked before.
What they did: Andy Carvell turns four retention strategies (activation, frequency, feature adoption and re-engagement) into concrete push, in-app and email tactics. He covers push pre-permission and "push win-back" prompts, onboarding drop-off reminders, intent-based nudges, gamification reminders and stats summaries, and segmented reactivation. He closes with how to measure the whole program with a long-term holdout group.
Results: At SoundCloud, "we were able to increase re-activation rates 5x (albeit from a low base) by personalizing re-activation pushes with information about the last track a user had 'liked' in the app." In an example meditation-app funnel (fake data), "around 60% of users complete the app onboarding flow within 2 minutes." On realistic goals: for monthly retention, "a 1 or 2 percentage point increase over a year should be considered a significant win in most cases."
Takeaways: Ask for push permission before users churn, with a primer; Win back users who declined push via Settings; Remind onboarding drop-offs within minutes and deep-link back; Use onboarding intent to time nudges; Use push to protect streaks and goals; Personalize reactivation with past favorites; Measure with a long-term holdout
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: show an in-app primer ("Get your daily plan and streak reminders") before the iOS/Android permission dialog, and only show the system dialog to users who tap yes. Notifications: if a user leaves onboarding or a practice set midway, send one push a few minutes later that deep-links back to the same question. Streaks: send a "your streak ends at midnight" push only to users who have not studied today, and a weekly stats summary of questions done and accuracy.

Key points.title: Get push permission before most new users churn
Key points.detail: Often more than half of a new cohort fails to activate and leaves after the first session. Without push or email there is no way to bring them back. So ask early, but warm users up first with an in-app "pre-permission" message, and only show the one-time system prompt to those who say yes. Users who say "Not Now" can be asked again later with a different benefit.

Key points.title: Win back users who declined push
Key points.detail: Users who tapped "Don't Allow" can still be shown an in-app message asking them to enable push, with a deep link to the Settings app. Carvell calls this a "Push Win-Back" and says it "typically yields strong results," because people reconsider once they see the app's value. Doing both prompts as in-app messages lets you A/B test timing and copy.

Key points.title: Remind onboarding drop-offs within minutes
Key points.detail: Map each activation step as an event and look for steps with large drop-offs or long gaps. In the example, about 60% finish onboarding within 2 minutes, so a reminder push a few minutes after someone stalls is safe and catches them while intent is fresh. The push or email must deep-link back to the exact step they left. Headspace shows a stronger version: nudges built from the time and reason the user chose in onboarding.

Key points.title: Use push to protect streaks and goals
Key points.detail: Gamification covers goals with progress, streaks of regular use, and congratulations on personal bests and milestones. Messaging supports it by reminding users "when a streak is about to expire or a goal is in danger of being missed," congratulating achievements and sending regular stats summaries (Whistle's weekly pet-fitness email). Teams can even prototype goals and streaks with in-app messages before building them natively.

Key points.title: Personalize win-back with what users liked before
Key points.detail: SoundCloud raised reactivation 5x by naming the last track a lapsed user had liked. They split lapsed users into those who liked a track, those who only played one, and those who never did either. Formerly active users respond to a reminder of past value; never-activated users need more education or social proof. Carvell warns that "We miss you!" messages and vouchers alone won't work at scale.

Key points.title: Judge the whole program with a long-term holdout
Key points.detail: Keep a holdout group that never receives CRM messages to see the true effect on slow metrics like monthly retention. Campaign tests only show short-term effects. Low opt-in rates mean messaging may reach under half of users, so set modest goals: 1 to 2 percentage points of monthly retention in a year is a big win.
