Title: Managing Retention Rate Benchmarks & Expectations
Creator: Phiture (Anastasia Karpikhina)
Bottom line: Education apps have some of the lowest Day 30 retention of any category, so OnCourse should judge itself against education benchmarks and focus first on a first-session win and early activation.
What they did: Phiture explains what Day 1, Day 7 and Day 30 retention each tell you, then gives a 2025 to 2026 table of retention by app category compiled from Statista, AppsFlyer, Adjust, Business of Apps and Sendbird (updated March 2026). It adds the Lenny Rachitsky and Casey Winters six-month benchmarks, a DAU/MAU guide, and advice on product-market fit, traffic quality and how long retention tests take.
Results: Cross-industry averages are "roughly 25–26% on Day 1, 11–13% on Day 7, and 5–7% on Day 30." Education: "~14–15%" on Day 1, "~6%" on Day 7 and "~2–3%" on Day 30, one of the lowest rows in the table. iOS averages about 24% on Day 1 and 3.7% by Day 30; Android about 21% and 2.1%. For DAU/MAU, "around 20% is generally considered good, while above 25% is considered excellent." In-app messages and personalized experiences "have been shown to boost retention by as much as 30%" (source not named).
Takeaways: Education apps drop off steeply by Day 30; Day 1, Day 7 and Day 30 each test something different; Good retention depends on business model; Track DAU/MAU for stickiness; A first win in the first session lifts D1 and D7; Work on one or two things at a time; Day 30 tests take one to two months
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: set OnCourse retention targets against the education row (about 14–15% D1, 6% D7, 2–3% D30) rather than all-app averages, and track DAU/MAU against the 20% good / 25% excellent bar. Onboarding: make sure the first session ends with a finished lesson or practice set, the "first win" Phiture links to better D1 and D7. Today's plan: because learning "happens in structured bursts," give users a steady small daily task that bridges the gaps between their study bursts.

Key points.title: Education apps lose users fastest by Day 30
Key points.detail: In the category table, education apps keep about 14–15% on Day 1, 6% on Day 7 and 2–3% on Day 30. News reaches 11–13% on Day 30 and banking 6–11%. Phiture says education and travel drop most because "learning tends to happen in structured bursts" and travel is episodic. OnCourse is fighting the hardest category curve, so small gains matter.

Key points.title: Each checkpoint tests a different stage
Key points.detail: Day 1 shows users did not delete the app and that onboarding gave enough value to return within 24 hours. Day 7 shows activation is working and a habit is starting. Day 30 suggests a strong habit and is "widely regarded as a proxy for product-market fit." Reading the three together tells you which stage to fix.

Key points.title: Good retention depends on the business model
Key points.detail: Phiture cites the Lenny Rachitsky and Casey Winters six-month benchmarks: consumer SaaS such as Netflix or Spotify is good at 40% and great at 70%, while consumer social is good at 25%. A number that is excellent for one model can be worrying for another. iOS also retains better than Android, and region matters.

Key points.title: DAU/MAU shows how often retained users return
Key points.detail: Retention only says whether users came back. DAU/MAU ("stickiness") shows how often. About 20% is good and above 25% is excellent. For a daily-study product, this is a useful second number next to D30.

Key points.title: A first win lifts Day 1 and Day 7
Key points.detail: Phiture names three levers working in 2025 and 2026: personalized onboarding and messaging, push strategy (users who get even one push in their first 90 days are "significantly more likely to remain active"), and a meaningful "first win" in the first session, such as "finishing a lesson." It also advises working on one or two initiatives at a time, starting with onboarding and activation.

Key points.title: Retention tests take one to two months
Key points.detail: To read D30 after a new onboarding flow, you must wait for old users to finish the old flow and new users to complete the new one. This alone can take one to two months, depending on onboarding length and sample size. Plan OnCourse experiment timelines with this in mind.

Title: What is good retention
Creator: Lenny's Newsletter (Lenny Rachitsky, with Casey Winters)
Bottom line: For a consumer subscription product, about 40% of paying users still active after 6 months is good and about 70% is great, but the bar should be read alongside your acquisition costs and stage.
What they did: Lenny Rachitsky and Casey Winters asked 20 experienced growth leaders what they consider GOOD and GREAT user retention at 6 months and net revenue retention at 12 months. They combined the answers with public company figures to set benchmarks for five business types. Each type lists every expert's answer, the denominator to use, and public comps.
Results: Six-month user retention: "Consumer SaaS: ~40% is GOOD, ~70% is GREAT" (denominator: users who started a paid subscription); "Consumer social: ~25% is GOOD, ~45% is GREAT." Public comps: Spotify "72% 6-month customer retention", Netflix "66% 12-month customer retention", Hulu "53% 12-month customer retention", Amazon Prime "93% 12-month customer retention." Twelve-month net revenue retention for consumer SaaS: "~55% is GOOD, ~80% is GREAT."
Takeaways: Measure six-month retention with the right denominator; Consumer subscriptions: 40% good, 70% great; Experts disagree a lot; Public comps give a reality check; Low retention can be OK early or with cheap acquisition; Startups rarely raise retention significantly
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: report six-month retention of paid subscribers by cohort and compare it with the ~40% good / ~70% great consumer-subscription bar. Renewal: judge Renewal screen experiments by their effect on paid cohort retention, using net revenue retention (~55% good, ~80% great for consumer SaaS) as the second check. Design process: because exam prep ends at the exam, also track retention up to each user's exam date, since a fixed six-month window may not fit OnCourse (our interpretation, not the article's).

Key points.title: Define retention at six months, with clear denominators
Key points.detail: User retention here means the share of users who signed up and are still active six months later. The denominator changes by type: registered users for social, users with at least one transaction for transactional, and users who started a paid subscription for consumer SaaS. Using the wrong denominator makes comparisons meaningless.

Key points.title: Consumer subscriptions: 40% good, 70% great
Key points.detail: Consumer SaaS covers products like Netflix, Spotify and Hulu that sell monthly or yearly plans. The consensus is about 40% of paying users still active at six months as good and about 70% as great. This is the closest category to OnCourse's paid plans.

Key points.title: Experts disagree widely on the bar
Key points.detail: For consumer SaaS, Dan Hockenmaier says over 40% is good and over 60% great, while Elena Verna says over 70% is good and over 80% great. For consumer social, Andrew Chen sets the bar at over 50% good and over 75% great, double some others. The ranges show these are rough guides, not targets.

Key points.title: Public companies give a reality check
Key points.detail: Spotify has 72% six-month customer retention and Netflix 66% at twelve months. Hulu is at 53% and Amazon Prime at 93% at twelve months. These are some of the most-used subscriptions in the world, which shows how high the "great" bar is.

Key points.title: Low retention can be OK in some cases
Key points.detail: The authors say lower retention is acceptable if you are just starting out, if your acquisition and marginal costs are low, or if you are not building a venture-scale business. Fareed Mosavat: "what matters is that your retention supports sustained growth." They also warn that "startups rarely increase retention significantly."

Title: What is a good activation rate
Creator: Lenny's Newsletter (Lenny Rachitsky and Yuriy Timen)
Bottom line: Pick an early activation milestone that predicts at least 2x better retention, then raise it mainly by cutting onboarding steps and showing value sooner.
What they did: Lenny Rachitsky and Yuriy Timen surveyed over 500 products about their activation rate and what most improved it. They define activation rate, list example milestones, give averages and GOOD (60th percentile) and GREAT (80th percentile) rates by product type, and group hundreds of reader answers into eight common tactics. They close with the common mistakes in choosing a milestone.
Results: "the average activation rate is 34%, and the median activation rate is 25%." For SaaS only, "the average activation rate is 36%, and the median is 30%." A good milestone means activated users "retain at a rate at least 2x better" than others. About 6% of respondents had a time-bound activation definition, "with a median of 10 days and a mode of 7 days." B2C freemium products such as Duolingo and Calm have the highest activation rates because their milestone is low-friction. The per-type numbers are in a chart image that we could not read as text.
Takeaways: Activation is the earliest point that predicts retention; B2C freemium activates best with low-friction milestones; Fewer onboarding steps is the most common win; Smart defaults and earlier value reduce friction; Don't set the milestone too early or too late; Pick a milestone, then prove it with experiments
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: define activation as an early, concrete action such as "answered 10 MCQs and read one explanation on day 1" and check that activated users retain at least 2x better. Onboarding: remove steps between sign-up and the first question, and pre-fill exam and subjects with smart defaults. Home: hide secondary buttons for brand-new users so the only clear action is starting today's first set.

Key points.title: Activation is the earliest point that predicts retention
Key points.detail: Activation rate is users who hit the milestone divided by users who finished sign-up. The milestone (the "aha moment") is the earliest step that shows the product's value and predicts long-term retention. It must be predictive, with activated users retaining at least 2x better, and actionable by the team. Good examples include "First day of food and weight logged" and "First listen to 3+ sessions in the first week."

Key points.title: B2C freemium activates best with easy milestones
Key points.detail: Across 500+ products, the average activation rate is 34% and the median 25%. Most of the variance comes from how the milestone is defined. B2C freemium products like Duolingo and Calm have the highest rates because their milestone is low-friction, such as starting a meditation session. Marketplaces and e-commerce are lowest because their milestone is a first purchase.

Key points.title: Fewer onboarding steps is the most common win
Key points.detail: "Simpler onboarding UI/UX" tops the eight most-cited tactics. Answers include "Changed the flow to have fewer steps and improved it 20%," "Removing distracting CTAs between sign-up event and activation event," and "Hiding a confusing button on home page for new users." Another: "Driving all attention into one seeded task for guided completion."

Key points.title: Defaults and earlier value reduce friction
Key points.detail: Other common wins are smart recommendations and defaults, templates, removing login gates from first interactions, and showing core value as early as possible. Readers also credit personalized emails and push for new users, and checklists that limit early actions. For OnCourse, a pre-built first set based on the chosen exam is the template equivalent.

Key points.title: Avoid milestones that are too early or late
Key points.detail: The most common mistake is setting the milestone at sign-up (too early) or at several purchases (too late). The milestone should be "a leading indicator of having built a habit, not having proven the habit." Other mistakes: weak prediction, not actionable, or too complicated. About 10% use two-part milestones like "2+ bookings within 7-day time frame."

Key points.title: Pick a milestone, then prove it causes retention
Key points.detail: At first, the milestone is a hypothesis that only correlates with retention. Run experiments that raise activation and watch whether later retention also rises; if it does, causality is shown. The advice is to "not overthink it": choose an early milestone that strongly correlates with retention and start.

Title: Why Retention Is The Silent Killer
Creator: Reforge (Brian Balfour)
Bottom line: Measure retention at the product's natural frequency and on one real core action, and track how often people use it, not just whether they are still around.
What they did: Brian Balfour shows with a simple growth model why higher retention beats double the acquisition over three years. He then walks through three ways teams mis-define retention: wrong unit (revenue instead of usage), wrong frequency (monthly instead of daily, as with Viddy) and wrong core action (Pinterest's blended WARC metric). Finally he argues that retention (breadth) must be paired with engagement depth.
Results: Modelled example: Company A gets 1M new users a month with 85% monthly retention; Company B gets 2M with 65%. "After 6 months, Company A has approximately 4.2M MAUs. Company B has approximately 5.3M MAUs." After 3 years, "Company A has approximately 6.6M MAUs and Company B has approximately 5.7M MAUs." Viddy looked healthy at "35M MAU's and 5M DAU's" before collapsing.
Takeaways: Retention beats acquisition over time; Measure at your product's natural frequency; Pick one real core action; Revenue retention hides usage problems; Retention is breadth, engagement is depth; The wrong metric makes teams build the wrong things
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: define the core action as "answered at least one question or reviewed one flashcard," and track it daily, not app opens or monthly actives. Renewal: flag paid users whose weekly study days drop well before renewal and show them a progress recap in the app, since revenue retention hides that they will churn at renewal. Progress & streaks: report study days per week as a depth measure next to the streak count.

Key points.title: Higher retention beats double the acquisition
Key points.detail: In the model, Company B gets twice the new users but has 65% monthly retention against Company A's 85%. B leads at six months with about 5.3M vs 4.2M MAU. After three years, A leads with about 6.6M vs 5.7M. Balfour adds that higher retention also improves acquisition, monetization and payback, so the real gap would be even bigger.

Key points.title: Measure at your product's natural frequency
Key points.detail: Ask whether a user needs to engage daily, weekly or monthly to count as active. Viddy's MAU looked like a hockey stick, but its DAU told the real story, and the app collapsed. For most habit products, measuring monthly hides problems. A daily-study app like OnCourse should measure daily.

Key points.title: Pick one real core action
Key points.detail: Pinterest once used WARC, a weekly active repinner or clicker. Combining two actions let experiments trade one for the other while the metric rose, and could even reward clickbait. It also ignored new content supply. Choose a single action that truly means the user got value.

Key points.title: Revenue retention hides usage problems
Key points.detail: Revenue is the output of engaged users; usage is the input. A subscriber who has stopped using the product still pays until renewal, then churns. Once a paying subscriber has churned, "winning them back is almost impossible." So watch usage retention first, especially before renewals.

Key points.title: Retention is breadth, engagement is depth
Key points.detail: Retention only says whether a user is active in a period, not how active. Shaun Clowes says that at Atlassian, Jira installs where most users were engaged "would practically never churn." More visits per user also drive revenue, like 4 visits a day vs 1. For OnCourse, study days per week is a good depth measure.

Key points.title: The wrong metric makes teams build the wrong things
Key points.detail: A wrong definition both hides problems and points the team at the wrong goals. If you measure monthly when the product should be daily, the team will build "features, notifications, and solutions to encourage monthly engagement." Balfour calls hidden problems plus wrong incentives "silent death."

Title: Mobile App Push Notification Benchmarks for 2025
Creator: Airship
Bottom line: Education app users opt in to push more than almost any other category, and even the busiest education apps send only about one push a day, so OnCourse should prime the opt-in well and spend its budget on relevant daily reminders.
What they did: Airship analysed 2024 data from apps with at least 1,000 active users across 13 verticals (more than 9 billion app users) to benchmark push opt-in rates, direct open rates and monthly pushes per user at the 90th, 50th and 10th percentiles. Each benchmark has Android and iOS charts by vertical, a year-over-year comparison and three practical tips. Customer spotlights cover Hawaiian Airlines, ASDA and TNT Sports.
Results: Education, 90th percentile: Android direct open rate 12.3%, iOS 9.5%; top education apps send 28 pushes per user per month on Android and 24.5 on iOS. On the opt-in chart, Education has the highest iOS bars of any vertical (about 90% at the 90th percentile and about 75% at the median, read from the chart, not printed). Android median opt-in fell from 71.3% (2023) to 59.5% (2024); iOS median held at 49.1% and 49.4%. Apps running onboarding campaigns see opt-in rates "as high as 40% above their category average." "in-app messages drive a 14% average increase in opt-in rates among opted-out users." Personalization gives "a 37% increase on average" in open rates; rich push gives "+22% average lift in direct open rates." Hawaiian Airlines "increased push notification opt-ins by 23%."
Takeaways: Education users opt in to push more than most; Use a soft prompt before the system dialog; Explain push value during onboarding; Re-ask opted-out users with in-app messages; Top education apps send about one push a day; Personalization is the biggest lever on opens; iOS open rates trail Android
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: add a soft prompt that explains what OnCourse will send (daily plan, streak reminder, revision due) before the system permission dialog, and let users explore before asking. Notifications: cap growth pushes near one a day, the level of top education apps (24.5 to 28 per month), and personalize each one with the user's subject or due cards. Today's plan: after a user finishes the plan, show an in-app card to users who declined push, explaining the reminder they are missing, with a link to turn it on.

Key points.title: Education users opt in more than most
Key points.detail: On the iOS opt-in chart, Education has the longest bars of all 14 verticals, around 90% for top apps and around 75% at the median (read from the chart; the report does not print these values). Android Education is also high, around 87% for top apps. Students accept reminders if the value is clear. OnCourse should aim for top-percentile opt-in, not settle for the cross-app median of about 49% on iOS.

Key points.title: Use a soft prompt, then explain value in onboarding
Key points.detail: Airship's first tip is "Don’t Jump the Gun with a Generic Prompt" on first open. Show a soft prompt first and let new users explore so they feel confident when the real prompt comes. Apps running onboarding campaigns that explain push benefits see opt-in rates "as high as 40% above their category average." Hawaiian Airlines raised opt-ins 23% by explaining its new "Ready to Board" alerts.

Key points.title: Re-ask opted-out users inside the app
Key points.detail: A declined prompt is not final. In-app messages drive a 14% average increase in opt-in among opted-out users. The tip is to show contextual prompts when users are most engaged. Android 13 now requires consent too, and Android median opt-in dropped from 71.3% to 59.5% in a year, so re-asking matters more on both platforms.

Key points.title: Top education apps send about one push a day
Key points.detail: At the 90th percentile, education apps send 28 pushes per user per month on Android and 24.5 on iOS, about one a day. Media sends about 293 and sports 221 at the top end. Airship notes the top reasons people opt out are messages that are too frequent or not relevant. A daily study reminder fits the norm for education; more than that needs strong relevance.

Key points.title: Personalization is the biggest lever on opens
Key points.detail: Tailored messages are "the single most important driver" of opens, at a 37% average increase. Segmenting sends lifts direct open rates by 18% to 65%, and rich push adds +22%. Top education apps reach 12.3% direct opens on Android and 9.5% on iOS. Collect preferences like exam date, weak subjects and study time and use them in each push.

Key points.title: iOS open rates trail Android
Key points.detail: Android notifications stay on the lock screen until swiped, while on iOS they vanish from the lock screen as soon as the phone is unlocked. So iOS direct open rates are lower in every vertical. Compare OnCourse's iOS and Android open rates separately, not as one number.

Title: Getting Your Product Into the Habit Zone
Creator: Nir Eyal (Nir and Far)
Bottom line: A product becomes a habit when an action happens often enough and feels useful enough, so make the core action frequent, familiar and clearly valuable.
What they did: Nir Eyal explains habits as actions the brain does without deliberating, and argues that frequency is the main driver, citing a University College London flossing study. He uses Google vs Bing to show habits as a switching cost, and Amazon's in-site price comparison to show how high perceived utility can build a habit for less frequent actions. He ends with the "Habit Zone": plot frequency against perceived utility.
Results: Eyal says Progressive used the price-comparison tactic "to drive over $15 billion of annual insurance sales, up from just $3.4 billion before the tactic was implemented." The UCL flossing study "concluded that the more frequently the new behavior occurred, the stronger the habit." A 2003 study by Trifts and Hubl "demonstrated that consumer's preference for an online retailer increases when they are offered competitive price information."
Takeaways: Habits are actions without deliberation; Frequency builds habit strength; Familiarity is a switching cost; Infrequent actions need high perceived utility; Plot frequency against perceived utility
Ideas for OnCourse: Today's plan: keep the daily task small enough to do every single day, since frequency is what builds the habit, and let extra study be optional. Home: keep the start button and layout in the same place every day so the routine stays automatic, and avoid moving it in redesigns without reason. Practice: show why each set is worth it (for example "high-yield for NEET-PG" or "your weakest topic") to raise perceived utility on days motivation is low.

Key points.title: Habits are actions done without deliberation
Key points.detail: Neuroscientists believe habitual behaviours move to the basal ganglia, which handles actions needing little thought. A habit forms when the brain stops deliberating and repeats what worked before. Nail biting is the example: a stress trigger, a quick relief, and a strong loop. For a study app, the goal is that opening OnCourse each day stops being a decision.

Key points.title: Frequency builds habit strength
Key points.detail: A University College London study followed people trying to start flossing and found that the more often the behaviour happened, the stronger the habit. The same applies to apps: frequent use raises the chance of a habit forming. Daily study is a strong fit if each session is easy enough to repeat.

Key points.title: Familiarity is a switching cost
Key points.detail: Eyal argues Google and Bing give nearly identical results, yet switching feels slower because even small changes in "pixel placement" force users to relearn. Habit, not speed, keeps users loyal. Google's results also improve with use, creating a cycle. For OnCourse, a stable Home layout protects the habit.

Key points.title: Infrequent actions need high perceived utility
Key points.detail: When a behaviour is less frequent, it can still become a habit if users see high value, from gaining pleasure or avoiding pain. Amazon shows competitors' lower prices on its own pages, which costs some sales but makes Amazon the default place to compare. Progressive used the same idea in insurance.

Key points.title: Plot frequency against perceived utility
Key points.detail: The "Habit Zone" is where an action has enough frequency and perceived utility to become the default behaviour. Teams can estimate their product's habit potential by plotting the two. OnCourse's daily practice is high frequency; making its value obvious each day (progress toward the exam) moves it further into the zone.

Title: Google: How can we reduce customer churn?
Creator: Irrational Labs
Bottom line: When results come slowly, frame the start as a fixed multi-month plan and get users to pre-commit to future dates, so early weak results don't feel like failure.
What they did: New AdWords customers who called Google's call centre for the first time were randomly split into two groups. The control got the usual call. The treatment group was told they were in "My 3 Month AdWord Expert Access Plan": reps repeated "three months" often, asked about long-term goals, and booked five future free optimisation calls that the customer pre-committed to on the first call.
Results: "Retention rates for AdWords users in the '3-Month Expert Access Program' group increased by 14 percent."
Takeaways: Slow results cause early churn; Set a long time frame from day one; Pre-commit to future sessions on the first call; Repeat the time frame so it sticks
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: frame the start as "your 90-day NEET-PG plan" with week markers, and say that early mock scores are expected to be low. Today's plan: on day 1, ask the user to pick their next three study slots and show them as booked sessions. Notifications: remind users of the session they committed to, in their own words, not a generic nudge

Key points.title: Slow results cause early churn
Key points.detail: New AdWords users design an ad and then wait to see if it works. Their first ad is often weak, and "without seeing immediate, positive ad results, some new AdWords users were churning in their first two months." Irrational Labs compares this to dieting, where effort does not show up right away. Exam prep is the same: the first mock scores are low, and progress is hard to see for weeks.

Key points.title: Set a long time frame from day one
Key points.detail: The team wanted to move users from a short-term mindset ("I need to see results ASAP!") to a long-term one ("I am investing to get a great return in the future"). They picked three months on purpose, to give a "mental benchmark that advertising requires time to learn." A clear time frame changes what a bad early result means. For OnCourse, a named multi-month plan can make a low first score feel normal, not like proof the app doesn't work.

Key points.title: Pre-commit to future sessions on the first call
Key points.detail: The expert set up a series of five future calls to help optimise the account for free. "On the first call, the customer pre-committed to these future dates." Booking the dates made the long-term approach concrete. OnCourse could ask new users to book their next few study sessions during onboarding.

Key points.title: Repeat the time frame so it sticks
Key points.detail: Reps "repeated the 'three months' phrase often" and asked customers about their long-term advertising goals. The plan had a name and a number, not just a promise of help. That framing, plus the booked calls, lifted retention by 14% against a randomly assigned control group.

Title: Livongo: How can we get people with chronic conditions to better take care of their health?
Creator: Irrational Labs
Bottom line: Framing a free benefit as something the user already owns and only has to claim ("Claim Your Welcome Kit") more than doubled sign-ups compared with "Join the Program".
What they did: Livongo emailed people with diabetes who were eligible for its free program through their employer. The control email said "Join the Program." The test email used "Claim Your Welcome Kit" in the subject line, headline, button and body, using the endowment effect and a hint that others are claiming a limited resource.
Results: Over 15,000 people were emailed. "The 'Claim Your Welcome Kit' condition increased open rates by 25% and click-through rates by 88%." "The experiment increased registration rate within 1 week of the email outreach by more than 120%."
Takeaways: Many people skip benefits they already have for free; Claim framing beats join framing; Change the frame everywhere, not just the button; Small copy changes can double sign-ups
Ideas for OnCourse: Notifications: for lapsed users, write "Your plan for today is ready. Claim it" instead of "Come back and study." Renewal: frame the win-back offer as "your saved progress and 1,200 solved MCQs are waiting", things they already own. Onboarding: after the diagnostic, show a "Your personal study plan" card to claim, not a generic "Start learning" button

Key points.title: Many people skip benefits they already have for free
Key points.detail: Many eligible people get the Livongo program, with a connected glucose meter, unlimited strips and a diabetes educator, at no cost through their employer. Yet "many eligible people fail to sign up, forfeiting potentially life-saving resources." Free is not enough to get people to act. That gap is the same for a free trial or a free daily plan in OnCourse.

Key points.title: Claim framing beats join framing
Key points.detail: The test changed "Join the Program" to "Claim Your Welcome Kit." Irrational Labs based this on the endowment effect (the new framing "creates a sense of ownership") and social proof and scarcity (it implies "other people are claiming this limited resource"). Joining feels like a new commitment, while claiming feels like taking what is already yours.

Key points.title: Change the frame everywhere, not just the button
Key points.detail: The "Claim Your Welcome Kit" framing was used "in the subject line, headline, call-to-action button, and email body." A single consistent message did the work, not just a button label change. When OnCourse tests framing in a notification or win-back email, the headline, body and button should all carry the same idea.

Key points.title: Small copy changes can double sign-ups
Key points.detail: With over 15,000 recipients, the claim email lifted open rates by 25%, click-through by 88% and one-week registration by more than 120%. People in the treatment "signed up ... at more than double the rate of the control group." Livongo then planned to use the theme in direct mail, landing pages and other emails.

Title: How to Boost Product Engagement with the Endowment Effect: A Case Study in Bitcoin
Creator: Irrational Labs
Bottom line: Giving people something tiny that is already theirs (a fraction of a cent of Bitcoin) beat education by 700%, because the feeling of ownership, not the money, drove action.
What they did: Irrational Labs recruited 1,200 Americans who had never owned crypto and split them into groups. One group got 1 Satoshi ($0.0003) placed in a free wallet they only had to open; another was just told about the free wallet; a third got about $1 of Bitcoin. They then measured how many created the wallet, which takes several steps and verifications.
Results: Endowing participants "vastly increased wallet creation (700%!)." "There was no statistical difference between the small and large endowment conditions." The piece also cites Livongo's claim framing increasing registration "by 120%" and One Medical's streamlined sign-up increasing "conversion to bookings by 20%."
Takeaways: When friction can't drop, raise motivation; A near-worthless gift still worked; Ownership feeling, not value, drives action; Free trials, samples and gifts all create endowment; Tell users the product is already theirs to activate
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: put a pre-built "Your Day 1 plan" with the user's name on Home before sign-up finishes, so it already feels theirs. Paywall: give free users one premium mock test already unlocked in their account ("1 Grand Test is yours") rather than a locked preview. Renewal: remind lapsing users of what is theirs (notes, bookmarks, streak history) instead of listing features

Key points.title: When friction can't drop, raise motivation
Key points.detail: The team listed four barriers to crypto adoption: negative mental models, ambiguity aversion, cognitive overload and logistical friction. They say "reducing friction is usually the simplest way to drive behavior change," but opening a wallet was "just hard and hard to change." So the only lever left was motivation. Some OnCourse steps, like a long mock test, can't be made much shorter, so motivation has to carry them.

Key points.title: A near-worthless gift still worked
Key points.detail: One group got 1 Satoshi, about $0.0003, put into a free wallet. Another only learned about the wallet. The endowed group created wallets at a much higher rate, a 700% increase. The team "was skeptical going in" because the amount was "less than 1 cent for some people."

Key points.title: Ownership feeling, not value, drives action
Key points.detail: A third group got about $1 instead of a fraction of a cent, and there was "no statistical difference" between the two. So "people weren't just after the money." The intervention "made people feel like they already owned Bitcoin, even before they had opened a wallet." The article says perceived ownership is what matters, so a small, personal thing given early can be enough.

Key points.title: Free trials, samples and gifts all create endowment
Key points.detail: The piece lists examples: Warby Parker's home try-on, Salesforce's 30-day trial with no card, Tinder's one free Super Like a day, and AR try-ons. It sums up four ways to use the effect: free trials, samples, mental models and gifts ("Hi, here's a $5 credit you can use"). For OnCourse, one unlocked premium test or a personal plan are cheap forms of endowment.

Key points.title: Tell users the product is already theirs to activate
Key points.detail: One of the four tactics is to "remind users that the product is already theirs and they just need to activate, or 'claim ownership'." Livongo did this and saw registrations rise by 120%. In OnCourse, activation copy can say "your plan is ready" rather than "create a plan."

Title: Merit America: Doubling Career Track Course Completion Rates
Creator: Irrational Labs
Bottom line: Learners drop out when a scary payment step is vague and badly timed; tell them early, show a clear timeline, break the task into a checklist and set an early deadline.
What they did: Merit America's training programs cost $0 upfront but need students to sign up for a loan they repay after getting a job. Students froze at the loan details. Irrational Labs changed when payment was introduced (at application, with a pre-commitment), drew a repayment timeline, turned the paperwork into a checklist, cut the information to three key questions and set a deadline before the real one.
Results: "Course completions for the September Data Analytics cohort doubling (100% increase, with 42% completion vs. 21% before)." This is a before/after comparison of cohorts, not a randomised test.
Takeaways: Vague payment info causes decision paralysis; Tell people early and ask them to pre-commit; Show a timeline to make the future concrete; Chunk big tasks into a checklist; Set a deadline before the real deadline
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: add a simple timeline showing what is paid today, when the plan renews and when the exam is, so cost feels concrete. Today's plan: break a long Grand Test or revision block into a checklist of small steps with visible ticks. Design process: for any scary step (payment, mock test), show only three things: what it costs, when, and who it's for

Key points.title: Vague payment info causes decision paralysis
Key points.detail: Students were excited about the program, "then they froze" when they saw the loan. They didn't know when they would repay, if they owed anything now, or what happened if they didn't get a job. The team names the barriers as ambiguity, cost salience, cognitive scarcity and present bias. Loan options were framed as "payment" decisions, which made people think they had to pay upfront.

Key points.title: Tell people early and ask them to pre-commit
Key points.detail: The team moved payment information to the time of application "to prevent situations of distrust in the future." They asked people to "pre-commit to completing the loan application at the time of application." They also gave a dedicated time during the program to do the paperwork and ask questions. For OnCourse, renewal and price details should appear early and clearly, not as a surprise.

Key points.title: Show a timeline to make the future concrete
Key points.detail: They "revisualized the repayment timeline for students at the time of application." The picture made it clear "that actual loan repayment would not begin until after the course was completed." Making the future concrete reduced fear. A paywall timeline (today, trial end, renewal, exam date) can do the same.

Key points.title: Chunk big tasks into a checklist
Key points.detail: People handle information better when it is "chunked" into small pieces. The team built a checklist for the loan application so people could "check off each completed item to make progress salient." They advise asking people "to complete one small step at a time." OnCourse can split big study tasks the same way.

Key points.title: Set a deadline before the real deadline
Key points.detail: They enforced "a deadline that is prior to the actual deadline to encourage early action." They also cut the information down to three questions: how much it costs, when repayment starts and who qualifies. Course completion went from 21% to 42% for the September Data Analytics cohort.

Chapters.summary: Ambiguity and salient cost made students defer the loan decision.

Title: Doubling New Engagement With Lyft’s Women+ Connect Feature
Creator: Irrational Labs
Bottom line: Follow-up reminders more than doubled feature opt-ins, but the message that got the most taps was not the one that drove the most usage, so pick the message for the behaviour you actually want.
What they did: About half of eligible Lyft drivers had not opted in to Women+ Connect. Irrational Labs randomly assigned them to three push message styles (Neutral, Confirm Settings, Concreteness) or a no-message control, and each driver got a series of notifications in their assigned style. They measured opt-ins, taps, driver hours and shift starts.
Results: "The messages increased opt-ins between 83-173% relative to the no message control group." "The Confirm Settings message led to 173% more opt-ins." The Concreteness message had the fewest opt-ins but drivers "started around one additional driving shift per week relative to control." "The average tap rate on the first push was approximately 10%, while the second push got around 7%."
Takeaways: One announcement is not enough; Ask users to check their settings; Concrete when-and-why messages drive real usage; Decide the goal before picking the winner; The second push still works
Ideas for OnCourse: Notifications: test a concrete "when and why" reminder ("Before your 7 pm revision, do 10 Pharmacology MCQs you got wrong") against a generic one, and measure sessions, not just taps. Notifications: send a second reminder to users who ignored a new feature like Flashcards, then stop once they act. Design process: for each message test, pick the success metric (opens vs. study minutes) before choosing the winner

Key points.title: One announcement is not enough
Key points.detail: Women+ Connect was highly requested, yet about half of eligible drivers had not opted in. People get a flood of notifications ("an average of 376 daily notifications"), and drivers also track incentives and demand. All three follow-up messages raised opt-ins by 83–173% over no message. A single launch notice is easy to miss.

Key points.title: Ask users to check their settings
Key points.detail: The Confirm Settings message asked drivers to double-check their settings, to make them "pause and reflect on their choices." The team avoided words like "verify" or "attention!", which feel like fraud warnings. It had the highest tap rate and 173% more opt-ins than control.

Key points.title: Concrete when-and-why messages drive real usage
Key points.detail: The Concreteness message gave "a specific example of the 'when and why' of the feature." It got the fewest taps and opt-ins, but drivers who got it "drove more hours and started around one additional driving shift per week relative to control." The authors think it made drivers "think more concretely about their next ride." For OnCourse, a specific reminder about the next study session may build more habit than a catchy one.

Key points.title: Decide the goal before picking the winner
Key points.detail: There may be "a trade off between attracting attention to a new feature, and getting people to use the feature (and the product overall) in the long term." The best tactic "depends on the overall goal of the messaging campaign." Lyft now sends both the Concreteness and Confirm Settings messages as automated campaigns.

Key points.title: The second push still works
Key points.detail: The first push had a tap rate of about 10% and the second about 7%. The authors recommend sending a follow-up "only to eligible users who haven't acted, and stop once they do," and tracking opt-outs alongside opt-ins. That gives a clear rule for OnCourse reminder cadence.

Title: Creating Habits in Healthcare: How We Helped a Large Pharma Partner Design Better Symptom Tracking for Cancer Patients
Creator: Irrational Labs
Bottom line: Instead of relying on a fixed weekly routine people forget, tie the habit to a natural cue, make the in-the-moment action two questions long, and reward it right away with useful help.
What they did: Irrational Labs redesigned a symptom-tracking app for patients with liver, kidney and breast cancer. Research showed patients forgot symptoms by the weekly report, so they built a two-tier system: a two-question report when a symptom happens, plus a short weekly review that shows recent symptoms up front. Each report returns tips voted on by similar patients, and reminders come from trusted messengers like family or the doctor.
Takeaways: Fixed weekly routines fail when memory fails; Use the natural cue as the reminder; Cut the in-the-moment task to two questions; Reward the action immediately with useful help; Pick a trusted messenger for reminders
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: when a user gets a question wrong, offer a one-tap "add to revision" in the moment, so the weekly review starts pre-filled. Today's plan: show recently weak topics first so the user doesn't have to remember what to revise. Notifications: test reminders framed from a mentor or topper ("Dr. X's tip for today") against app-voice reminders

Key points.title: Fixed weekly routines fail when memory fails
Key points.detail: A routine at the same time each week is often a good strategy, but the diagnosis "highlighted the shortcomings of that approach" for cancer symptoms. Patients suffer "prospective memory failure": they intend to report and then forget, made worse by treatment and stress. By Friday a patient feels fine and only vaguely remembers Tuesday's pain. Busy exam aspirants have the same problem remembering what they got wrong.

Key points.title: Use the natural cue as the reminder
Key points.detail: The team found that "the symptoms themselves are a natural reminder – salient and immediate." They changed the mental model to "Report When You Don’t Feel Well." The habit is tied to a moment that already happens, not to a calendar slot.

Key points.title: Cut the in-the-moment task to two questions
Key points.detail: In-the-moment reporting went "from five or more questions to just two." Patients are often unwell when they notice a symptom, and "a short survey is more likely to get completed when energy is low." The weekly review then shows "previously reported symptoms ... as low-friction selections."

Key points.title: Reward the action immediately with useful help
Key points.detail: "Immediate, positive reinforcement is key to fostering consistent product engagement." After logging a sudden headache, the app quickly suggests relief, like drinking water or a specific medicine. Tips "proposed and voted on by similar others" were more trusted. The advice also changes each time, so it stays useful.

Key points.title: Pick a trusted messenger for reminders
Key points.detail: Using the messenger effect, reminders were designed to come "from someone close to the patient, like a family member, or their doctor." The source makes the task feel more important. The piece reports no numbers, so treat this as a design pattern to test.

Title: Activation metric or motivation detector?
Creator: Retention.Blog (Daphne Tideman, guest post for Jacob Rushfinn)
Bottom line: A good activation metric is the behaviour that splits retention curves for good and that enough users can reach, at the right frequency, and you must check it isn't just spotting people who were already motivated.
What they did: Daphne Tideman, a growth lead for wellness subscription apps, shares a five-step method from her workshop: interview recent subscribers, cohort only the last 13–17 weeks of sign-ups, compare 3–5 candidate behaviours on D7/D30/D90 retention, check the right frequency, and check if timing matters. She then lists checks for survivorship bias and three causes of drop-off: trust, context and value.
Results: "Duolingo: learners who reach a 7-day streak are 3.6x more likely to complete their course." One audited app had "90%+ onboarding completion" but "most users still churned by day two." At one wellness app "the metric that predicted retention was 2 pieces of content in the first 14 days," which beat weekly opens. At one fitness app "four workouts was the sweet spot," but whether by day 7, 8 or 15 "barely mattered."
Takeaways: Onboarding completion is activity, not activation; Use only recent cohorts; Pick the behaviour with lift and volume; Daily isn't always the right frequency; Your magic number may just detect motivation; Drop-off is trust, context or value
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: compare D30 retention for users who did 1, 2, 3 or 5 Today's plan completions in week one, using only the last 13–17 weeks of sign-ups, and keep a holdout for reminders. Today's plan: like Finch, start day 1 with a task the user can tick off at once (e.g. "set your exam date") before the first new MCQ set. Notifications: if timing doesn't matter, nudge gently after two missed days instead of pushing a week-one target

Key points.title: Onboarding completion is activity, not activation
Key points.detail: One app had 90%+ onboarding completion on iOS and Android, but most users still churned by day two. "Activation is the moment value clicks, not the steps completed." A strong metric points to something downstream, like Duolingo's 7-day streak (3.6x more likely to finish a course). For OnCourse, finishing onboarding says little; finishing a first real study session may say more.

Key points.title: Use only recent cohorts
Key points.detail: Old users joined a different product, from different channels, at different prices. At one meditation app, long-time customers used it about once a month, unlike newer subscribers. Tideman cohorts "the last 13 to 17 weeks of signups" and warns against "averaging everyone since launch."

Key points.title: Pick the behaviour with lift and volume
Key points.detail: Split users into did vs didn't for 3–5 behaviours and compare D7, D30 and D90. Look for the one that "splits the curve, and the gap never closes," because some gaps close later. It also needs volume: for a friendship app, more friends was always better, but "five friends in a week" was where lift was real and enough people could reach it.

Key points.title: Daily isn't always the right frequency
Key points.detail: "Most apps are not daily-habit apps, and that's okay." At one wellness app, 2 pieces of content in the first 14 days predicted retention better than weekly opens. At a fitness app, four workouts mattered but the day didn't, so they stopped pushing a week-one target and instead "nudg[ed] them back, gently" after two days without a workout. Also check which days people act: Monday was the top day to log a workout.

Key points.title: Your magic number may just detect motivation
Key points.detail: Motivated users do everything more, so "your magic number might just be a motivation detector." Keep a holdout group for lifecycle emails, ask if the metric is gameable, and sometimes test removing something. One founder changed "completes 2 coaching sessions" to "starts 1 session with personal context set, within 7 days."

Key points.title: Drop-off is trust, context or value
Key points.detail: Drop-off before activation is usually trust (asking for data or payment before any win), context (users don't get what it is) or value (they never felt it). Finch's starter plan is mostly things you've already done, like brushing your teeth, so you get an "oh, I'm already doing this" win first. Ask: "what's the version of 'a goal you've already achieved' in session one?"

Title: Life of a birb
Creator: Retention.Blog (Jacob Rushfinn)
Bottom line: Finch hooks users on screen one with play instead of forms, pre-fills easy goals so everyone reaches the reward loop on day one, and uses a real-time 8-hour adventure to pull users back the same day.
What they did: Jacob Rushfinn walks through Finch's onboarding from January 2024 to January 2026. Finch starts by having you pick a colour and hatch a bird, lets you earn points while answering questions, adds a 'Starter plan' after a loading screen, splits its paywall into several screens, and adds streaks. It now auto-fills goals on Home so a few taps earn enough energy to send the bird on an adventure.
Results: Finch made "$30M+ last year" (context, not a test result). The bird is "gone for 8 hours of real time," which builds "an instant habit loop."
Takeaways: Hook on screen one with play, not forms; Personalise the pet, not the person; Let users earn rewards during onboarding; Close the loop with a generated plan; Pre-fill easy goals to solve cold start; A real-time timer pulls users back the same day
Ideas for OnCourse: Home: never land a new user on an empty plan; pre-fill Today's plan with 3 short, easy tasks so they hit the first reward in minutes. Onboarding: give a small reward (XP or a badge) for answering setup questions, so the first minutes feel like the real app. Today's plan: after the first set, start a timed unlock (e.g. "your revision set unlocks in 4 hours") to create a second visit on day one

Key points.title: Hook on screen one with play, not forms
Key points.detail: "You have some of the highest drop off rates on your first screen." Finch's first screens are pick a colour and hatch a bird, with a hatching animation. It asks for no user info, just "a fun and easy interaction, that inserts a bit of personalization." OnCourse's first screen could be a single fun choice instead of a form.

Key points.title: Personalise the pet, not the person
Key points.detail: You then pick your bird's gender, name and trait. Finch is "building investment in the product, but without you sharing any information on yourself." A "Shuffle" button gives preset names so nobody gets stuck on a text field.

Key points.title: Let users earn rewards during onboarding
Key points.detail: Answering a question earns points and rainbow stones. "Your onboarding should give people a feeling of what the real product will be like," and this simulates earning things just like the real app. Later versions added questions about the user; Jacob thinks the sunk cost of answering "make[s] people more committed once they see the paywall."

Key points.title: Close the loop with a generated plan
Key points.detail: Finch added a loading screen and a "Starter plan." It "makes you feel like they took into account everything you shared," though the plans are "pretty much the same for everyone." The paywall became multi-screen to repeat "FREE", the trial reminder and the discount: "If it's important, don't be afraid to say it twice."

Key points.title: Pre-fill easy goals to solve cold start
Key points.detail: Before, users picked their own goals. If they picked too few, they couldn't earn enough energy and might never reach the "Send your Finch on an adventure" moment. Now Finch auto-fills many goals, so "you tap a few times, and you're pretty much guaranteed to reach that 'Aha' moment." OnCourse's Today's plan should never start empty.

Key points.title: A real-time timer pulls users back the same day
Key points.detail: The bird goes on an adventure for 8 hours of real time, and "you have to come back into the app to see what they got." This forces several opens on day one and builds "an instant habit loop." Finch also added streaks after the paywall.

Title: One question to increase retention
Creator: Retention.Blog (Jacob Rushfinn)
Bottom line: Ask for notifications right after the user commits to a goal or streak and frame the choice as which reminders to get, because saying no would contradict what they just committed to.
What they did: Jacob Rushfinn compares how 8 top apps ask for push and other permissions. Headway asks for a daily goal, then an X-day streak commitment, then a preferred time, then shows toggles for notification types. Flo frames the prompt as better predictions, Opal builds excitement first, RISE explains all data use in one flow, and Impulse and JustFit just show the system prompt right away.
Results: Jacob "recently saw" showing the push prompt immediately "increase the opt-in rate by 44%. It was low initially." His benchmarks for opt-in: "Good: 40-50%", "Great: 50-65%", "Wonderful: 65%+", measured on all new installs, not just users who reach the prompt.
Takeaways: Commit first, then ask for notifications; Ask which reminders, not whether; Sell the value, not the notification; Build excitement before a big ask; Showing the prompt right away can work too; Measure opt-in on all installs
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: ask for daily question goal, then "commit to a 7-day streak", then "what time do you study?", then show toggles for reminder types (daily plan, streak saver, weekly mock) before the system prompt. Notifications: frame the permission as "so we can save your streak and tell you when your mock results are ready." Design process: track opt-in as a share of all new installs

Key points.title: Commit first, then ask for notifications
Key points.detail: Headway's opt-in is tied to choosing a daily goal in minutes, then committing "to growing with an X-day streak." Only then does it ask about notifications. This uses cognitive dissonance: "If you said you wanted to commit to your goal, but you don't want notifications to stay on track, then do you really want to commit?" Imprint uses a simpler version of the same order.

Key points.title: Ask which reminders, not whether
Key points.detail: Headway asks "When do you like to find out about new ideas" instead of picking a time. It then shows toggles for different notification types. This "switches the choice away from, 'Should I turn on notifications?' to 'Which notifications should I turn on?'"

Key points.title: Sell the value, not the notification
Key points.detail: Flo's request "is not about the notifications. It's about making better predictions for you." Flo starts calculating cycle predictions, builds suspense, then says it needs more data. This leans on reciprocity: Flo promises to do something for you first.

Key points.title: Build excitement before a big ask
Key points.detail: Opal asks for Screen Time access right after showing how much time it can give back. It also reassures that data won't leave the phone. RISE explains all its data needs in one flow and asks for push last, because it's the lowest-friction request.

Key points.title: Showing the prompt right away can work too
Key points.detail: Impulse and JustFit show the system prompt immediately, and Jacob calls this "an underrated tactic": people are used to tapping Allow. He saw it lift opt-in by 44% from a low base. Measure opt-in across all new installs, with 40–50% good and 65%+ wonderful.

Title: 2nd Offers and Re-engagement
Creator: Retention.Blog (Jacob Rushfinn)
Bottom line: Returning users show intent, so greet them with a 'welcome back' flow, a 'why didn't you buy?' survey or a more detailed paywall, and use discounts as one option, not the only one.
What they did: Jacob Rushfinn reopened 16 apps after not paying or after a period of inactivity and recorded what each showed. Examples: Headway's "Why?" survey after a declined paywall, Flo's detailed value paywall and 365-day celebration, Zing's staged tooltips, Fabulous and Finch's welcome-back flows, Elevate's widget push, and Calm's "special gift" spinner.
Results: No test results. The post notes the opportunity is "the 90%+ of users who don't convert immediately."
Takeaways: Most users don't buy at the first paywall; Ask why before you discount; Returning users want more detail, not less; Welcome them back and ask what path they want; Stage tooltips instead of stacking them; Keep offers fresh with in-app messages
Ideas for OnCourse: Renewal: after a declined renewal, ask "What stopped you?" (price, exam date passed, not enough time) and answer each reason before showing any discount. Home: for users back after 7+ days, show a welcome-back card that asks which exam and date they're aiming for now, then rebuilds Today's plan. Home: show one tooltip at a time, and only show the next if the user doesn't engage

Key points.title: Most users don't buy at the first paywall
Key points.detail: The first paywall matters most, but there is "still an opportunity to get the 90%+ of users who don't convert immediately." The goal is a product good enough that people "who don't pay immediately have a reason to come back." Jacob looked at 16 apps to see what they do next.

Key points.title: Ask why before you discount
Key points.detail: If you don't convert at the first paywall, Headway shows "a mini-survey that asks you 'Why?' and then tries to address those needs." It is "an attempt to convert more users without a discount." Only then does it fall back to discount offers. MyFitnessPal rarely discounts and reframes its 30-day trial as a "free premium pass."

Key points.title: Returning users want more detail, not less
Key points.detail: After inactivity, Flo shows a paywall that explains each value prop "in decent detail." Returning users "are likely more familiar with the product, and coming back is a decent signal of intent, so don't be afraid to give more detail." Flo also celebrates "365 days since I first opened the app."

Key points.title: Welcome them back and ask what path they want
Key points.detail: "Fabulous welcomes me back into the app after a period of inactivity to ask me what path I want to take." Finch acknowledges you've been gone and runs a mini re-engagement flow, plus monthly live-ops themes. Ahead puts expired-trial users through a simplified onboarding with goal-personalised paywall titles.

Key points.title: Stage tooltips instead of stacking them
Key points.detail: Zing shows a "What's new" message, then tooltips one at a time. "The 2nd tooltip only appeared after Zing saw I wasn't engaging." Jacob's rule: "Don't overwhelm users with messages, but also don't let them get lost." Zing also shows a "Retry" modal if a purchase fails.

Key points.title: Keep offers fresh with in-app messages
Key points.detail: LingoKids and Ladder use in-app messages from their CRM to link to the paywall or App Store offer codes. This lets them change "the creative and copy so users can see the same offer many times without feeling 'stale'." Elevate skips discounts and pushes its widget instead, and Calm uses a "special gift" spinner that lands on a free premium piece.

Title: Win back more users with re-onboarding
Creator: Retention.Blog (Jacob Rushfinn)
Bottom line: Treat a returning user like a friend you haven't seen in a while: acknowledge the gap, show what's new, and for the biggest win, run a short re-onboarding that asks why they stopped and points them to one feature.
What they did: Jacob Rushfinn lays out three levels of re-onboarding. Level one is a "Welcome back!" in-app message after 20–30+ days away (and on reinstall). Level two adds what's new, level two and a half is a video of new features (as Duolingo did after a redesign), and level three is a full returning-user flow, like Fabulous's.
Takeaways: Acknowledge the gap; Start with a simple welcome-back message; Show what's new to signal progress; Run a full returning-user flow; Ask why they stopped and recommend one feature
Ideas for OnCourse: Home: after 20+ days away (or a reinstall), show "Welcome back" with the days left to their exam and a one-tap "Restart with an easy set." Onboarding: build a returning-user flow that asks "What got in the way?" (time, motivation, exam moved), then suggests one feature, like a shorter daily plan. Notifications: send an email on the first app open after a long gap

Key points.title: Acknowledge the gap
Key points.detail: "If you haven't seen a friend in a year, do you act like you saw them yesterday? No, you acknowledge it's been a while." Users who return after a long time won't remember everything from onboarding. Jacob calls the return "a strong positive signal" of an unmet need, and a "second chance."

Key points.title: Start with a simple welcome-back message
Key points.detail: Level one: show a "Welcome back!" in-app message if users "haven't used your app in 20-30+ days." You can also trigger an email on the app open event, and "make sure to do this for reinstalls too." It's "fast and easy to get live if you have a decent CRM tool."

Key points.title: Show what's new to signal progress
Key points.detail: Level two adds new features or tooltips, which "conveys value since it shows you're constantly improving." Level two and a half is a video of new features. Duolingo did this after a redesign so returning users "aren't confused which in turn helps retention."

Key points.title: Run a full returning-user flow
Key points.detail: Level three is "a full returning user flow that asks questions about their goals and experience similar to onboarding." Contextualise it for a returning user, and lead them to features that "lead to better retention."

Key points.title: Ask why they stopped and recommend one feature
Key points.detail: Fabulous has "one of the best" re-onboarding flows. It opens with "Your story isn't finished…", asks why they stopped their habit, asks questions to understand how to help, and "recommends a specific feature based on the responses." For OnCourse, a lapsed aspirant could get a reason-based restart.

Title: Why retention is so hard for new tech products
Creator: Andrew Chen
Bottom line: Retention decays at a predictable rate and is very hard to win back, so the first days matter most, and notifications or small A/B tests can't rescue a product people don't value.
What they did: Andrew Chen, a16z partner and former Uber growth lead, shares nine patterns from 15+ years of looking at retention curves. They include: you can't fix bad retention with notifications, retention halves from D1 to D7 and again to D30, retention depends on the category's natural frequency, churn is asymmetric, and early users are the best users.
Results: Typical curve: "Whatever the D1, it drops by 50% on D7. Whatever the D7, it drops by another 50% at D30." "Most products churn 90% or more in the first 30 days." D1 of 40% aiming for 50% "is great and potentially workable"; D1 of 10% means "you probably just have built something that nobody wants." He sees "a 50% D30" about "once every couple years."
Takeaways: Notifications won't fix bad retention; Retention halves at a predictable rate; Fixing retention takes a big home-screen change; Category sets the natural frequency; Churn is asymmetric; Later users retain worse
Ideas for OnCourse: Home: if D1 is weak, test a big change (e.g. a structured step-by-step Today's plan instead of a library of content), not small copy tweaks. Notifications: don't use more reminders to fix weak early retention; spend the effort on the first session and first week. Design process: track retention by acquisition channel and region, since later and paid users will look worse than early organic ones

Key points.title: Notifications won't fix bad retention
Key points.detail: "No, adding more notifications will not fix your retention curve. You can't A/B test your way to good retention." Going from 40% to 50% D1 is workable, but at 10% D1 "all the local optimizations around A/B tests and notifications aren't actually enough." Reminders help a product people already value, but can't replace it.

Key points.title: Retention halves at a predictable rate
Key points.detail: Many curves look like this: D1 drops by 50% at D7, and D7 drops by another 50% at D30. "What you never see is a curve that starts high, then goes low, then becomes high again." So "you need to start strong in order to end strong." For OnCourse, the first day and first week deserve most of the design effort.

Key points.title: Fixing retention takes a big home-screen change
Key points.detail: "The type of pivot that fixes retention involves a complete new redesign of the app's home screen." His example: "If it looks like a feed, maybe it needs to be a structured step-by-step flow." The bigger the change, "the better, in order to have a chance at changing retention."

Key points.title: Category sets the natural frequency
Key points.detail: "There's nature, and there's nurture." Some products are naturally daily, others weekly or rare, and "it's just hard to fight nature." Exam prep has a natural daily rhythm in the months before the exam, which helps OnCourse, but also a natural end when the exam is over.

Key points.title: Churn is asymmetric
Key points.detail: "It's incredibly easy to churn users," and "most products churn 90% or more in the first 30 days." Winning back a user who quit is so hard it's "often easier to simply try to acquire a new user." Discount-led resurrection "tends to be extremely painful and expensive"; what works better is existing users bringing others back through normal use, like a coworker inviting you.

Key points.title: Later users retain worse
Key points.detail: "The best users show up early," often by word of mouth. As you add Android, international and paid users, "all of your metrics get worse." The question becomes whether these users are still valuable and whether you keep the early "Golden Cohort."

Title: Family Values
Creator: Benji Taylor
Bottom line: Family feels simple and calm because it shows one thing at a time in trays, connects every screen with motion, and saves its biggest delight for the features people use least.
What they did: Benji Taylor explains the three principles behind the Family crypto wallet: simplicity, fluidity and delight. Simplicity comes from a "dynamic tray system" that shows one piece of content or one action per tray. Fluidity comes from linking every screen with motion, down to chevrons and button labels that morph. Delight is placed on purpose, with more of it on rare features and only small touches on daily ones.
Takeaways: Show one piece of content per tray; Vary tray height so each step is clearly new; Motion should map where you came from; Morph labels to flag an important step; Removing motion makes flows feel like whiplash; Delight goes up as feature use goes down
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: when the user taps "Submit", morph the button label into "Next question" instead of swapping it, so the change of step is visible. Today's plan: open plan details, streak freezes and warnings in a tray from the bottom, one item per tray, each tray a different height. Progress & streaks: save the big celebration for rare moments (finishing a full mock test, a 30-day streak), and keep daily MCQ feedback small and quick

Key points.title: Show one piece of content per tray
Key points.detail: Family's trays are small sheets that "expand, contract, and adapt" to the user's actions. Each tray holds "a singular piece of content" or "a primary action", has a title and an icon that closes it or goes back. Trays are used for short, transient steps like confirmations and warnings, and they keep the screen behind them in view. For OnCourse, short steps like "Use a streak freeze?" or "Why this answer?" can live in a tray instead of a new screen.

Key points.title: Vary tray height so each step is clearly new
Key points.detail: "Each subsequent tray is designed to vary in height" so that moving to the next step is unmistakable. The team sometimes rewrote content or tweaked a design just to make the height change visible. This is a cheap trick that tells users something changed without any extra text.

Key points.title: Motion should map where you came from
Key points.detail: Switching tabs in Family slides left or right in the direction of the tab you tapped: "We fly instead of teleport." A chevron morphs into a different icon as you move through steps, and wallet cards travel between screens instead of being duplicated. Benji's rule is that if a component stays on screen in the next step, it should stay the same object and not re-appear.

Key points.title: Morph labels to flag an important step
Key points.detail: Family animates "Continue" into "Confirm" by keeping the shared letters ("Con") and morphing the rest. A static swap "could leave the user unaware of the significant step they're about to take". The same approach updates numbers and counts on buttons as the user adds wallets. OnCourse could use this when a button moves from "Next" to "Submit test".

Key points.title: Removing motion makes flows feel like whiplash
Key points.detail: Benji built versions of Family with the motion removed to compare. Without the animation, the swap approval tray "loses" its connection to the swap screen, and wallet grouping makes the outcome "much less clear". He calls the static version "digital whiplash". After a send, a spinner moves into the bottom tab to show where the pending transaction now lives.

Key points.title: Delight goes up as feature use goes down
Key points.detail: Benji's "Delight-Impact Curve" says "the potential for delight increases as the frequency of feature usage decreases." Rare moments like creating a wallet get a full interactive animation, and backing up a wallet ends with confetti. The daily send flow only gets small touches, like commas that shift as you type. He also says every part of the app must get the same polish, or it is like "a fancy restaurant" with "a dirty bathroom".

Title: Honkish
Creator: Benji Taylor
Bottom line: Honk shows how presence, sound, haptics, colour and small physical details can make simple actions feel alive, and when deliberate friction is worth adding.
What they did: Benji Taylor looks back at Honk, a real-time messaging app with no send button and no chat history. The team built features around showing that a friend is present: avatar borders that fill when they arrive, a dashed outline when they look away, and reactions placed exactly where you tap with a shared haptic. They also added custom sounds and typefaces, colour-coded trays and deliberate pauses like signing your name before chatting with strangers.
Results: Before it was shut down, Honk "facilitated over 2.6 billion characters typed, 170 million Honks sent, and hundreds of millions of images, audio, and videos exchanged." Asking users to sign their name before random chats "noticeably reduced bad behaviour" (no number given).
Takeaways: Make presence visible with motion and sound; Put feedback exactly where the finger landed; Small physical details make actions feel like toys; Use background colour to signal how serious an action is; Add friction on purpose where it builds accountability; Custom sound and type give an app its voice
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: show the correct-answer feedback right where the user tapped (a small ring and a light haptic on the chosen option) instead of a generic banner. Renewal: tint the cancel or downgrade tray background red, the way Honk did for destructive actions. Progress & streaks: when the user writes a daily commitment on the streak screen, ask them to type or sign their name to add a sense of commitment

Key points.title: Make presence visible with motion and sound
Key points.detail: When a friend entered a chat, "a border around their avatar filled up" with a sound. When they left, a burst of waving emojis appeared. If they looked elsewhere in the app, their avatar became a dashed outline to show partial attention. These details created a "snap-to-attention" effect and made the friend feel present.

Key points.title: Put feedback exactly where the finger landed
Key points.detail: Double-tapping a bubble placed a heart "exactly where you tapped", with a faint animated circle and "a simultaneous haptic felt by both users." The team stored the spot as relative coordinates (for example "10% X, 20% Y") so it matched on every screen size. For OnCourse, feedback on an answer should start from the option the user tapped.

Key points.title: Small physical details make actions feel like toys
Key points.detail: As you typed, a tiny trash can slowly filled, "shaking when the chat bubble was full, and emptying when cleared." Emojis flew across the screen and collided using "a tiny physics engine", which users turned into "emoji battles". In-app notifications had animated borders counting down how long they would stay visible.

Key points.title: Use background colour to signal how serious an action is
Key points.detail: "Destructive actions, like deleting your account, turned the background red, emphasising the seriousness of the action." The colour coding carried through to chat themes too. This is a simple way to make risky steps feel different from normal steps.

Key points.title: Add friction on purpose where it builds accountability
Key points.detail: Before chatting with strangers, users signed their name on screen. "It wasn't legally binding", but it "noticeably reduced bad behaviour in random chats by making users pause." Finding new people used a slot-machine animation to create anticipation. Not every moment needs to be fast.

Key points.title: Custom sound and type give an app its voice
Key points.detail: Honk had two custom typefaces: Honk Sans for UI and Honk Chat only for message bubbles. A sound designer composed audio "to precisely match the timing of each interaction", often after the feature was designed. Benji's footnote also warns to record high-quality videos of features while they are live, as it is hard to do later.

Title: Designing Depth
Creator: Rauno Freiberg
Bottom line: Interfaces feel deeper and clearer when you blur what is behind, sequence motion in steps near the trigger, and stagger similar items instead of moving everything at once.
What they did: Rauno Freiberg takes the film idea of "dirtying the frame" and applies it to UI. He breaks down iOS interactions frame by frame: the Home Screen swipe-down to Search in four states, the tap version where the order is reversed, staggered app icons on unlock, and the iPad Dock sliding away. He shows how blur, delays and stagger signal which layer is active and where the user's input landed.
Takeaways: Blur the backdrop to show only the overlay is active; Choreograph motion as a sequence of states; Start the motion near where the user acted; Stagger similar items so updates feel natural; What moves vs what blurs tells you what stays usable
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: when the explanation sheet opens after an answer, blur and dim the question behind it so only the sheet looks tappable. Home: when today's plan cards load, fade them in with a small stagger instead of all at once. Flashcards: when a card flips or a new deck opens, start the motion near the user's finger and delay secondary elements (counts, buttons) slightly

Key points.title: Blur the backdrop to show only the overlay is active
Key points.detail: Dimming or blurring the backdrop when an overlay opens simulates depth of field. On the iOS Home Screen, a context menu "would feel fairly awkward" without de-emphasis, and it would wrongly suggest the apps behind are still tappable. Only the menu is actionable, and tapping the backdrop closes it.

Key points.title: Choreograph motion as a sequence of states
Key points.detail: Rauno splits the Home Screen swipe-down into 4 states. The Home Screen blurs first, then Siri suggestions appear, then the Search field turns into an input while the keyboard peeks in, and the keyboard fully expands on release. The suggestions are "intentionally delayed" so layers don't overlap oddly, and the keyboard is delayed so it doesn't compete with them.

Key points.title: Start the motion near where the user acted
Key points.detail: When Search opens by tapping the button at the bottom, the order flips. The button turns into an input immediately, and the suggestions follow after a slight delay. Prioritising the transition near the trigger "promptly communicate[s] that the interface understood you." For a swipe from the top, feedback starts at the top.

Key points.title: Stagger similar items so updates feel natural
Key points.detail: OpenAI "staggers the fade in of loaded content in a grid layout." The interface does not feel slower, and users are not left wondering how many items changed. iOS also staggers app icons on unlock, and Control Centre rows use "slightly staggered spring" settings for rubber banding.

Key points.title: What moves vs what blurs tells you what stays usable
Key points.detail: On iPad, swiping to Today View blurs the Home Screen but the Dock slides off at full opacity. This says the Dock "retains interactivity and can be brought back with a swipe." When Control Centre opens, the Dock is blurred with the Home Screen instead, because it is no longer usable.
