Title: Animate with springs (WWDC23)
Creator: Apple (Jacob)
Bottom line: Use springs with a duration and a bounce of 0 by default, add up to about 15–30% bounce for playful or gesture-driven moments, and avoid going above about 0.4.
What they did: Jacob from Apple explains why springs are the best default for UI animation. He compares ease-in-out, linear and spring curves on a toggle knob, shows how springs keep the finger's velocity when a gesture ends, and introduces a simpler way to set springs with two values: duration and bounce. He ends with practical guidance on picking values.
Takeaways: Avoid linear motion except for spinners; Springs keep the finger's speed after a gesture; Set springs with duration and bounce, not physics; A spring doesn't need to bounce; Pick duration first, then add bounce carefully; Different properties can finish at different times
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: write motion specs for OnCourse as spring duration and bounce (for example 0.35s, bounce 0) instead of bezier curves, and use the same values in React Native Reanimated. Flashcards: when the user lets go of a swiped card, use a spring that keeps the swipe's speed so the card flies off naturally. Progress & streaks: allow a small bounce (around 15%) only on celebratory elements like the streak flame, and keep everyday transitions at bounce 0

Key points.title: Avoid linear motion except for spinners
Key points.detail: Linear animation has "a sharp corner and a jump in velocity" at start and end. Apple says it can be useful for "a repeating spinning indicator", but be cautious with it elsewhere, "especially for movement". Good animation keeps both position and velocity continuous.

Key points.title: Springs keep the finger's speed after a gesture
Key points.detail: When you throw a toggle knob, an ease-in-out animation "jerks to a halt as the gesture ends" because a fixed curve can't take an initial velocity. A spring "can start with any initial velocity", so the animation "picks up right where the gesture ends." Springs also stay smooth when an animation is interrupted and retargeted mid-way.

Key points.title: Set springs with duration and bounce, not physics
Key points.detail: Mass, stiffness and damping are hard to reason about. Apple now uses "just 2 parameters: duration and bounce" across its design and engineering. Bounce above 0 overshoots (bouncy), 0 gives a smooth long tail (smooth), and negative values are "flattened".

Key points.title: A spring doesn't need to bounce
Key points.detail: "A spring animation doesn't only mean a bouncy animation." Non-bouncy springs "are used in animations all over iOS." What makes them feel natural is the way they "very slowly and gradually" come to rest, with no single moment where the object abruptly stops.

Key points.title: Pick duration first, then add bounce carefully
Key points.detail: Start with a duration that gives the pacing you want, then tune bounce. "A small bounce, like around 15%" feels brisk, around 30% feels noticeably bouncy, and you "should be cautious about using values higher than around 0.4" for UI. When unsure, "use a spring with bounce 0". Add bounce for playful moments or the end of a gesture, and keep values consistent with the app's character.

Key points.title: Different properties can finish at different times
Key points.detail: With springs, properties don't all stop together, and that is fine because real objects slow down at their own pace. Apple's app launch animation uses "different springs, different start times, and different end times" to feel natural.

Title: The details of UI typography (WWDC20)
Creator: Apple (Loïc Sander and Jiang)
Bottom line: Small text needs more letter spacing and big text needs less, line height should change with the context, and custom fonts should still scale with the user's text size.
What they did: An Apple type designer explains optical sizes, tracking and leading, and why SF Pro's spacing changes with point size. A second speaker shows text styles, emphasized (bolder) variants, tight and loose leading, rounded and serif designs, and how to make custom fonts and spacing scale with Dynamic Type.
Results: Tight leading takes the 22 pt body line height down to 20 pt; loose leading takes it up to 24 pt. In iOS and macOS the change is 2 points; on watchOS it is 1 point. SF Pro now "transitions from Text to Display between 17 and 28 points."
Takeaways: Small text needs more space between letters; Use size-specific tracking, never one value; Let strings tighten before you truncate; Change leading to match how much text there is; Use a bolder weight of the same style for emphasis; Custom fonts and spacing should scale with text size
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: give long explanation text loose leading (body 17/24) and keep tight leading only for short, one- or two-line option labels. Design process: add a tracking value to each OnCourse text style token (tighter for large headings, looser for captions) instead of one letter-spacing for all sizes. Lessons: make custom fonts and the padding around paragraphs scale with the phone's text size setting

Key points.title: Small text needs more space between letters
Key points.detail: "When type becomes smaller, letters tend to need more space between them, so that the eye can more easily tell them apart." SF was first split into SF Text (below 20 points) and SF Display (20 points and above). Now the variable SF Pro moves smoothly from Text to Display "between 17 and 28 points".

Key points.title: Use size-specific tracking, never one value
Key points.detail: Apple publishes tracking tables because "if you want to accurately reproduce a system font's behavior, you need to know how much tracking to apply for each point size." If you add custom tracking, "it should be size specific", or what works for small sizes "may not look good on large sizes."

Key points.title: Let strings tighten before you truncate
Key points.detail: For a string that doesn't fit, the best fix is to let the system tighten it using a tight tracking table, within a range "reasonable for legibility." Use the tracking API, not kerning, since tracking also breaks apart ligatures. "There is such a thing as too much tracking", and then it is better to truncate.

Key points.title: Change leading to match how much text there is
Key points.detail: Tight leading suits dense areas like the Fitness app. Loose leading suits long reading, like Maps. In the demo, a long body paragraph went from 22 pt to 20 pt line height, which was "too tight for such a long paragraph", then to 24 pt, which looked "much better". Apple also adds leading for Arabic and other tall scripts.

Key points.title: Use a bolder weight of the same style for emphasis
Key points.detail: "Emphasized text styles" keep the size of a text style but use a heavier weight. Calendar uses them for year and month headers, and Mail for its large title. The actual weight can be medium, semibold, bold or heavy, depending on the style.

Key points.title: Custom fonts and spacing should scale with text size
Key points.detail: Custom fonts can follow Dynamic Type by scaling "relative to" a text style, and spacing can scale too. The demo set a 20-point padding around body text that grows with the text size "instead of a fixed size."

Title: Typography
Creator: Apple Human Interface Guidelines
Bottom line: On iPhone, use 17 pt as the default text size and 11 pt as the minimum, avoid light weights, build hierarchy from a few text styles, and test every screen at the largest text sizes.
What they did: Apple's typography guidelines give default and minimum sizes for each platform, the full table of iOS text styles at every Dynamic Type size, and tracking values for SF Pro. They explain how to show hierarchy with weight, size and colour, when to change leading, and how layouts should adapt when people turn text size up.
Results: iOS and iPadOS: default size "17 pt", minimum "11 pt". Default (Large) iOS text styles: Large Title 34/41, Title 1 28/34, Title 2 22/28, Title 3 20/25, Headline 17/22 semibold, Body 17/22, Callout 16/21, Subhead 15/20, Footnote 13/18, Caption 1 12/16, Caption 2 11/13 (size/leading in points).
Takeaways: Default 17 pt, minimum 11 pt on iPhone; Avoid Ultralight, Thin and Light weights; Build hierarchy from few typefaces and set styles; Use loose leading for long text, never tight for 3+ lines; Adapt the layout at large text sizes; Spacing between letters changes with size
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: set question and option text at 17 pt or more, and make sure no label (timers, tags, counts) drops below 11 pt. Lessons: at the largest accessibility text sizes, stack secondary items (time, tags) under the title instead of beside it, and avoid truncating explanation text. Design process: map OnCourse's type tokens to the iOS text styles so size, weight and line height stay consistent

Key points.title: Default 17 pt, minimum 11 pt on iPhone
Key points.detail: Apple's table gives iOS and iPadOS a default size of 17 pt and a minimum of 11 pt. If a custom font is thin, "aim for larger than the recommended sizes". For OnCourse, MCQ text and options should sit at body size or above.

Key points.title: Avoid Ultralight, Thin and Light weights
Key points.detail: "In general, avoid light font weights." Prefer Regular, Medium, Semibold or Bold, because thin weights "can be difficult to see, especially when text is small."

Key points.title: Build hierarchy from few typefaces and set styles
Key points.detail: Use weight, size and colour to show what matters, and "minimize the number of typefaces you use." Text styles bundle weight, size and leading, and they scale together when people change text size. Body is 17/22 and Headline is 17/22 semibold, so headline and body differ by weight, not size.

Key points.title: Use loose leading for long text, never tight for 3+ lines
Key points.detail: Loose leading in wide columns or long passages helps people "keep their place while moving from one line to the next." Tight leading can fit text in constrained rows, but "if you need to display three or more lines of text, avoid tight leading even in areas where height is limited."

Key points.title: Adapt the layout at large text sizes
Key points.detail: Test at the largest accessibility sizes. Keep truncation to a minimum, and "consider using a stacked layout where text appears above secondary items" when inline items crowd text. Keep primary elements at the top so people don't lose them. Only grow the content people care about, not every label.

Key points.title: Spacing between letters changes with size
Key points.detail: Apple publishes tracking values for SF Pro at every size. For example, 11 pt uses +6 (1/1000 em), 17 pt uses -26, and 28 pt uses +14. Mockups with the system font may need these values to match the real app.

Title: Practice audio haptic design (WWDC21)
Creator: Apple (Camille Moussette)
Bottom line: Haptics and sound work when the cause is obvious, the haptic matches the look and sound, and they are saved for moments that matter.
What they did: An Apple designer walks through adding haptics and sound to a small demo game, HapticRicochet. She sets out three principles (causality, harmony and utility), then fixes a 500 ms shield animation whose haptic and sound did not match by combining the continuous haptic from one asset with the sound from another. She also makes a rolling texture loop and matches the visual dot pattern to the haptic density.
Takeaways: Causality: make it obvious what caused the feedback; Harmony: it should feel the way it looks and sounds; Utility: don't add feedback just because you can; Match the haptic's shape to the sound's shape; Match visual detail to haptic detail
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: play one light haptic on a correct answer and a different, firmer one on a wrong answer, each tied exactly to the option's colour change. Progress & streaks: let the streak-extended animation, sound and haptic share the same rhythm (for example one rising haptic with a rising sound), not three separate effects. Design process: list every haptic in the app and remove any that does not mark a meaningful moment

Key points.title: Causality: make it obvious what caused the feedback
Key points.detail: "For feedback to be useful, it must be obvious what caused it." The ball's haptic plays as it hits the wall. The rolling texture haptic only plays when the dotted background is visible, so people understand the grid caused it.

Key points.title: Harmony: it should feel the way it looks and sounds
Key points.detail: Senses work best together. "A small ball should feel small and sound small. A large ball ought to sound and feel heavier." The iOS Flashlight button is the example: animation, sound and haptic in one "clear, precise, and succinct" moment.

Key points.title: Utility: don't add feedback just because you can
Key points.detail: "Don't add feedback just because you can. It can quickly become overwhelming and unpleasant." Reserve haptics and audio "for significant moments in your app", like the ball growing.

Key points.title: Match the haptic's shape to the sound's shape
Key points.detail: The first shield asset had a haptic of three sharp taps but a sound that was "continuous and progressive", so "there's no harmony." The fix kept the continuous haptic from the second asset and swapped in the preferred sound. The visual animation was 500 ms, and the final haptic and sound "support and reinforce each other."

Key points.title: Match visual detail to haptic detail
Key points.detail: The texture haptic had "nearly 100 entries over 2 seconds", but the background had only a few dots. Switching to a denser dot pattern made the experience feel more realistic, because what you see now matches what you feel.

Chapters.summary: Causality, harmony and utility, with the Flashlight button as the model.

Title: A calmer interface for a product in motion
Creator: Linear (Charlie Aufmann and Maxime Heckel)
Bottom line: Linear's 2026 refresh calmed a dense product by dimming navigation, cutting icons and borders, and warming the greys, using in-app tools to compare and tune changes quickly.
What they did: Linear's two-person team refreshed the interface by following two rules: "Don't compete for attention you haven't earned" and "Structure should be felt not seen". They dimmed the sidebar, made tabs smaller, cut and shrank icons, removed coloured icon backgrounds, and softened borders. They shipped behind feature flags with a dev toolbar to flip between old and new, and built an in-app colour tool with coding agents to tune hue, chroma and lightness of tokens.
Takeaways: Navigation should recede once you have arrived; Cut icons that don't earn their place; Structure should be felt, not seen; Warm greys, but not too warm; Build tools to compare and tune in the real app; Good refreshes go mostly unnoticed
Ideas for OnCourse: Home: dim the bottom tab bar and secondary labels a step so today's plan and the start button carry the most weight. Practice: remove dividers between options and rely on spacing and soft card backgrounds instead. Design process: build a hidden in-app panel (behind a flag) to tweak OnCourse colour tokens on a real phone and copy the values back into Figma

Key points.title: Navigation should recede once you have arrived
Key points.detail: The sidebar "used to appear bright enough that it remained visually prominent even after a user had reached their destination." Now it is "a few notches dimmer" so the main content takes precedence. Tabs were made more compact with smaller icons and text.

Key points.title: Cut icons that don't earn their place
Key points.detail: Icons help people recognise projects and statuses, but "in some views their presence had grown excessive." The refresh reduced icon use, scaled sizes down and removed "colored team icon backgrounds".

Key points.title: Structure should be felt, not seen
Key points.detail: Borders and separators "had quietly proliferated across the platform, sometimes appearing without clear reason." The team used fewer separators, rounded their edges and softened their contrast so the page still has structure without clutter.

Key points.title: Warm greys, but not too warm
Key points.detail: The old palette was "a cool, blue-ish hue". The aim was "a warmer gray that still feels crisp, but less saturated." "Go too warm, though, and the interface risks looking muddy", so it took many rounds to get right.

Key points.title: Build tools to compare and tune in the real app
Key points.detail: A dev toolbar toggles the refresh flag so "it took us just one click to compare it with the previous version." A colour tool, built with Claude Code "in a couple of hours", exposes hue, chroma and lightness of each token, and the values are imported into Figma as JSON. Feature flags let them ship small changes instead of one big release.

Key points.title: Good refreshes go mostly unnoticed
Key points.detail: "If most people don't immediately notice what changed, that's probably a good sign." Most of what makes software feel good "is what you aren't likely to see".

Title: Get to know the new design system (WWDC25)
Creator: Apple (Maria)
Bottom line: Apple's Liquid Glass design system asks for concentric corners, sheets that grow out of the control that opened them, hierarchy from grouping instead of decoration, and text labels where an icon is unclear.
What they did: An Apple designer explains the new design system across visual design, structure and continuity. She covers updated colours and bolder, left-aligned type, three shape types for concentric layouts, action sheets that spring from their source, dimming for modal tasks, bar grouping rules, scroll edge effects instead of dividers, and when to use text labels instead of symbols.
Takeaways: Nest shapes concentrically to avoid pinched corners; Sheets should grow from the thing you tapped; Dim for interruptions, not for parallel tasks; Show hierarchy through grouping, not decoration; Replace hard dividers with a soft scroll edge; Use a text label when an icon is ambiguous
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: make the "Report question" or "More" menu grow out of the button that opened it, not slide up from the bottom of the screen. Paywall: give the plan cards and the inner price chips concentric corners (inner radius = outer radius minus padding) and use a capsule button with extra margin from the screen edge. Home: replace hard dividers under the sticky header with a soft fade, and use text labels like "Edit plan" where an icon could be misread

Key points.title: Nest shapes concentrically to avoid pinched corners
Key points.detail: Apple uses three shapes: fixed (constant radius), capsules ("half the height of the container"), and concentric shapes that take "their radius by subtracting padding from the parent's." Watch for corners "that feel too pinched— or flared", often in "artwork in a card". On phones, use "a capsule with extra margin" for buttons near the screen edge.

Key points.title: Sheets should grow from the thing you tapped
Key points.detail: "Take the Action Sheet. It used to appear at the bottom of the screen, no matter where the action came from. Now, it springs from the action itself." This keeps the link between a surface and its source clear.

Key points.title: Dim for interruptions, not for parallel tasks
Key points.detail: "When a task interrupts the main flow, pair Liquid Glass with a dimming layer" to centre attention. When a task happens in parallel, no dim is needed. As a sheet is dragged up, it becomes more opaque and grows to show deeper engagement.

Key points.title: Show hierarchy through grouping, not decoration
Key points.detail: Extra backgrounds and borders on bar buttons are now unnecessary. "Instead of relying on decoration, hierarchy should be expressed through layout and grouping." Group by function and frequency, move secondary actions to a menu, and "not group symbols with text", since they could read as one button. The primary action stays separate and tinted.

Key points.title: Replace hard dividers with a soft scroll edge
Key points.detail: "Scroll edge effects reinforce that boundary, replacing hard dividers with subtle blur". They are "not decorative" and should only appear where floating UI meets content. Soft is the default on iOS; use only one per view.

Key points.title: Use a text label when an icon is ambiguous
Key points.detail: "A pencil might suggest annotate, and a checkmark can look like confirm", so actions like Select or Edit are easy to misread. "When there's no clear shorthand, a text label is always the better choice." Typography is also now "bolder and left-aligned" in alerts and onboarding.

Title: Color
Creator: Apple Human Interface Guidelines
Bottom line: Give each colour one meaning, never rely on colour alone, provide light, dark and high-contrast versions, and remember colour meanings differ by culture.
What they did: Apple's colour guidelines cover using colour consistently, supporting light, dark and Increased Contrast modes, testing in different lighting, inclusive colour, semantic system colours, and how to use colour on Liquid Glass. For iOS they define layered background colours (primary, secondary, tertiary) and label colours by role.
Takeaways: One colour, one meaning; Never rely on colour alone; Colour meaning changes across cultures; Supply light, dark and high-contrast versions; Test colours in real light; Use colour by role, and sparingly on controls
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: show correct and wrong answers with an icon (tick or cross) and a text label as well as green and red, so colour-blind users can tell them apart. Design process: give every OnCourse colour token a light, dark and high-contrast value, and test the Practice screen outdoors in bright light. Paywall: use the accent colour only on the main subscribe button, not on secondary links or plan tags

Key points.title: One colour, one meaning
Key points.detail: "Avoid using the same color to mean different things." If the brand colour marks a tappable button, using it on text that is not tappable is confusing. For OnCourse, the accent colour should only mean "you can tap this".

Key points.title: Never rely on colour alone
Key points.detail: "Avoid relying solely on color to differentiate between objects, indicate interactivity, or communicate essential information." Use text labels or glyph shapes too, so people with colour blindness can understand. This matters for green/red correct and wrong states in MCQs.

Key points.title: Colour meaning changes across cultures
Key points.detail: "Red communicates danger in some cultures, but has positive connotations in other cultures." Apple's Stocks app shows a positive trend in green in English and in red in Chinese.

Key points.title: Supply light, dark and high-contrast versions
Key points.detail: Every custom colour needs light and dark variants, plus "an increased contrast option for each variant" with much more difference. Apple adds: "Even if your app ships in a single appearance mode, provide both light and dark colors" for Liquid Glass.

Key points.title: Test colours in real light
Key points.detail: "In bright surroundings, colors look darker and more muted. In dark environments, colors appear bright and saturated." Test on different devices too, since True Tone shifts the white point.

Key points.title: Use colour by role, and sparingly on controls
Key points.detail: iOS defines background colours by level (primary for the view, secondary for groups, tertiary for groups inside groups) and label colours by importance. Don't reuse a role, like using separator colour for text. On Liquid Glass, "apply color sparingly" and "refrain from adding color to the background of multiple controls."

Chapters.summary: Consistent meaning, light/dark/high-contrast variants, lighting and device testing.

Title: Gestures
Creator: Apple Human Interface Guidelines
Bottom line: Keep standard gestures doing standard things, give feedback during the gesture, show when a gesture isn't available, and always offer a button alongside any custom gesture.
What they did: Apple's gesture guidelines explain how to use familiar touch gestures, when custom gestures are worth adding, and what makes them learnable. They list iOS gestures people already expect (three-finger swipe to undo, shake to undo) and warn against clashing with system gestures.
Takeaways: Standard gestures should do standard things; Give feedback while the gesture is happening; Show clearly when a gesture won't work; Custom gestures need four qualities; Shortcut gestures supplement buttons, never replace them; Offer more than one way to act
Ideas for OnCourse: Flashcards: if swipe left/right rates a card, also show visible "Again" and "Good" buttons, and tilt or tint the card during the swipe so users can predict the result. Practice: when an option can't be changed after submit, give a small shake or haptic on tap so it doesn't look frozen. Lessons: keep a visible back button even if edge-swipe back works

Key points.title: Standard gestures should do standard things
Key points.detail: "People expect tap to activate or select an object." Avoid using a familiar gesture like tap or swipe "to perform an action that's unique to your app", and avoid inventing a gesture for a standard action like scrolling.

Key points.title: Give feedback while the gesture is happening
Key points.detail: "Handle gestures as responsively as possible." As people perform a gesture, give feedback "that helps them predict its results" and shows "the extent and type of movement required to complete the action."

Key points.title: Show clearly when a gesture won't work
Key points.detail: If you don't explain why a gesture doesn't work, "people might think your app has frozen." A locked object that can't be dragged, or a disabled button that looks like an enabled one, both cause confusion.

Key points.title: Custom gestures need four qualities
Key points.detail: Add custom gestures "only when necessary". They must be "Discoverable", "Straightforward to perform", "Distinct from other gestures", and "Not the only way to perform an important action". If it is hard to explain the gesture in simple words, it will be hard to learn.

Key points.title: Shortcut gestures supplement buttons, never replace them
Key points.detail: Many apps let people swipe from the edge to go back, but they still keep the Back button. People "need simple, familiar ways to navigate and perform actions, even if it means an extra tap or two."

Key points.title: Offer more than one way to act
Key points.detail: "Don't assume that people can use a specific gesture to perform a given task." Some people use voice, a keyboard or Switch Control. Also avoid clashing with system gestures.

Chapters.summary: Multiple inputs, consistent gestures, responsive feedback, and unavailable gestures.

Title: How we learn how you learn
Creator: Duolingo Blog (Burr Settles)
Bottom line: A per-item memory model that predicts when each fact will be forgotten made Duolingo's practice sessions and strength meters work better, and lifted daily retention.
What they did: Duolingo replaced its Leitner-style strength meters with half-life regression (HLR), a model that estimates how long each word stays in a learner's memory. It uses each learner's history with a word (times seen, times correct, time since last practice) plus traits of the word itself. The model picks each learner's weakest words for a custom practice session and drives the strength meter on each skill. They compared it with older methods on 12 million practice sessions, then A/B tested it with users.
Results: HLR had the lowest prediction error; "the HLR error rate is nearly half that of the Leitner system method." In the A/B test, "We saw a 9.5% increase in retention for practice sessions, a 1.7% increase for lessons, and a whopping 12% increase for overall activity." Mean absolute error for HLR was 0.13. The student model is updated "3,000 times per second."
Takeaways: Show memory strength per skill so learners know when to review; The best time to review is right before forgetting; Model each item, not a fixed schedule; Item difficulty is learnable from data; Better review scheduling lifted daily retention
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: build a "Weak topics" session that picks the questions a student is most likely to get wrong today, based on their history with each topic. Lessons: show a strength meter on each topic that decays over time, so students can see when a topic needs review. Today's plan: fill part of the plan with topics that are due for review, not only new ones

Key points.title: Strength meters tell learners when to review
Key points.detail: Each Duolingo skill had a strength meter. It is full right after a skill is finished, and "once the meter slips to half-full, though, you know it's time to practice." Tapping a skill showed the words that most needed practice, with a custom session built from them. For OnCourse, a decaying meter per topic turns a hidden algorithm into something a student can see and act on.

Key points.title: Review right before you would forget
Key points.detail: The model treats memory as a forgetting curve: recall probability is p = 2^(-Δ/h), where Δ is time since last practice and h is the item's half-life. When Δ equals h, there is only a 50% chance of recall. "The best time to practice is when you are on the verge of forgetting." Each correct answer makes h longer and each mistake makes it shorter.

Key points.title: Fixed schedules lose to models learned from data
Key points.detail: Pimsleur used a fixed schedule for every word (5 seconds, then 25 seconds, then 2 minutes, then 10 minutes, and so on). Leitner doubles the interval after a correct answer and halves it after a mistake, and that is what Duolingo shipped in 2012. HLR learns weights from millions of learners instead. Its prediction error was "nearly half that of the Leitner system."

Key points.title: The model also learns which items are hard
Key points.detail: HLR can use the word itself as an input, so it learns which words fade fast. Easy words tended to be cognates or short, common, regular words. Hard words were rare or irregular, or used complex grammar. The same idea could flag MCQ topics that most students forget quickly and schedule them more often.

Key points.title: Better scheduling lifted retention in A/B tests
Key points.detail: Duolingo "secretly ran A/B tests" of HLR against the old algorithm. Daily retention rose 9.5% for practice sessions, 1.7% for lessons and 12% for overall activity. After that they moved everyone to HLR. Good review scheduling helps learning and also brings people back the next day.

Title: How we adjust in-app messaging for learners in different languages
Creator: Duolingo Blog (Eva Raimondi)
Bottom line: Small copy changes on high-traffic, high-friction screens can cut lesson quits and raise opt-ins, but a winning line in one language may not win in another.
What they did: Duolingo built Expurrimenter, a tool that lets the localization team A/B test 2–3 versions of interface copy without engineering time. They target the screens people use most, especially where a learner might feel stuck or need motivation. Tests included a warmer quit-lesson message in Spanish, a notification opt-in prompt in German, and more descriptive subscription feature names in Chinese.
Results: "Within the first three months with Expurrimenter, we more than doubled our all-time volume of copy tests." The German opt-in copy "yielded an 8% increase in opt-in to notifications for German learners"; the same test in Spanish "had no significant impact." The Spanish quit message reduced "the number of people that quit sessions" and increased time spent learning (no figure given). The Chinese feature names "increased free trial sign-ups for Plus" (no figure given).
Takeaways: Make copy testable without engineers; Test copy where learners feel stuck; A warm quit message keeps people in the session; Tie the notification ask to the learner's goal; Winning copy does not always travel; Spell out what premium actually does
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: when a student tries to leave a test midway, test a warmer message such as "Only 4 questions left. Leave anyway?" against the plain confirm. Notifications: in the permission pre-prompt, link reminders to the exam goal (for example, "Students who get reminders keep their NEET-PG plan on track") instead of asking for permission plainly. Paywall: describe each premium feature by what it does for the student, for example "See why every option is wrong" instead of "Detailed explanations"

Key points.title: Make copy testable without engineering time
Key points.detail: Copy A/B tests used to need engineers, so "just changing the localized text was a small step that took outsized effort." Expurrimenter plugs into Duolingo's analytics so writers can set up tests for one language or for all languages. In the first three months, Duolingo more than doubled its all-time number of copy tests. For OnCourse, keeping key strings behind a remote-config or experiment flag would let copy change without a release.

Key points.title: Test copy on screens where learners stall
Key points.detail: The team picks "the screens that people interact with the most, particularly those where a learner might feel stuck, or need extra motivation or instruction to continue." Then they write a hypothesis about tone or clarity. This keeps tests on moments that matter rather than random strings.

Key points.title: A warmer quit message kept people learning
Key points.detail: The Spanish quit-lesson prompt was a plain "Do you want to end this session?" They tested "Don't give up! Do you really want to end this session?", which speaks to the learner and admits they may feel discouraged. Fewer people quit sessions and time spent learning went up. OnCourse's leave-test confirm is a similar moment.

Key points.title: Tie the notification ask to the goal
Key points.detail: German learners opted into notifications less often. The old copy said "Duolingo needs to send you notifications." The winner said "notifications are proven to foster learning success!" Opt-in rose 8% for German learners, but the same test in Spanish had no significant effect. Explain the benefit, and retest in each market or language rather than assuming a win carries over.

Key points.title: Spell out what premium actually does
Key points.detail: Chinese has room for more description, so the team expanded "Unlimited Hearts" to "No heart loss on errors" and "Mastery quiz" to "Test your knowledge anytime." This "increased free trial sign-ups for Plus by giving learners a much clearer idea of how to make the most of their subscription." Feature names that describe the benefit can beat short labels on a paywall.

Title: Two simple tricks for remembering what you’ve learned on Duolingo
Creator: Duolingo Blog (Lucy Portnoff)
Bottom line: Slipping one old question into a new lesson is a cheap way to measure real recall, and it showed that studying a topic at a harder level and moving forward both help memory.
What they did: Duolingo adds a Review Exercise from an earlier skill into lessons from a later skill, and uses the answer as a measure of whether the learner still remembers it. Learners answer about 300,000 of these a day. The assessment team compared learners who got them right with those who got them wrong, using a regression discontinuity design to isolate the effect of doing one extra, harder level.
Results: "Together, learners answer around 300,000 Review Exercises every single day!" Learners who completed the additional level "were significantly more likely to answer the Review Exercise for that content correctly later." Learners who answered correctly "had completed more lessons in the next skills"; there was "no significant difference" for time spent on previous skills. No exact percentages are given.
Takeaways: Embed one old item in new lessons to measure recall; Harder levels of the same content improve later recall; Moving forward reinforces what came before; Use careful methods to separate effect from habit
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: mix one or two questions from topics the student finished weeks ago into each new set, and track how often they get them right as a retention metric. Lessons: after the basic quiz on a topic, offer a harder "level 2" set of clinical-vignette questions and nudge students to do it before moving on. Design process: use the recall rate on these embedded questions as a north-star learning metric next to engagement

Key points.title: One old question in a new lesson measures recall
Key points.detail: A Review Exercise is randomly sampled from an earlier skill (for example Animals) and shown inside a later lesson (for example Places). Right means remembered and wrong means forgotten. Across the app this gives about 300,000 recall measurements a day without a separate test. OnCourse could measure retention the same way inside normal practice sets.

Key points.title: Harder levels of the same topic boost recall
Key points.detail: Each skill has levels that teach the same material in harder contexts, from matching a picture to translating a sentence. Only the first level is required, so some learners never try harder ones. Learners who did the next level were "significantly more likely" to get the later Review Exercise right. Depth on a topic, not just finishing it once, helps memory.

Key points.title: Moving forward reinforces what came before
Key points.detail: Learners who got Review Exercises right had done more lessons in the next skills, because later skills reuse earlier concepts. Time spent going back to earlier skills showed no significant difference. A well-sequenced curriculum does part of the review for you.

Key points.title: Separate the effect from the type of learner
Key points.detail: Keen learners do more of everything, so a plain comparison would mislead. The team used regression discontinuity: they compared learners who usually complete the extra level and did, with similar learners who usually do but didn't this time. Any difference can then be put down to that one extra level. This is a useful model for reading OnCourse's own analytics.

Title: How we developed our addictive and delightful widget
Creator: Duolingo Blog (Osman Mansur, Jackson Shuttleworth)
Bottom line: A home-screen widget that shows only today's status and the streak worked as a habit reminder, but it only took off once Duolingo taught people how to install it right after a lesson.
What they did: The widget started as a hackathon project and took over a year to ship. Testing showed that the only data worth showing was whether today's lesson was done and the current streak. Installs were the main problem, so they tested an in-app promo with an animated install guide after a lesson. Later they made Duo's illustration change through the day and get more desperate near midnight, so the widget would not feel like just another notification.
Results: "Half of the learners with the widget installed have a streak of at least 6 months!" After the post-lesson promo with an animated explainer, "we saw widget installs skyrocket." Widget users had "far better retention on Duolingo, even when controlling for the fact that learners who add the widget tend to be more committed to begin with." No exact lift is given.
Takeaways: Show only what drives action: done today and streak; Installation, not building, was the hard part; Promote the widget right after a lesson, with an animated guide; Make the widget feel different from a notification; Widget users retained better even after controls
Ideas for OnCourse: Home: ship a home-screen widget that shows only "Today's plan: done / not done" and the streak, with a tap that opens straight into the next question. Today's plan: after a student finishes the plan, show a one-time promo with a short animated guide to adding the widget. Streaks: change the widget's illustration and tone through the day as the streak gets closer to breaking

Key points.title: Show only what makes people act
Key points.detail: Most widgets are passive, but Duolingo's had to get people to tap and do a lesson. So it shows just whether today's lesson is done and the current streak. Research and feature tests found that "simply reminding a learner of their current streak, and whether or not it's at risk, is hugely valuable." Extra stats were not needed.

Key points.title: Getting installs was the real challenge
Key points.detail: After the iOS launch in July 2022, some early adopters installed it on their own. The team soon saw that awareness and knowing how to install it were the main problem. If people didn't install it, months of engineering would be wasted. Any OnCourse widget needs a plan for getting it installed, not just a design.

Key points.title: Promote it after a lesson with an animated guide
Key points.detail: They tested an in-app promo shown after learners finished a lesson, with an animated explainer of how to add the widget. "We saw widget installs skyrocket." The team now keeps working on the content, placement and frequency of these promos. Right after a finished session is a good moment to ask.

Key points.title: Make it feel unlike a notification
Key points.detail: Learners said the widget worked as well as push notifications, which worried the team: why keep something that feels like extra notifications? They used the larger space for illustrations of Duo's mood across the day, and he "gets more and more desperate as it nears midnight." Personality gives people a reason to keep it installed.

Key points.title: Widget users retain better, even with controls
Key points.detail: Half of learners with the widget have a streak of at least 6 months. Duolingo says widget users had far better retention "even when controlling for" the fact that committed learners are more likely to add it. They later added Android and an iOS lock-screen streak widget.

Title: Elevating craft: How we refreshed our core tabs
Creator: Duolingo Blog (Leah Lee, Lokesh Fulfagar)
Bottom line: Duolingo made its tabs feel like one family by exploring four extreme directions, then building a small system that balances consistency with purpose and simplicity with clarity.
What they did: Duolingo's tabs had been built one at a time and had different header sizes, weak type hierarchy and uneven spacing. The team ran a quick divergent sprint, then pushed four directions to extremes (Punchy, Soft, Modular, Flat) and tested scrappy prototypes on phones. They then built tiered header sizes by tab purpose, a smaller type scale and spacing rules, and ran QA with engineers using design overlays.
Results: "We see higher engagement across tabs while maintaining our core learning metrics." No figures are given. It was live on iOS, with Android to follow.
Takeaways: Small inconsistencies add up to an unpolished app; Explore extreme directions before converging; Consistency must serve each tab's purpose; Simplicity must not cost clarity; Tier headers by purpose, keep titles in one place; Use whitespace instead of forced containers; QA with design overlays
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: audit Home, Practice, Lessons and Flashcards side by side for header size, title position, type styles and spacing, then write a small tiered header system. Design process: before polishing one direction, mock all main tabs in three or four extreme styles and compare them on a real phone. Lessons: remove container cards that only add boxes, and group content with spacing instead

Key points.title: Small inconsistencies add up to an unpolished app
Key points.detail: Each tab "worked fine on their own, but together they didn't feel like part of the same family." Headers varied in size, typography lacked hierarchy and spacing was uneven. These small details added up to an experience that didn't feel polished. Apps that grow tab by tab, like OnCourse, drift the same way.

Key points.title: Push four directions to extremes first
Key points.detail: The team first suspended assumptions and "went wild" with divergent ideas for each tab. Then they scaled the best into four extremes: Punchy (solid bright headers), Soft (gradients), Modular (cards) and Flat (heavy white space). Quick prototypes on phones and early feedback showed what worked before they committed.

Key points.title: Balance consistency with each tab's purpose
Key points.detail: Putting artwork in every tab header is consistent, "but it can also feel forced, especially if it occupies significant space without signaling anything useful." Likewise, "simplicity is good but not at the expense of clarity." Good design means knowing what to remove and what to keep.

Key points.title: Build a system: tiered headers, fewer type styles
Key points.detail: Headers come in tiered sizes based on each tab's purpose, with titles always in the same position. The type system was cut to a minimal number of styles. Spacing was cleaned up by "purposefully using the whitespace around the components instead of forcing containers around them."

Key points.title: Polish needs engineering partners and overlays
Key points.detail: A cross-functional team built QA processes, including self-QA with design overlays, on top of dogfooding across languages and devices. The result was higher engagement across tabs with core learning metrics unchanged. Craft work can be shipped and measured, not just admired.

Title: Why Duolingo switched to Energy and how it helps you learn
Creator: Duolingo Blog (Duolingo Team)
Bottom line: Duolingo replaced Hearts, which charged free users for each mistake, with Energy, which is spent per lesson and earned back by answering correctly, because punishing mistakes stalled beginners.
What they did: Under Hearts, every mistake cost a free learner one heart. Under Energy, each lesson uses a little energy, streaks of correct answers earn it back, and reviewing mistakes at the end of a lesson is free. It refills in about a day, and learners can refill with a rewarded ad or gems. Bonus energy rewards small wins such as perfect lessons or adding a friend. At the time of writing it was being tested with a small number of users.
Results: Beginners were "2X more likely to run out of hearts mid-lesson." "Our data shows it helps more learners complete lessons," especially "newer users and less engaged users who previously got stuck on mistakes." No exact figures are given.
Takeaways: Charging for mistakes stalls beginners; Spend per session, not per error; Earn energy back with correct streaks; Never charge for reviewing mistakes; Reward small wins with bonus energy; The free-tier limit still supports the business
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: if free users have a daily limit, count it in questions or sets attempted, never in wrong answers, so a struggling student is not locked out mid-test. Practice: always let students review their wrong answers and explanations for free, even after the free limit is reached. Paywall: when a free user hits the limit, offer an ad- or streak-based refill next to the upgrade, so the limit feels like a pause rather than a wall

Key points.title: Charging for mistakes stalled beginners
Key points.detail: With Hearts, each mistake cost a free learner one heart. Beginners, "who were still figuring things out," were "2X more likely to run out of hearts mid-lesson." Duolingo calls this discouraging, "especially since mistakes are a natural part of learning." A mistake-based limit hits hardest the people who most need practice.

Key points.title: Spend per lesson, earn back with right answers
Key points.detail: Energy works like a battery: each lesson uses a little and it fully recharges in about a day. Getting multiple answers right in a row earns energy back. This rewards effort and success instead of punishing errors. Duolingo says its data shows more learners complete lessons with Energy.

Key points.title: Reviewing mistakes is always free
Key points.detail: "Reviewing your mistakes at the end of a lesson doesn't use energy." The most valuable learning moment is not taxed. For an MCQ app, reading explanations of wrong answers should stay open even when free practice runs out.

Key points.title: Small wins earn bonus energy
Key points.detail: Learners get bonus energy for things like perfect lessons, adding a friend and reward chests. Running low can be fixed with a rewarded ad or gems. The limit becomes part of the game loop, not just a paywall. It still "helps us sustain" the free model.

Title: Improving Duolingo, one experiment at a time
Creator: Duolingo Blog (Lavanya Aprameya)
Bottom line: Duolingo runs hundreds of A/B tests at once, writes a hypothesis first, always checks learning and engagement guardrails, and kills changes that raise revenue but hurt retention.
What they did: Duolingo built a company-wide experiments service. Each test sets out what it does, how many arms it has, who sees it and what results are expected. Rollouts ramp up over a few days, and nightly reports compute a curated list of metrics per experiment plus universal metrics. The post shows two outcomes: Leaderboards on iOS, which shipped, and an offline-lesson upsell for Duolingo Plus, which was killed.
Results: "A few hundred experiments running simultaneously" in a given week; "over 2,000 experiments in total" in three years. The iOS Leaderboards test increased "the number of lessons that learners started" and "the number of lessons they completed." The offline Plus promotion: the experiment group "signed up for Plus at a much higher rate" and there was "a slight increase in revenue," but "a decrease in user retention" and "a slight decrease in daily active users," so it was shut down.
Takeaways: Write the expected result before running the test; Some tests need more than two arms; Ramp rollouts and watch for breakage; Curate metrics per test, plus universal guardrails; Never ship a revenue win that hurts learning habits
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: for every paywall or upsell test, add Day-7 retention and questions answered as guardrail metrics, and do not ship a winner that lowers them. Design process: write a one-line hypothesis and the expected metric change before each experiment goes live in PostHog. Practice: when testing a leaderboard or social feature, measure tests completed, not just tests started

Key points.title: Every change is tested, big or small
Key points.detail: "Test everything" is a Duolingo operating principle. Animated skill icons, five extra leagues and how many tears Duo cries in emails were all experiments. In a given week there are a few hundred running at once, and over 2,000 ran in three years.

Key points.title: Hypothesis first, and sometimes more than two arms
Key points.detail: Each experiment answers four questions: what it does, how many arms, who sees it and what results are expected. "Before running an experiment, we always come up with a hypothesis." Adding Leaderboards on desktop clashed with Friends, so the test had two branches: Friends kept in the sidebar, or moved to the profile.

Key points.title: Curated metrics plus universal guardrails
Key points.detail: Showing every metric in every report "creates unnecessary clutter," so each report template lists the relevant metrics. Universal metrics are always included, because "we never want to launch experiments that negatively impact the learning experience or cause lower engagement." Rollouts ramp over a few days and broken tests are paused.

Key points.title: Leaderboards won on both starts and completions
Key points.detail: The iOS Leaderboards test raised lessons started and lessons completed. Duolingo saw this as wins "for both engagement and learning," so it launched to everyone. Completions matter more than starts for a learning product.

Key points.title: A revenue win was killed for hurting retention
Key points.detail: An experiment let users tap skills while offline, then showed an ad for Plus when they tried to start a lesson. Plus sign-ups were "much higher" and revenue rose slightly, but retention and daily active users dropped because some users were discouraged from using the app offline. Duolingo shut it down and iterated. OnCourse should judge paywall tests on retention too.

Title: Why Khan Academy will be using “skills to proficient” to measure learning outcomes (and you should too!)
Creator: Khan Academy Blog (Bogdan Yamkovenko)
Bottom line: Reaching a high mastery level on fewer skills tracks real test scores better than touching many skills lightly, so Khan Academy now measures learning by skills brought to proficient.
What they did: Khan Academy compared mastery progress on its platform with students' scores on the nationally normed MAP Growth maths test. Skills move through four levels: attempted, familiar, proficient and mastered. They found that the share of skills reaching proficient or mastered correlated with MAP scores, whatever the number of skills worked on or time spent. They made "skills to proficient+" their internal learning metric.
Results: Prior studies suggest "spending 30+ minutes per week on Khan is associated with better learning outcomes." "The proportion of math skills completed at a proficient/mastered level correlated with MAP Growth mathematics scores," and "this pattern held regardless of the overall number of skills a learner worked on or the amount of time spent." "In a typical 30-minute session, a learner can work on two exercises and level up to proficient on two skills." These are correlations, not experiments.
Takeaways: Measure mastery, not just time spent; Use visible mastery levels per skill; Depth beats breadth; Retry to reach proficient before moving on; Pick a learning metric that matches an outside test
Ideas for OnCourse: Lessons: give each topic visible mastery levels (for example Attempted, Familiar, Proficient, Mastered) based on accuracy across sets. Practice: when a student finishes a topic set below proficient, suggest "Try this topic again" as the main button and "Next topic" as secondary. Design process: track "topics brought to proficient" each week as a learning metric, and check that it matches students' mock-test scores

Key points.title: Measure learning, not only time spent
Key points.detail: Edtech should be judged "not only by time spent on a platform but also by learning." Khan Academy earlier found 30+ minutes a week was associated with better outcomes. The newer finding is that skill mastery adds a stronger signal on top of time. Minutes or questions answered alone can hide shallow learning.

Key points.title: Four visible mastery levels per skill
Key points.detail: Skills move from attempted to familiar to proficient to mastered. Learners level up by getting more questions right on exercises, quizzes, unit tests and course challenges. Mastery learning research says working until a high score is reached gives better long-term retention.

Key points.title: Proficiency matched an outside test
Key points.detail: Khan Academy compared its data with MAP Growth, a valid external maths test. The share of skills at proficient or above correlated with MAP scores, regardless of how many skills or how much time. This held across grades. Researchers call this convergent validity: the in-app metric matches a trusted outside measure.

Key points.title: Depth beats breadth, so retry first
Key points.detail: "It is better to focus on fewer skills but reach at least proficient levels on those skills than to try and work on multiple skills but only reach a familiar level." Stopping at familiar may be the difference between shallow and deep learning. A typical 30-minute session covers two exercises and two skills to proficient. If the first try falls short, Khan Academy recommends trying again rather than moving on.

Title: Spacing Retrieval is More Important than Extra Retrieval
Creator: The Learning Scientists (Cindy Nebel)
Bottom line: Spreading the same quiz questions across several weeks helped long-term memory, while doubling the number of questions helped only in the short term.
What they did: The post reviews a study of pre-engineering students in a precalculus course who were followed into calculus the next semester. Each topic was quizzed in one of four ways: baseline (3 questions in one weekly quiz), extra spacing (3 questions spread over 4 weekly quizzes), extra quizzing (6 questions in one quiz), or both (6 questions spread over 4 quizzes). Every student got all four conditions on different topics.
Results: On the final exam, "spacing and retrieval practice were both equally good and adding them together provided an extra punch." Four weeks into the next semester, "the positive effects of spacing stayed the same" but "the benefits of increased quizzing disappeared": "Students were no better having been quizzed with three items vs. six items." Also, "increased spacing reduced quiz performance" at first. Only about half the class took all quizzes and was analysed.
Takeaways: Spacing beat extra volume for long-term memory; Same effort, better spread, better results; Spaced practice feels harder and scores lower at first; Keep spaced quizzes low-stakes; Retrieve old material, not just this week's
Ideas for OnCourse: Today's plan: instead of adding more questions on today's topic, spread a few questions from topics studied 1, 2 and 4 weeks ago through the plan. Practice: when spaced review questions lower a student's score, label them "Review" and do not count them against accuracy streaks, so a dip doesn't feel like failure. Lessons: end each lesson with 2–3 questions from earlier lessons rather than only the lesson just finished

Key points.title: Four ways of quizzing the same topics
Key points.detail: Topics in a precalculus course were quizzed as baseline (3 items in one week), extra spacing (3 items over 4 weeks), extra quizzing (6 items in one week) or both. It was a within-subjects design, so each student experienced all four on different topics. This made it possible to compare methods within the same person.

Key points.title: Spacing lasted, extra quizzing faded
Key points.detail: On the final exam, spacing and extra quizzing helped equally, and both together helped most. Four weeks into calculus, the spacing benefit remained but the extra-quizzing benefit was gone. Three items spread out did as well as six items bunched together. "It isn't about how much you study, but about how you study."

Key points.title: Same effort, just spread out
Key points.detail: Taking the questions from one normal quiz and spreading them across a few quizzes beat writing and answering more questions. Students don't need to double their study time if they space their retrieval. For OnCourse, a review set can stay short as long as it pulls from older topics.

Key points.title: Spaced practice scores lower at first
Key points.detail: "Increased spacing reduced quiz performance." Students remember more later but don't like it at the time because it is harder. The author says quizzes should be low or no stakes, and learners need to understand why it is harder. OnCourse should explain review questions and not punish a lower score on them.

Chapters.title: The experiment
Chapters.summary: Four quizzing conditions in a precalculus course, followed into calculus.

Chapters.title: Results
Chapters.summary: Both helped on the final; only spacing still helped a semester later.

Chapters.title: So what
Chapters.summary: Spread existing questions out instead of adding more.

Chapters.title: Caveats
Chapters.summary: Limited sample, and spaced quizzes lower early scores, so keep them low-stakes.

Title: GUEST POST: The Dark Side of Interleaving
Creator: The Learning Scientists (Miko M. Wilford)
Bottom line: Switching back and forth between quizzing old material and learning new material on every item hurts the new learning, so finish the quiz block, review, then teach the new part.
What they did: A 2013 paper found that retrieval practice on face–name pairs hurt learning of new related facts (face–profession pairs) when the two were alternated item by item. The author's lab then tested how often learners switched between retrieving old information and studying new information: 0 switches, then switching every 10, 5 or 2 faces, up to every face (39 switches across 40 faces).
Results: "As task-switch frequency between retrieval practice of original learning and studying new information increased, new learning would decrease" (the prediction, which the results supported). With 0 switches, retrieval practice "actually helps students learn the new information"; with 39 switches, "retrieving original learning hurt new learning, compared to restudying." The restudy group did not show this effect.
Takeaways: Retrieval practice still beats restudying; Constant switching between quiz and new content hurts new learning; With no switching, quizzing helps new learning; Review after a quiz before teaching new material; Feedback alone is not enough review
Ideas for OnCourse: Lessons: put the recall questions on earlier material in one block at the start or end of a lesson, not between every new concept card. Lessons: after a recall block, show a short summary of the answers before starting the new concept. Practice: keep review sets and new-topic sets as separate blocks in Today's plan rather than alternating question by question

Key points.title: Item-by-item switching hurt new learning
Key points.detail: In a 2013 seven-study paper, students learned face–name pairs, then either restudied or tried to recall the names. Between each, they were shown new related facts: the same face with a profession. Recalling names helped remember names, but it hurt learning of the professions compared with restudying. This was replicated in all their studies.

Key points.title: The cost grows with how often you switch
Key points.detail: The author's follow-up varied how often learners switched between retrieval and new learning: 0, every 10, 5 or 2 faces, or every face (39 switches). New learning dropped as switching increased in the retrieval group. The restudy group did not show this drop. The problem is the switching, not retrieval itself.

Key points.title: With no switching, quizzing helps new learning
Key points.detail: When all retrieval practice came first and new learning came after (0 switches), retrieval practice actually helped students learn the new information. So the same activities in a different order give the opposite result. Lesson structure matters as much as the activities in it.

Key points.title: Review after the quiz, before new material
Key points.detail: "The benefits of retrieval practice still far outweigh the costs." The advice is to include some review of earlier material right after a quiz and before new material. This needs to be more than feedback on answers, because participants already got feedback. For OnCourse, a short recap screen between a recall block and a new concept fits this.

Chapters.summary: Retrieval practice hurt learning of new related facts when alternated item by item.

Chapters.title: The follow-up study
Chapters.summary: Varying switch frequency from 0 to 39 switches.

Chapters.title: Results
Chapters.summary: New learning fell as switching rose; with no switching, retrieval helped.

Chapters.title: Practical applications
Chapters.summary: Keep retrieval, but review fully after a quiz before introducing new material.

Title: Exam Wrappers with Resources Enhance Metacognition
Creator: The Learning Scientists (Cindy Nebel)
Bottom line: Asking students to reflect right after a test and pointing them to evidence on better study methods shifted them away from re-reading toward retrieval practice.
What they did: The post reviews a study in an intro college biology course. After four exams, students could earn extra credit for an exam wrapper, a short reflection on how they did and how they studied. On the first and last wrappers, students ranked the strategies they had used. On the middle ones, they were sent to a Learning Scientists blog post and a podcast about retrieval practice and metacognition, and answered questions about them.
Results: "There was a large decrease in the number of students who reported re-reading." Students "reported more 'forced recall' demonstrating an increased use of retrieval practice." They also reported more summarising in their own words, group work and drawing. No exact figures are given; results are self-reported.
Takeaways: Students default to weak strategies like re-reading; Reflect right after a test, when it stings; Show the evidence, not just the advice; Reflection plus resources changed study habits
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: after a mock test, show a short "How did you prepare?" check with 3–4 options, then a one-line, evidence-backed tip based on the answer (for example, swap re-reading notes for a flashcard review). Practice: on the test result screen, link the weakest topics straight to a retrieval set rather than to re-reading the lesson. Flashcards: show a small chart from research comparing re-reading with self-testing the first time a student opens flashcards

Key points.title: Students pick weak strategies by default
Key points.detail: "Left to their own devices students most often choose less than desirable strategies, like re-reading instead of retrieval." Reasons include not knowing better, what has "always worked in the past," and the easy feeling re-reading gives. An exam-prep app can't assume students will choose testing over reading.

Key points.title: Exam wrappers ask students to reflect
Key points.detail: An exam wrapper asks students to reflect on their score, what they did well and badly on, and what strategies they used or could change. In this study they were worth extra credit after four exams. Students ranked the strategies they had used on the first and last wrappers.

Key points.title: Pointing to evidence shifted habits
Key points.detail: On the middle wrappers, students read a blog post with a chart on retrieval practice and listened to a podcast, then answered questions. Afterwards, far fewer reported re-reading and more reported "forced recall." They also did more summarising, group work and drawing.

Key points.title: Teach the alternative at the moment of failure
Key points.detail: Students "don't always know what the alternatives could be." Sharing better strategies "while they are realizing their strategy didn't work well may increase" adoption. For OnCourse, the mock-test result screen is that moment.

Title: When “almost right” is catastrophically wrong: Evals for AI learning games
Creator: Brilliant (Blake Farrow)
Bottom line: When AI writes practice problems, one broken problem can teach the wrong idea and shake confidence, so Brilliant runs automated checks for correctness, solvability and clarity before any human review.
What they did: Brilliant uses LLMs to generate thousands of interactive STEM puzzles. It built an evals framework that tests each puzzle for mathematical correctness, unique solvability, visual clarity, state consistency, impossible states and physical plausibility. For balance-mobile puzzles, early AI output compiled but was often unsolvable or visually unclear. Changing the puzzle representation the LLM generated improved pass rates a lot. Puzzles that fail never reach human reviewers.
Results: "Today, our success rate sits in the 80-90% range across all dimensions for foundational problems." "What once took weeks of careful handcrafting and testing now happens in hours, with higher quality results." Harder multi-layer problems "remain difficult even for frontier models."
Takeaways: An unsolvable problem is the worst problem; Compiling is not the same as correct; Check several quality dimensions automatically; Changing the representation improved AI output; Filter before human review; Humans still own the final call
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: if MCQs or explanations are drafted with AI, run automatic checks before review: exactly one defensible correct option, the explanation agrees with the key, no option overlaps another, and figures match the stem. Practice: add a one-tap "Report a problem with this question" on every question and explanation, and pull flagged items quickly. Design process: track the share of AI-drafted questions that pass checks and human review, by subject, to see where AI drafts are reliable

Key points.title: An unsolvable problem is the worst kind
Key points.detail: The post opens with a pool-shot momentum puzzle that can never be solved, however well you reason. "An unsolvable problem is about as bad a problem as you can have in a learning environment." The learner may build the wrong mental model, "or even worse, lose confidence in their ability to learn." A wrong answer key on an MCQ does the same harm.

Key points.title: At scale, small error rates mean many broken items
Key points.detail: With thousands of puzzles across dozens of concepts, "even a small percentage of errors means multiple broken puzzles in every course." Checking every puzzle by hand would make scaling impossible. That is why automated evals come before human review.

Key points.title: Test many dimensions, not just 'does it run'
Key points.detail: The evals check mathematical correctness, unique solvability, visual clarity, state consistency, impossible states and physical plausibility. For logic puzzles they check that every puzzle has exactly one solution. Code that compiles can still give a bad learning item. MCQs have their own versions: one correct answer, clear wording and a matching explanation.

Key points.title: Changing what the AI generates fixed quality
Key points.detail: Early mobile puzzles "compiled correctly. But, the puzzles still sucked": they were unclear or unsolvable. Changing the puzzle representation the LLM produced "dramatically improved the metrics," to 80–90% success on foundational problems. Harder puzzles still challenge frontier models, but they are also too hard for most users.

Key points.title: Filter automatically, then humans review
Key points.detail: Puzzles that fail evals "never even make it to the human review process," so learning designers spend time refining the best candidates. Work that took weeks now takes hours. Brilliant says human experts are still essential to its quality standards.

Title: Flat UI Elements Attract Less Attention and Cause Uncertainty
Creator: Nielsen Norman Group (Kate Moran)
Bottom line: Buttons and links that look like plain text or ghost outlines make people look longer and doubt more, so tappable things need clear, strong signifiers, especially on busy screens.
What they did: NN/g took 9 web pages, made two near-identical versions of each (strong vs weak clickability signifiers), and gave 71 participants a find-the-target task while tracking their eyes. Each person saw one version of each page. They measured fixations, time and heatmaps.
Results: On weak-signifier pages, participants spent "22% more time" and had "25% more fixations" (p < 0.05). 6 of 9 page pairs showed different gaze patterns. On the jewelry page, 86% (25 of 29) went from heading to the "Shop Pearl" link on the strong version vs "only 50% (12 out of 24)" on the weak one (p < 0.005); 9 of 24 stopped at the subheading.
Takeaways: Weak signifiers cost 22% more time to find targets; Users see weak buttons but don't trust them; Links styled as plain text get skipped; Flat works with low density, standard layout, contrast; Strong signifiers matter most for discovery
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: make answer options and "Next" look unmistakably tappable (filled container, clear contrast), never like plain text. Home: keep the main "Start today's plan" button solid and high-contrast; reserve ghost or text styles for low-priority actions. Design process: audit dense screens (Lessons, Flashcards) for text-styled links and give them a contrasting colour

Key points.title: Weak signifiers cost 22% more time to find targets
Key points.detail: 71 participants looked for one element on each page while eyetracking recorded them. On pages with weak signifiers they spent "22% more time" and made "25% more fixations", both statistically significant. NN/g notes this is extra effort, not engagement: people struggled to find the target or weren't sure when they saw it.

Key points.title: Users see weak buttons but don't trust them
Key points.detail: Heatmaps on weak versions spread across more of the page in 6 of 9 pairs. Often participants looked right at the target but moved on, because it didn't look clickable. NN/g calls this "click uncertainty": the problem is not that users never see the element, but that they don't feel confident it's the one.

Key points.title: Links styled as plain text get skipped
Key points.detail: On a jewelry page, the "Shop Pearl" link was either blue and underlined or styled like body text. With the strong link, 86% (25 of 29) moved from the heading to the link; with the weak one only 50% (12 of 24) did, and 9 of 24 stopped at the subheading, thinking it was clickable. For OnCourse, text-only links under lesson cards risk being missed.

Key points.title: Flat works with low density, standard layout, contrast
Key points.detail: 3 of 9 pairs showed no gaze difference. Those pages had little content and lots of white space, elements in standard positions, and high-contrast targets with room around them. NN/g says all three should be met, not just one or two. In-line links in a contrasting colour worked even without an underline.

Key points.title: Strong signifiers matter most for discovery
Key points.detail: The tasks were short, focused findability tasks, so real-world slowdown may be smaller. But NN/g stresses that strong signifiers are "absolutely crucial" when you want users to discover a feature they didn't know existed. New OnCourse features need obvious affordances, not subtle ones.

Title: Scrolling and Attention
Creator: Nielsen Norman Group (Therese Fessenden)
Bottom line: People scroll more than they used to, but most attention still goes to the top of the page, so put the most important content and action first.
What they did: NN/g analysed over 130,000 eye fixations from 120 participants in an eyetracking study across news, ecommerce, blog, FAQ and encyclopedia pages on 1920×1080 screens. They compared where viewing time fell with their 2010 study on 1024×768 screens.
Results: "Users spent about 57% of their page-viewing time above the fold" (vs 80% in 2010). "74% of the viewing time was spent in the first two screenfuls." The second screenful got "17%"; "81% of the viewing time is spent in the first three screenfuls." On general sites, "more than 42% of the viewing time fell within the top 20% of the page." Above the fold, "more than 65%" of time went to the top half of the viewport.
Takeaways: Above-the-fold content still gets 57% of attention; Attention drops sharply after the first screen; People scroll only when they have a reason; Put high-priority content and CTAs at the top; Beware false floors in airy layouts
Ideas for OnCourse: Home: put today's plan and its start button in the first screenful; push secondary cards (articles, offers) lower. Lessons: start each lesson with its key points in the first screen, since later screenfuls get far less attention. Home: avoid big decorative headers or spacing that create a false floor; let the next card peek in so users know to scroll

Key points.title: Above-the-fold content still gets 57% of attention
Key points.detail: Across 120 participants and over 130,000 fixations, users spent about 57% of viewing time above the fold. That's down from 80% in 2010, likely because long pages taught people to scroll. But the sharp drop in attention after the fold is the same as in 2010.

Key points.title: Attention drops sharply after the first screen
Key points.detail: The second screenful got about 17% of viewing time, and the remaining 26% spread thinly below. 74% of time fell in the first two screenfuls and 81% in the first three. NN/g says the fold as a barrier has moved down to the third screenful. On a phone, screenfuls are short, so this matters even more.

Key points.title: People scroll only when they have a reason
Key points.detail: "People will scroll if they have a reason to do it," but the interaction cost of scrolling lowers the chance lower content is seen. Even within the first screen, more than 65% of above-fold time went to the top half. Bigger screens didn't reduce scrolling, because designers spread content further apart; NN/g says designs now tend to be "too sparse."

Key points.title: Put high-priority content and CTAs at the top
Key points.detail: Reserve the top for key business and user goals and keep major calls to action above the fold. Use distinct, consistent headings and bold text so people can find new sections. For OnCourse Home, the one daily action belongs in the first screen.

Key points.title: Beware false floors in airy layouts
Key points.detail: Minimal designs with lots of white space can create an "illusion of completeness", so people think the page has ended. Add signifiers such as cut-off text to show there's more below. Then test with real users to find the right page length.
