Title: F-Shaped Pattern of Reading on the Web: Misunderstood, But Still Relevant (Even on Mobile)
Creator: Nielsen Norman Group (Kara Pernice)
Bottom line: When text has no formatting, people scan the top and left edge and miss the rest; headings, bold keywords, bullets and front-loaded words steer their eyes to what matters.
What they did: NN/g revisited the F-shaped reading pattern it found in 2006 with new eyetracking research on desktop and mobile. The article explains the F-pattern, lists other scanning patterns (layer-cake, spotted, marking, bypassing, commitment), when the F appears, why it hurts, and how formatting prevents it.
Results: The article states the F-pattern "is alive and well in today's world — both on desktop and on mobile," and that right-to-left readers scan in a flipped F. It gives no numeric results.
Takeaways: The F-pattern still happens on desktop and mobile; F-scanning appears when text has no formatting; Users miss content just because of where it falls; Other patterns: layer-cake, spotted, marking, bypassing, commitment; Front-load headings and bold key words
Ideas for OnCourse: Lessons: break each lesson into short sections with information-bearing subheadings so students scan in a layer-cake pattern, not an F. Practice: put the key point first in each MCQ explanation and bold the one fact to remember. Design process: when a list's items start with the same words ("Anatomy – …"), move the distinct part first, since readers skip repeated starts

Key points.title: The F-pattern still happens on desktop and mobile
Key points.detail: People read across the top of the content, then a shorter line lower down, then scan down the left side. NN/g's recent eyetracking shows the pattern "is alive and well" on both desktop and mobile. First lines and the first words of each line get the most fixations.

Key points.title: F-scanning appears when text has no formatting
Key points.detail: It happens when three things are true: a wall of text with no bolding, bullets or subheadings; a user trying to be efficient; and a user not committed enough to read every word. NN/g says the F is the default pattern "when there are no strong cues to attract the eyes."

Key points.title: Users miss content just because of where it falls
Key points.detail: With F-scanning, people skip big chunks that may be the most important, simply because they sit on the right. In responsive layouts text reflows, so a phone user fixates on different words than a desktop user. NN/g calls the F-pattern "bad for users and businesses."

Key points.title: Other patterns: layer-cake, spotted, marking, bypassing, commitment
Key points.detail: Layer-cake means scanning headings and skipping body text; spotted means hunting for links, digits or a keyword. Marking (eyes fixed while the finger scrolls) happens more on mobile. Bypassing skips list items that start with the same words, and commitment is reading almost everything when highly motivated.

Key points.title: Front-load headings and bold key words
Key points.detail: NN/g's fixes: put the most important points in the first two paragraphs; use visible headings that start with the words carrying the most information; group related content; bold key phrases; use descriptive link text; use bullets and numbers; cut unneeded content. These apply directly to OnCourse lesson and explanation text.

Title: Banner Blindness Revisited: Users Dodge Ads on Mobile and Desktop
Creator: Nielsen Norman Group (Kara Pernice)
Bottom line: People ignore anything that looks like an ad, sits where ads usually go, or sits next to an ad; making a promo card look different to stand out often makes it invisible.
What they did: NN/g ran a new eyetracking study on desktop and mobile and compared it with findings from 1997 and 2007. It shows three triggers of banner blindness (location, ad-like visual treatment, proximity to ads), the "hot potato" pattern, and how mobile users treat inline ads and ad-like content.
Results: In one session, of 132 fixations in the content area "only one is within the right rail: that's 0.8% of the user's attention within 25% of the content area", "33 times smaller than its size might have warranted." 26 participants on two task pages looked very little at ads or ad-styled promotions.
Takeaways: People ignore anything in ad positions; Looking different can make content look like an ad; Ads poison the content next to them; One glance can make users avoid an area for good; On mobile, standout images get mistaken for ads
Ideas for OnCourse: Home: style important cards (today's plan, streak, mock test reminder) like the rest of the content, not as colourful banners, so they don't read as ads. Home: keep upgrade or offer cards in their own section, away from study content, so they don't poison nearby cards. Design process: test whether students actually notice any promo or announcement card before relying on it

Key points.title: People ignore anything in ad positions
Key points.detail: Ignoring ads is learned: users skip the top banner and right rail, and some even skipped the ad at the top of Google results. In NN/g's study, 26 participants on a how-to page read the text but barely looked at the ads. Banner blindness has now been documented across 3 decades.

Key points.title: Looking different can make content look like an ad
Key points.detail: An inline promotion in an article was ignored by 26 participants because it was a small rectangle, fancily formatted, with a blue background and text in the image. NN/g warns that making content look different to raise its salience "often has the opposite effect." For OnCourse, a bright promo card on Home may be skipped.

Key points.title: Ads poison the content next to them
Key points.detail: By the Gestalt law of proximity, items close together are seen as one group. One participant glanced at a right rail once, saw sponsored stories, and never saw the useful craft videos next to them. Mixing offers and real content in one section hides the content.

Key points.title: One glance can make users avoid an area for good
Key points.detail: NN/g's "hot potato" pattern: users glance at something irrelevant, look away, and avoid that area on this page and others. One user's right rail held 25% of the content area but got 0.8% of her attention, "33 times smaller than its size might have warranted."

Key points.title: On mobile, standout images get mistaken for ads
Key points.detail: Mobile inline ads are hard to avoid because they fill the screen. But people also scroll past big images or graphics before looking, assuming they're ads, a behaviour NN/g first saw on mobile in this study. Anything that stands out from what's around it on a small screen risks being skipped.

Title: Placeholders in Form Fields Are Harmful
Creator: Nielsen Norman Group (Katie Sherwin)
Bottom line: Don't use placeholder text as a field's label; keep labels and hints visible outside the field, because placeholders vanish, hide errors, look like filled data and hurt accessibility.
What they did: Drawing on NN/g's user testing and eyetracking, the article lists 7 problems when placeholders replace labels, problems that remain when placeholders are used with labels, accessibility issues, and how floating labels fix some but not all of them.
Results: No numbers. NN/g says "user testing continually shows that placeholders in form fields often hurt usability more than help it," and "eyetracking studies show that users' eyes are drawn to empty fields."
Takeaways: Disappearing hints strain short-term memory; Without labels, users can't check or fix answers; Filled-looking fields get skipped or mistaken for defaults; Light grey placeholders fail accessibility; Floating labels help but don't solve everything
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: give every field (name, college, exam attempt, target year) a visible label above it; use placeholders only for an example, never the label. Onboarding: show format hints (e.g. phone number format, OTP length) as persistent helper text under the field. Paywall: keep labels visible on any billing or coupon field so users can check before paying

Key points.title: Disappearing hints strain short-term memory
Key points.detail: Once the user types, the placeholder is gone, so they must delete their text to see the hint again. NN/g's mobile research shows people are often distracted and interrupted, so they lose their place. Even a simple login without labels leaves people unsure whether to enter a username or an email.

Key points.title: Without labels, users can't check or fix answers
Key points.detail: A filled form with no labels can't be reviewed at a glance, and autofill mistakes go unnoticed. When an error message appears, users must go back into each field to recall what it wanted. Keyboard users tabbing quickly also never see hints that vanish on focus.

Key points.title: Filled-looking fields get skipped or mistaken for defaults
Key points.detail: "Eyetracking studies show that users' eyes are drawn to empty fields," so fields with text in them are less noticeable and can be overlooked. Some users think the placeholder is a default value and skip the field. Others try to delete placeholder text by hand, adding effort.

Key points.title: Light grey placeholders fail accessibility
Key points.detail: Default light grey placeholder text has poor contrast. Not all screen readers read placeholders aloud. People with cognitive or motor impairments bear the extra memory and interaction load most.

Key points.title: Floating labels help but don't solve everything
Key points.detail: Floating labels (used in Material Design) move the label above the field on focus, which saves space on mobile and fixes the memory problems. But fields still look filled and less noticeable, and accessibility issues may remain. NN/g's conclusion: "if you have the screen space, placing the label and hint outside the field is still the best way to go."

Chapters.summary: Memory strain, no review, unclear errors, skipped fields and more.

Title: Touch Targets on Touchscreens
Creator: Nielsen Norman Group (Aurora Harley)
Bottom line: Make every tappable element at least 1cm × 1cm on screen, space competing targets apart, and make primary actions bigger still.
What they did: The article sets a minimum touch target size from published research (Parhi, Karlson and Bederson; MIT Touch Lab) and illustrates problems with examples from NN/g's usability testing: crowded stacked buttons, tiny dismiss buttons, view–tap asymmetry and well-sized targets in apps used on the move.
Results: Minimum target "1cm × 1cm (0.4in x 0.4in)" (Parhi et al.). Average fingertip "1.6–2cm (0.6–0.8 in)" wide; thumb impact area "an average of 2.5cm (1 inch)." Instagram's dismiss button was "only 2mm — 0.08in — wide"; David Yurman's swatches were "only 1mm." Target's in-store buttons are about "2cm × 2cm"; Glow Baby's nursing timers "2.3cm" wide.
Takeaways: Minimum touch target is 1cm × 1cm; Small targets are slower to hit; Crowded targets cause wrong taps; Visible but untappable is view–tap asymmetry; Primary and on-the-move actions need bigger targets
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: make each MCQ option a full-width row, well over 1cm tall, with clear gaps so students don't tap the wrong answer. Flashcards: keep "Again/Hard/Good/Easy" buttons large and spaced, since students often study one-handed on the move. Design process: replace tiny carousel dots or small icon-only buttons with targets of at least 1cm, and check them on a real phone

Key points.title: Minimum touch target is 1cm × 1cm
Key points.detail: Based on a study by Parhi, Karlson and Bederson, targets should be at least 1cm × 1cm (0.4in) for quick, accurate taps. This is a physical size, so pixel values are misleading across screen densities. MIT Touch Lab found fingertips are 1.6–2cm wide and the thumb's impact area about 2.5cm.

Key points.title: Small targets are slower to hit
Key points.detail: Fitts' law says the time to reach a target depends on its distance and size, so small targets take longer. In Glow Baby, short sleep or feeding events were drawn as thin bars, so their tap targets became too small. The same risk applies to any chart where size encodes data.

Key points.title: Crowded targets cause wrong taps
Key points.detail: Kate Spade's stacked thin buttons were too close together, while White House Black Market's links were spaced well. Instagram's dismiss button was 2mm wide, so people ignored bad suggestions rather than risk following an account by mistake. Targets must be big enough first, then spaced; side-by-side pairs give more room than stacked ones.

Key points.title: Visible but untappable is view–tap asymmetry
Key points.detail: Elements big enough to see can still be too small to tap, like iOS carousel dots. David Yurman's 1mm colour swatches worked with a mouse but on tablets often opened the product page instead. Desktop patterns need resizing for touch.

Key points.title: Primary and on-the-move actions need bigger targets
Key points.detail: 1cm is the minimum. Target's app gives in-store search and scan buttons about 2cm × 2cm for people walking. Glow Baby gives most of the screen to two 2.3cm-wide nursing timers with lots of space. Children, older users and busy one-handed users also need larger targets.

Chapters.title: Size matters
Chapters.summary: The 1cm minimum and why physical size is what counts.

Chapters.summary: Seeable but not tappable, like carousel dots.

Title: Trello User Onboarding: 7 Tactics To Inspire You
Creator: Growth.Design
Bottom line: Let new users build something real in the first minutes, using their own input, and push every unavoidable chore (like email confirmation) until after they have seen value.
What they did: The comic walks through Trello's sign-up while the author builds a content calendar. Trello strips header links from the landing page, skips forced email confirmation, asks one use-case question, then has the user type their own tasks into form fields that appear live as cards on a board. A one-tap background makes the board feel owned, and a link opens Gmail straight away for the confirmation email.
Results: Removing header navigation on critical pages "may increase your conversion rate by 28%." Deferring email confirmation "can increase your 'Signup' to 'First Key Action' rate by up to 100%." "Trello later reported a +36% lift in activation through a mix of personalization experiments." Appcues reported persona-based onboarding "improved their users' activation time by 74%." (These are cited figures from other sources, not tests run by Growth.Design.) Overall experience score: A.
Takeaways: Fewer links on the path means fewer leaks; Let people use the product before confirming email; One self-segment question beats a long quiz; Teach new concepts by building from the user's own input; A small customisation makes the app feel like theirs; Send people straight to the confirmation email
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: ask one question (target exam and date) and then drop the user into a real first question, not a feature tour. Onboarding: build the user's first Today's plan live on screen from their answers, so they see their own plan take shape. Onboarding: defer account verification (OTP or email) until after the first practice set, and watch activation, not just sign-up rate

Key points.title: Fewer links on the path means fewer leaks
Key points.detail: Trello's landing page removed nearly all menu links except Log in and Sign up. Growth.Design cites that removing header navigation on critical pages "may increase your conversion rate by 28%", because each link is a reason to leave (Hick's Law). OnCourse's onboarding and paywall screens should show one path forward, not tabs or extra links.

Key points.title: Let people use the product before confirming email
Key points.detail: Trello did not force an email confirmation step, so the author could start building right away. Deferred account creation "can increase your 'Signup' to 'First Key Action' rate by up to 100%." The comic warns to check activation and revenue too, because a lift at the top of the funnel has to carry through.

Key points.title: One self-segment question beats a long quiz
Key points.detail: Trello asks what you want to use it for, then tailors the setup. Trello "later reported a +36% lift in activation" from personalisation experiments, and Appcues saw activation time improve "by 74%." But Trello offered 15 options and two vague buttons ("Dive right in" vs "Help me get started"), which caused doubt. Keep the question short and the choices few.

Key points.title: Teach new concepts by building from the user's own input
Key points.detail: The user types tasks into plain form fields, and each one appears live as a card on a board preview. This moves them from a familiar mental model (a to-do list) to Trello's new one (boards, lists, cards). A later step that only showed a video of dragging cards felt like watching a friend play a game. For OnCourse, show a plan or a deck forming from the user's own answers instead of a demo.

Key points.title: A small customisation makes the app feel like theirs
Key points.detail: One tap set a calm photo as the board background, and the board suddenly felt like the author's own "zen hub." This is the Endowment Effect: a tiny investment of effort makes people value the thing more. The first board also kept the user's earlier input, which felt less scary than an empty board.

Key points.title: Send people straight to the confirmation email
Key points.detail: Trello linked directly to Gmail, but the author still got lost in the inbox for ten minutes. The "Sniper Link" fix pre-fills the inbox search (from:@trello.com, in:anywhere) so only the app's email shows, even if it is in spam. Any OnCourse flow that needs an email step can use the same trick.

Chapters.title: Landing page with no exits
Chapters.summary: Removing header links keeps people on the sign-up path.

Chapters.title: No forced email confirmation
Chapters.summary: Users explore first and confirm later, which can double the first-key-action rate.

Chapters.title: One use-case question
Chapters.summary: Self-segmenting lifts activation, but 15 options and vague buttons cause doubt.

Chapters.title: Live preview of your own board
Chapters.summary: Form fields turn into cards as you type, teaching Trello's concepts.

Chapters.title: One-tap background
Chapters.summary: A tiny customisation makes the board feel owned.

Chapters.summary: Pre-filled inbox search gets users to the confirmation email without distraction.

Title: How small UI delighters have a huge impact on UX
Creator: Growth.Design
Bottom line: Start new users on one easy action, and make the first bit of progress feel big, instead of showing it as 0% of a huge goal.
What they did: The comic tests Been, a travel-tracking app. Its intro lists features, then drops the user on an empty map with only a subtle hint of what to do. Adding a first country takes a complex, cold form, and the reward is a stat that still reads 0% of 195 countries. Growth.Design redesigns it with an easy first question, a photo in the form, and a delightful animation when a country is added.
Takeaways: Prime people with the value, not a feature list; Make the first action obvious and easy; Small touches make data entry feel warmer; A far-away goal at 0% kills motivation; Make the first progress moment a peak
Ideas for OnCourse: Progress & streaks: never show a new user "0% of 2,000 MCQs"; show a near goal (today's 20 questions, or this week's topic) and how close they are to it. Practice: give the first correct answer of a new user's first session a short, satisfying animation so the first progress moment is a peak. Onboarding: open with why tracking prep matters (exam date, rank goal) instead of listing features like widgets or premium

Key points.title: Prime people with the value, not a feature list
Key points.detail: Been's intro scrolls through features like widgets, zoom and premium mode. Growth.Design asks: "Have you ever been excited about widgets?" Priming says earlier information shapes how people react to what comes next, so the intro should set up the meaning of tracking trips. For OnCourse, the first screens should talk about the exam and rank, not features.

Key points.title: Make the first action obvious and easy
Key points.detail: After the intro the user lands on a map and asks, "That's it? What do I do now?" The only cue is a very subtle animation. The redesign asks one easy question to start, using the Spark Effect: people act when the effort is small. OnCourse's first Home screen for a new user should have one clear, easy first step.

Key points.title: Small touches make data entry feel warmer
Key points.detail: Adding a trip to Italy meant an "overly complex form" that felt cold. The author suggests a simple image that brings back memories of the trip. Aesthetic Usability means people believe things that look better work better, so a little warmth makes a chore feel lighter.

Key points.title: A far-away goal at 0% kills motivation
Key points.detail: After adding a country the stat still showed 0% out of 195 countries. The Goal-Gradient Effect says people speed up near a goal, but a goal that seems too far has the opposite effect. Growth.Design suggests Shaping: reward small steps toward the target. OnCourse should frame early progress against a near goal, not the whole syllabus.

Key points.title: Make the first progress moment a peak
Key points.detail: The redesign drops the far-away goal and adds a fun animation when a country is added, to boost the user's "psych" and nudge them to fill the rest of the map. The Peak-End Rule says people remember peaks and endings. The case study gives no numbers; it is a redesign proposal, and Been scores a C.

Chapters.title: Feature-list intro
Chapters.summary: The intro lists features instead of priming the value of tracking trips.

Chapters.title: An easy first step
Chapters.summary: One easy question makes it a no-brainer to start.

Chapters.title: Warmer screens
Chapters.summary: Colour and imagery make the experience feel better and seem to work better.

Chapters.title: 0% of 195 countries
Chapters.summary: A goal that is too far away discourages instead of motivates.

Chapters.title: A delightful first win
Chapters.summary: An animation turns adding a country into a memorable peak.

Start here.why: It directly warns against the "0% of the syllabus" progress bars that exam-prep apps tend to show new users.

Title: Adobe: The growing issue with “Free” trials UX
Creator: Growth.Design
Bottom line: Give people a taste of the product before any plan picker or card form; a trial wrapped in upsells, contracts and hidden fees burns the excitement that brought them in.
What they did: The author tries Photoshop's generative AI and hits a confusing three-plan upsell first, then a second plan picker where monthly and yearly cost the same and are both annual contracts. A "curated just for you" Acrobat upsell follows, then a card form whose fine print shows a cancellation fee of half a year's price. Growth.Design proposes a quick AI demo first and points to Rows, which drops visitors straight into a working file.
Results: Growth.Design cites that "~25-40%" of people "cancel their trial on day one to avoid this trap." Rows: after turning their product into a homepage, "conversion rate to sign-up rose 72%" and "the activation rate of people who converted from a 'sandbox account' is 30% higher" than other channels. Adobe's trial score: F.
Takeaways: A complex plan picker first drains excitement; Show the magic before asking for anything; Same price, different fine print, is fake choice; Fake personalisation feels exploitative; Many users cancel on day one to dodge trial traps; Product-first beats form-first
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: let a new user answer a few real MCQs with explanations before the paywall appears. Paywall: keep plans few and plainly different; state the real total, renewal date and cancellation terms on the same screen. Renewal: send a clear trial-ending reminder so users don't feel they must cancel on day one to stay safe

Key points.title: A complex plan picker first drains excitement
Key points.detail: Clicking to try Photoshop's AI opened a three-plan upsell where Photoshop plus Lightroom was cheaper than Photoshop alone, because it had less cloud storage and fewer "generative credits." The user could not tell how much they needed, or why Lightroom was there. That is Cognitive Load at the worst moment. An OnCourse paywall shown before any value should have very few, clearly different choices.

Key points.title: Show the magic before asking for anything
Key points.detail: The redesign lets the user type "a tiny elephant" and watch the AI add it to a photo. After that, the author is "super excited to jump into the real thing." For OnCourse, a few real questions with good explanations can be the taste before the trial.

Key points.title: Same price, different fine print, is fake choice
Key points.detail: The second picker offered monthly and yearly at the same price (£9.98 x 12 = £119.76), and both were annual contracts. The only difference was the cancellation fee: "Some fees" vs "No refund." Growth.Design calls complex plans that hide real costs unethical, and says they lead to frustrated customers, more support and a worse reputation.

Key points.title: Fake personalisation feels exploitative
Key points.detail: A "Step 1 of 3" screen offered Acrobat Pro as "curated just for me," which had nothing to do with the AI feature. Real curation signals care, but unrelated deals can leave people "feeling exploited." Any "recommended for you" label in OnCourse must be based on the user's actual data.

Key points.title: Many users cancel on day one to dodge trial traps
Key points.detail: To get the trial, the user had to pass upsells, decode fees, sign an annual contract and enter a card. The fine print showed a late cancel costs half a year's subscription. Growth.Design cites that "~25-40%" of people cancel their trial on day one to avoid such traps.

Key points.title: Product-first beats form-first
Key points.detail: Rows dropped visitors straight into a new spreadsheet. Its sign-up conversion "rose 72%," and people who came from a sandbox account had a "30% higher" activation rate than other channels. These are cited figures, not Growth.Design's own test.

Chapters.title: Upsell before anything
Chapters.summary: A confusing three-plan picker greets a user who just wanted to try one feature.

Chapters.title: Monthly vs yearly, both annual
Chapters.summary: Same price, both contracts; only the cancellation fee differs.

Chapters.title: "Curated just for me"
Chapters.summary: An unrelated Acrobat upsell pretends to be personal.

Chapters.title: Trial traps
Chapters.summary: Card, contract and steep fees push people to cancel on day one.

Chapters.title: Rows: product as homepage
Chapters.summary: Letting people use the product first lifted sign-ups 72%.

Start here.why: It has the only hard numbers and makes the case for letting OnCourse users practise before the paywall.

Title: Adobe: The Psychology of User Offboarding
Creator: Growth.Design
Bottom line: Make renewal and cancellation honest and easy: clear renewal emails, offers that match the reason someone gave, and a calm goodbye, because the last moment is what people remember.
What they did: The author gets a renewal email with the key word hidden, then tries to cancel a Photoshop plan unused for 6 months. Adobe asks for a fresh login, forces a feedback survey, warns about losing "favorite apps" never used, shows untailored discount offers (many pricier than the current plan), repeats warnings, and ends with a confusing confirmation and cross-sell. Growth.Design redesigns the email, the offers and the goodbye screen.
Results: Growth.Design's own LinkedIn poll: "n=328 people indicated that 97% of them did not think that Adobe's approach could be considered 'Ethical'." Offboarding score: E. No product metrics are given.
Takeaways: Renewal emails should state date, plan and cost plainly; Annual-paid-monthly plans confuse and anger; Don't warn people about losing what they never used; Tailor the save offer to the stated reason; Unjustified discounts train people to wait for deals; End with a clear, calm goodbye
Ideas for OnCourse: Renewal: send a renewal reminder whose subject line says "renewal", with the date, plan and price up front and one clear button. Renewal: if a user picks "exam is over" or "too expensive" as the reason, show an offer that fits it (pause until next attempt, a cheaper plan), not a generic discount. Renewal: end cancellation with a plain confirmation, an undo option and a kind goodbye, with no cross-sell

Key points.title: Renewal emails should state date, plan and cost plainly
Key points.detail: Adobe's email hid "renewal" at the end of the subject, used an all-caps preview, buried the deadline and link in paragraphs, and never said what the plan cost. The redesign shows a clear preview, an obvious date, plan and cost, and an easy button. Growth.Design ties hidden costs to Status Quo Bias, which keeps "Zombie Customers" paying for things they don't use.

Key points.title: Annual-paid-monthly plans confuse and anger
Key points.detail: The account page showed $9.99 per month, and the author was left "always confused by these 'annual paid monthly' plans." This lets Adobe charge penalty fees for early cancellation. Growth.Design says the revenue boost also hurts the brand, a reminder to weigh long-term costs of short-term tactics.

Key points.title: Don't warn people about losing what they never used
Key points.detail: Adobe warned the user they would lose their "favorite apps," though they had not opened them in 6 months, which Adobe tracks. The comic compares it to a gym owner warning about losing your "favorite weights." Loss warnings only work when they are true for that user.

Key points.title: Tailor the save offer to the stated reason
Key points.detail: Adobe forced a reason for leaving (the confirm button was disabled until you answered) and then showed generic offers, most "even more expensive" than the current plan. Growth.Design says forcing feedback and then not showing you listened "can be worse than not asking for any feedback at all." The redesign personalises options to the stated reason, using the Noble Edge Effect: visible care builds loyalty.

Key points.title: Unjustified discounts train people to wait for deals
Key points.detail: A wall of last-minute discounts felt like a TV infomercial. Reasonable discounts can help short-term sales, but "unjustified discounts lower brand perception over the long-term," which Growth.Design calls the "Sleazy Salesmen Effect." Extra screens repeating the same warnings were unreasonable friction, unlike Adobe's quick checkout.

Key points.title: End with a clear, calm goodbye
Key points.detail: After cancelling, Adobe said the user was "still part of their community" and showed more plans, hiding the confirmation. Growth.Design suggests a clear message that you can leave in peace, plus an "Undo" button for mistakes. Per the Peak-End Rule, "How you say goodbye is as important as how you say hello."

Chapters.title: The renewal email
Chapters.summary: Hidden keyword, hidden cost and a buried link keep people paying by default.

Chapters.title: Annual paid monthly
Chapters.summary: A pricing tactic that enables penalty fees but hurts the brand.

Chapters.title: The offer-fest
Chapters.summary: Untailored discounts make the brand look desperate.

Chapters.title: Forced feedback, ignored
Chapters.summary: Asking why and then not listening is worse than not asking.

Chapters.title: Unreasonable friction
Chapters.summary: Repeated screens make leaving much harder than joining.

Chapters.title: The goodbye
Chapters.summary: A clear confirmation and calm exit shape what people remember.

Start here.why: It shows how to make a cancel flow's offer match the user's reason, which is the core design choice for OnCourse's renewal and cancel screens.

Title: Spotify Wrapped: 6 psychology principles that make it go viral every year
Creator: Growth.Design
Bottom line: A personal recap works when it builds suspense, tells the user's own story with fresh visuals, frames their time as value, and ends with one clear next thing to do.
What they did: The case study walks through Spotify Wrapped from the teaser notification a week before release to the final screen. It names six principles: curiosity gap, anticipation (with variable reward), storytelling, delighters, positively framed numbers, and social value. It then redesigns the anti-climactic ending into a single personalised song you missed, hidden until you tap.
Takeaways: Tease the recap with the most emotional hook; Not knowing the result is part of the reward; Tell a story, not a summary table; New animations each year keep it memorable; Frame time spent as value gained; End on one personal next step, not a dead end
Ideas for OnCourse: Progress & streaks: build a weekly or post-mock "prep recap" in story format (top subject, toughest topic conquered, hours studied framed as progress toward the exam) with a shareable card. Notifications: tease the recap with a personal hook such as "Your strongest subject this month is…" rather than a raw question count. Progress & streaks: end the recap with one suggested next step (a single weak-topic set), not a list

Key points.title: Tease the recap with the most emotional hook
Key points.detail: Spotify's notification a week before release uses the curiosity gap to prime users. Growth.Design asks whether the total number of songs is the best hook, and suggests your favourite song would be more emotional. For OnCourse, a teaser about a student's strongest subject beats a count of questions answered.

Key points.title: Not knowing the result is part of the reward
Key points.detail: People wait all year, and some even change what they listen to midway through. The author had "no idea" who their top artist would be, so the reveal felt like a variable reward. Unexpected rewards are one of the "key ingredients" of Wrapped's success.

Key points.title: Tell a story, not a summary table
Key points.detail: Spotify could send a list or graph, but instead uses crafted copy to introduce each section and a timeline of when you listened to each artist. Stories engage more of the brain and are "more memorable than simple facts and statistics alone." A recap that tells a student how their prep unfolded will stick better than a stats page.

Key points.title: New animations each year keep it memorable
Key points.detail: Wrapped comes in new graphic styles and animated stories each year, because people remember playful pleasures better. The animations are what make the stories memorable. OnCourse recaps can keep the format but refresh the visual style each season.

Key points.title: Frame time spent as value gained
Key points.detail: Spotify ties minutes listened to memories and to how your taste grew. Growth.Design contrasts this with Screen Time, where big numbers feel bad. OnCourse can frame hours studied as questions mastered and progress toward the exam, never as time spent on a phone.

Key points.title: End on one personal next step, not a dead end
Key points.detail: Wrapped ends by priming next year's edition, which the author found anti-climactic. The redesign ends with one curated song you missed, hidden until tapped, using personalisation, FOMO, the Singularity Effect (one item is less effort than a playlist) and the curiosity gap. Sharing grows each year through the Bandwagon Effect, since music reflects identity.

Chapters.title: The teaser notification
Chapters.summary: A week-early notification primes curiosity; the hook could be more emotional.

Chapters.title: Anticipation and the reveal
Chapters.summary: Not knowing your top artist makes the reveal rewarding.

Chapters.title: Storytelling
Chapters.summary: Copy and a listening timeline turn data into a personal story.

Chapters.title: Fresh animations
Chapters.summary: New visual styles each year make it memorable.

Chapters.title: Numbers framed as value
Chapters.summary: Time spent is tied to memories, unlike Screen Time.

Chapters.title: Social sharing
Chapters.summary: Everyone posting makes others want to join in.

Start here.why: It shows how to present study time as progress rather than effort, the key choice in any OnCourse progress recap.

Title: 5 Deadly Onboarding Mistakes You Should Avoid
Creator: Growth.Design
Bottom line: In the first minute, deliver the promise the user came for; don't ask for notifications, push a fake-urgent sale, or punish a "no" before they've seen any value.
What they did: The comic follows a user who downloads a sleep-cycle alarm clock app with high hopes. In the first seconds it asks for notification permission with vague copy, hides how the promised optimal wake-up works, shows a full-screen discount with a countdown, then a "gift" offer and ads after the user says no. The user deletes the app, and the comic lists five mistakes.
Results: Growth.Design cites Localytics: "Almost 1 out of 4 people will delete your app after the first use" ("21% churn on the 1st use").
Takeaways: Ask for notifications after the first aha moment; Name exactly which notifications they'll get; Show the promised land in the first session; Fake scarcity in the first seconds destroys trust; Pushing again after a no triggers reactance
Ideas for OnCourse: Notifications: move the permission ask to right after the first completed practice set, and list the exact reminders (daily plan at a set time, streak at risk) instead of "relevant notifications". Onboarding: show the user's exam countdown and first plan before any paywall. Paywall: never open with a countdown discount in the first session, and don't re-show the offer as a "gift" right after a dismissal

Key points.title: Ask for notifications after the first aha moment
Key points.detail: The app asked for notification permission on the very first screen. Growth.Design: "Never ask for reciprocity if you haven't given anything." Ask after users have their first aha moment, when they trust you most with their attention. For OnCourse, that is after the first finished practice set.

Key points.title: Name exactly which notifications they'll get
Key points.detail: The prompt promised "relevant notifications," which made the user worry instead. Specific copy builds trust, so list each kind of notification instead of leaving people guessing. OnCourse can say exactly what it will send and when.

Key points.title: Show the promised land in the first session
Key points.detail: The user came to wake up refreshed, but nothing on the first screen explained the optimal wake-up time. Users arrive with a specific intent, so remind them in the first experience why they came. An OnCourse new user should see their exam, their date and a path to it right away.

Key points.title: Fake scarcity in the first seconds destroys trust
Key points.detail: Within about 10 seconds a full-screen pop-up showed a big discount, "limited time offer" and a countdown, with a sleeping child and cat. Scarcity drives purchases, but "nothing here justifies the sudden urgency." Faking it is a dark pattern.

Key points.title: Pushing again after a no triggers reactance
Key points.detail: After declining, the user saw a "gift" that looked like the same urgent offer, then ads that felt like punishment for not buying. When people feel their freedom is threatened, it can "trigger an angry motivation to regain it." The user deleted the app; Growth.Design cites that almost 1 in 4 people delete an app after the first use.

Chapters.title: Notifications too early
Chapters.summary: Asking before giving value breaks trust.

Chapters.title: Vague copy
Chapters.summary: "Relevant notifications" makes users suspicious.

Chapters.title: Missing the promised land

Title: Obsessing Over Onboarding for 10+ Years — The Architect of Superhuman's Onboarding Shares His Playbook
Creator: First Round Review (Gaurav Vohra)
Bottom line: Onboard early users by hand to learn what they need, then build self-serve onboarding that is opinionated, interruptive and interactive, not a corner checklist.
What they did: Superhuman ran 30-minute human onboarding calls for every new customer for five years, then spent three years turning those lessons into in-product onboarding. The self-serve version was modelled on video games: a Mario 1-1 style demo, full-screen setup steps that could not be skipped, and a fake inbox where users practise safely. They cut the first demo down to the one goal that mattered, Inbox Zero, and taught features like Undo Send at the moment they are useful.
Results: "Over 65% of new customers fully transitioned their email to Superhuman after their human-led onboarding", "more than double" what they saw with no onboarding. When the call was made optional, attendance was "15% — down from 100%". Focusing the demo on Inbox Zero: "'e' and 'h' usage increased by 50%, and self-serve activation rates improved by 25%, from 40% to 50%." A tucked-away checklist: "Only 50% of users completed each task, and only 30% of users completed all tasks", with "no change in activation rates". Rebuilt as full-screen steps: completion went "from 30% to over 98%" and feature opt-in "from 45% to nearly 80%". "57% of new users opt in to 'Get Me To Zero'."
Takeaways: Onboard users by hand before you automate it; Teach one opinionated goal, not every control; Hidden checklists did nothing; full-screen steps worked; Let users try a feature at the right moment; Pick one main user and job, then branch
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: replace any skippable tips or checklist with 3-4 full-screen setup steps (exam, exam date, daily time) that have smart defaults so aspirants can tap through fast. Practice: make the first session a real 5-question set where the app teaches one thing at a time at the moment it matters, like the explanation after the first wrong answer. Design process: run 10 live onboarding calls with new aspirants and log every point of friction before redesigning onboarding.

Key points.title: Onboard users by hand before you automate it
Key points.detail: Early calls ran 90 minutes: 30 minutes of discovery, then 60 minutes of onboarding. Each call produced "10 pages of notes, 5-10 feature requests, and 5-10 bugs". Human-led onboarding gave nearly 2x the activation of self-serve, though the author notes selection bias. For OnCourse, a few live onboarding calls with new aspirants would show where the first session breaks.

Key points.title: Teach one opinionated goal, not every control
Key points.detail: The first self-serve demo taught navigation keys like "j" and "k", which felt like making users "eat their vegetables". The next version taught only the controls for Inbox Zero: "e" (done) and "h" (remind). Activation rose from 40% to 50%. OnCourse's first session should teach the one action that matters most, such as answering a question and seeing the explanation.

Key points.title: Hidden checklists did nothing; full-screen steps worked
Key points.detail: Checklists, tooltips and timed nudges "yielded zero impact" at Superhuman. Moving the same steps into full-screen panels before the main product, with smart defaults so users could zip through, raised completion from 30% to over 98%. The golden rule: only interrupt for something extremely valuable, which filters out 90% of ideas.

Key points.title: Let users try a feature at the right moment
Key points.detail: Undo Send is taught in the split second after sending, and pressing "Z" in the alert really undoes the send. The core of onboarding is a synthetic inbox that is "fully interactive and entirely safe". The rule is do > show > tell. OnCourse could teach features like bookmarking a question or flagging a doubt right after a wrong answer, inside a real question.

Key points.title: Pick one main user and job, then branch
Key points.detail: Onboarding can only be opinionated if the product is. Teams fail when they lack conviction about who the main user is, fear backlash, or reach for drop-in widgets. Pick the main user and their main job, build the best flow for them, then branch by persona (like Netflix or Notion asking for interests or use case). Rapid tests make bold steps, like removing Skip, less risky.

Title: Defining Growth Design: The Guide to the Role Most Startups are Missing
Creator: First Round Review (Angel Steger)
Bottom line: Growth design is half design and half growth: cut choices, protect user intent, and judge experiments by the outcome that brings people back, not raw volume.
What they did: Angel Steger, who led growth design at Pinterest and Dropbox, explains what growth designers do differently. At Pinterest her team cut the send flow from about 11 actions to three, then added a personal-message step that slowed sending but raised responses. She also lists the questions she asks designers about any growth screen and how to staff the role.
Results: Pinterest's mobile send flow had "about 11 different sending actions". Cutting it to "just three categories of sending" "increased the original sending rate almost seven-fold". Adding a personal-message step "decreased the overall volume of sends slightly ... but it increased the response rate." Her growth design teams grew "from three to eight" at Pinterest and "from six to more than 20" at Dropbox.
Takeaways: Clear design makes experiments finish faster; Cutting 11 send options to 3 raised sending sevenfold; Keep friction that creates ownership; Measure the outcome that matters, not volume; Never replace the user's action with an upsell; Chainsaw first, then chisel
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: when a free user taps a locked item, open the item's preview first and show the upgrade inside it, so the upsell never replaces what they meant to do. Practice: judge any end-of-session experiment by next-day return and questions completed, not by taps on the share or extra-practice buttons. Design process: use Steger's five questions (problem, who and how often, emotional context, main action, why they care) as the opening checklist in every crit.

Key points.title: Clear design makes experiments finish faster
Key points.detail: Teams often trim design details to ship experiments sooner. Steger argues clearer screens let users act quickly, so tests reach statistical significance faster, and skipping design "can add weeks". For OnCourse, a rough paywall test may need longer to read than a clean one.

Key points.title: Cutting 11 send options to 3 raised sending sevenfold
Key points.detail: Pinterest found people "send" pins to a person rather than "share" them to many. The mobile flow had about 11 send actions. Cutting to three categories raised the sending rate almost seven-fold. Fewer decisions means more people decide.

Key points.title: Keep friction that creates ownership
Key points.detail: Not all friction is bad. Research showed that naming your own Pinterest board mattered, and auto-naming it made the product "less sticky". The job is to reduce cognitive load, not to remove every choice. An OnCourse aspirant choosing their own exam date may work the same way.

Key points.title: Measure the outcome that matters, not volume
Key points.detail: Adding a personal message to sends lowered send volume slightly but raised the response rate, which was the real value: "No one wants to share to a void." She also warns about wins where users in the lab showed a "bad hookup face". Judge OnCourse tests on things like next-day return, not taps.

Key points.title: Never replace the user's action with an upsell
Key points.detail: In an interview, a candidate showed an upsell where the share flow should be. Steger asked how that served the user's intent: "when someone is in the middle of something, they have very explicit intent." Her five review questions cover the core problem, who sees it, their emotional context, the most important action, and why they would care.

Key points.title: Chainsaw first, then chisel
Key points.detail: Like carving ice into a dolphin, start rough to find where the problem is, then refine. Sometimes the right tool is no design at all: pull data, talk to a user, or show a paper sketch. Speed means velocity with crisp execution, not haste.

Title: From Figma's design team: How to run a design critique
Creator: Figma (Noah Levin)
Bottom line: Agree what crits are for, then pick from six named formats (standard, jam, pair, silent, print-out, FYI) to fit the problem.
What they did: Figma's design team ran a "critique of critiques" after finding crits crowded, shallow and too nice. They set four goals for crit and ruled out roadmap decisions. They then wrote six named crit methods, each with when to use it and how to run it, plus ten tips such as two topics per hour and a timer.
Takeaways: Crits exist to unblock, not to decide roadmaps; Say what feedback you want, and what you don't; Round-the-room beats popcorn for quiet voices; Pair design gives a lone designer a copilot; Silent crits get the most feedback, fast; Two topics per hour, and plan 30 minutes ahead
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: open every OnCourse crit with one slide on the screen's goal, the feedback wanted and the feedback not wanted. Design process: for async review with PM and engineers, run a 20-minute silent crit where everyone comments in the Figma file at the same time. Design process: name a standing copilot (PM or engineer) for each big project such as the Paywall redesign, and pair with them weekly.

Key points.title: Crits exist to unblock, not to decide roadmaps
Key points.detail: The four goals are unblocking problems and generating ideas, raising quality, encouraging consistency, and sharing context. "Making major product decisions" is deliberately not a goal, so crit stays a safe space. The presenter owns the format because crit exists to help them.

Key points.title: Say what feedback you want, and what you don't
Key points.detail: A standard crit runs about 10-15 minutes of context, 2-5 minutes of clarifying questions, then 10+ minutes of feedback. The presenter includes a slide on "Here's the feedback I am looking for" and "Here's what I'm NOT looking for". If the goals are missed, "their feedback will be misdirected."

Key points.title: Round-the-room beats popcorn for quiet voices
Key points.detail: Round-the-room gives each person about two minutes with no interruptions, and people may pass. Popcorn is freeform and faster but "can reward the 'loudest voice'". The presenter should thank people rather than defend each point.

Key points.title: Pair design gives a lone designer a copilot
Key points.detail: Pair design in groups of two or three was the team's most popular alternative format. Because a small startup can't put several designers on one problem, they assign a part-time "copilot" so the lead feels "less alone while solving a problem." On a small team like OnCourse, a PM or engineer can play that role.

Key points.title: Silent crits get the most feedback, fast
Key points.detail: In a silent crit everyone reviews a file and comments in writing at the same time, so many threads run in parallel. It needs more prep because all context must live in the document. A scheduled slot makes sure people actually review the work.

Key points.title: Two topics per hour, and plan 30 minutes ahead
Key points.detail: Topics "always take at least 10 minutes more than people think", so Figma caps crits at two topics per hour and uses a timer. Presenters spend 30 minutes beforehand deciding what they need. A note-taker's summary worked better than raw transcripts.

Title: Figma on Figma: Our approach to designing UI3
Creator: Figma (Jenny Xie)
Bottom line: A redesign needs a clear vision, but beta metrics and feedback should be allowed to reverse even core decisions, and users need a way back while they adjust.
What they did: Figma spent over two years redesigning its interface (UI3) around keeping work at the centre. In open beta, feature adoption, performance data and feedback showed the new floating panels slowed heavy users, so the team re-docked them before full launch. They also reverted a dropdown to a checkbox, ran 60-minute "speed round" crits for two months, rebuilt labels for accessibility, and let users opt out during the beta.
Takeaways: Beta data reversed a headline design decision; An extra tap is a reason to revert; Speed-round crits for a large redesign; Accessibility can be a dealbreaker for a minimal idea; Give users a way back during a redesign
Ideas for OnCourse: Home: ship any big Home redesign behind a flag with a way back to the old layout for a few weeks, and track time to start the first question, not only opinions. Practice: in any new layout, count taps to answer and review a question; if the new version adds a tap, revert that control. Design process: for a multi-screen refresh, run 60-minute speed-round crits where everyone comments on all screens at once.

Key points.title: Beta data reversed a headline design decision
Key points.detail: Floating panels looked friendly but cramped the canvas on small screens and moved rulers away from designs. "The nail in the coffin was learning that they slowed people down," said PM KC Oh. The team re-docked the panels, still resizable, for the full launch. Speed counted as a feature.

Key points.title: An extra tap is a reason to revert
Key points.detail: Blend mode was hidden behind an icon, which forced users to wait for a tooltip. Clip content became a dropdown in beta but "caused an extra click", so it went back to a checkbox. "Better to have riffed and lost, than to never have riffed at all."

Key points.title: Speed-round crits for a large redesign
Key points.detail: Instead of the usual 30-minute crits, the team ran 60-minute "speed rounds" where everyone commented on each other's work at once, for two months. People self-selected into visual details or flows. It surfaced every context the slider component had to support.

Key points.title: Accessibility can be a dealbreaker for a minimal idea
Key points.detail: A minimal label and tooltip system looked promising but would have hurt accessibility, which UX writer Hoi Fung Ho called "a deal breaker". Visible labels now match screen reader labels. Having a clear reason, "This is what we're doing, and here's why", removed the team's doubts.

Key points.title: Give users a way back during a redesign
Key points.detail: Users could opt out of UI3 during the beta, so a Friday deadline didn't clash with a new interface. The gradual rollout also gave time to process feedback and write tutorials. When weighing criticism, ask if it is just a reaction to change, and if positive feedback balances it.

Title: 4 new ways to go from idea to product with AI tools
Creator: Figma (Emma Webster)
Bottom line: Choose where to start by the question you need answered: code for logic-heavy flows, an AI agent on the canvas for wide exploration, a prototype instead of a PRD, and MCP to carry the design system into code.
What they did: Figma talked to four teams about AI workflows. FloQast tested a multi-step accounting flow as a coded prototype with simulated data. Merkle used Figma's agent to generate about 50 layout variations. Accor built a working Make prototype to align leadership. Affirm prototyped payment-plan badges in Make and passed components and tokens through MCP into Cursor for production code.
Results: At Affirm, a PM went "from idea to working prototype in two days instead of the usual six weeks". At Merkle, the designer started with seven layouts and asked the agent for 10 variations at a time "until he'd generated about 50"; "production work that would have taken days was compressed into hours."
Takeaways: Prototype in code when the logic is the design; Use an AI agent to exhaust the options; A working prototype aligns people better than a deck; Pass the design system into code with MCP
Ideas for OnCourse: Today's plan: prototype the plan in code with realistic simulated students (missed days, weak subjects, exam in 30 days) before polishing mockups, to see where the logic breaks. Paywall: ask an AI agent for 30+ layout and copy variations of the Paywall header, then pick 3 to test. Design process: connect OnCourse's React Native components and tokens to the coding agent through MCP so prototypes use real components from the first prompt.

Key points.title: Prototype in code when the logic is the design
Key points.detail: FloQast's new page had steps where finishing one triggered the next, which a mockup couldn't show. A UX manager built a coded prototype with a simulated backend and data based on a real customer's workflow. The team found flows "that looked right on the surface but fell apart in practice". Use this when screens change with conditions you can't judge in a mockup.

Key points.title: Use an AI agent to exhaust the options
Key points.detail: Merkle's designer sketched seven loose directions, then asked the agent for 10 variations at a time until about 50 existed and it ran out of new combinations. He then used it for realistic placeholder copy, spec annotations, and a review that flagged missed screen reader issues. The win was depth of exploration, not just speed.

Key points.title: A working prototype aligns people better than a deck
Key points.detail: Accor's brand designer built a page that reshapes itself around what the user types, such as "golf". Within days it was concrete enough to start a real conversation with leadership. Use this when an idea is too nuanced for a document.

Key points.title: Pass the design system into code with MCP
Key points.detail: Affirm needed badges on payment plans across desktop, mobile web, Android and iOS. After designers refined the winner, the MCP server passed components, tokens and layout into Cursor, where an agent generated front-end code. Developers started from code that already matched the design, so "What shipped matched what the designers intended."

Title: Creating coherence: How Spotify’s design system goes beyond platforms
Creator: Figma (Juli Sombat, Spotify)
Bottom line: Spotify's design system moved from too much flexibility to shared cross-platform components, each started with a written outline of terms, anatomy, states and variants.
What they did: Spotify's Encore design system had a very flexible mobile catalogue, and by 2022 "the pendulum had swung too far towards flexibility". A new team built reusable cross-platform components. Each starts with platform audits, then a shared "component outline" before detailed design. Buttons were unified into primary, secondary and tertiary with a size framework built on Figma variables.
Takeaways: Too much flexibility breaks consistency; Write a component outline before you design it; One button hierarchy, one size framework; Aim for cohesion, not identical screens; One lead per component, few active projects
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: before redesigning a shared component like the MCQ option card, write a one-page outline with its anatomy, states (default, selected, correct, wrong, disabled) and variants. Design process: define primary, secondary and tertiary buttons with a size scale as tokens, and audit Home, Practice and Paywall against it.

Key points.title: Too much flexibility breaks consistency
Key points.detail: Encore Consumer Mobile was a "vast catalog of ever-growing and evolving UI components". By 2022 teams wanted more refined, reusable parts, so Spotify built a layer between the foundation and the mobile catalogue. Components were designed cross-platform from the start, not as an afterthought.

Key points.title: Write a component outline before you design it
Key points.detail: Each platform rep audits the component and diagrams what is unique to their surface. The group then agrees on naming, specs and accessibility needs. The outline "might include a glossary of terms, the anatomy of the component, or any variants we need to support", and it lays the foundation for detailed design.

Key points.title: One button hierarchy, one size framework
Key points.detail: Buttons used to differ in sizes, interactions, padding and type steps. Encore unified them into primary, secondary and tertiary, with a size framework and naming built on variables. The result was a family of buttons "right in the sweet spot between consistency and chaos".

Key points.title: Aim for cohesion, not identical screens
Key points.detail: Spotify treats cohesion as "the middle path between perfect consistency and total platform independence". Start from a shared foundation, then let platforms adjust for screen size or input. The advice: define what is non-negotiable.

Key points.title: One lead per component, few active projects
Key points.detail: Many platforms and teams make coordination hard. Encore picks one project lead per component who pulls in platform experts as needed. They also limit the number of active projects and communicate early.

Title: Sketch, Scroll, or Swipe?
Creator: Google Design (Garen Checkley, Phil Madeley, Aysha Siddique, Peter Finlan)
Bottom line: When testing in the field, choose paper, a printed scroll, an offline swipe-through or a motion prototype based on location, bandwidth and how people relate to technology.
What they did: Google's Next Billion Users researchers explain how to pick a prototype for field testing, starting from a research trip in India. They compare paper prototypes, printed "scrolls", digital prototypes and offline swipe-throughs, with pros and cons of each. They also describe a study where a static prototype confused people until motion was added.
Takeaways: The test device can distract from the design; Test copy on paper; A scroll walks people through a journey; Swipe-throughs work offline on common phones; Static prototypes can fail where motion succeeds
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: test new screens with aspirants on budget Android phones like the ones they use, with the prototype saved offline, since hostel Wi-Fi is often weak. Paywall: test Paywall and Renewal copy as paper printouts first, so students read the words instead of tapping through. Flashcards: prototype swipe gestures with real motion before testing, since a static mockup may confuse people about how to swipe.

Key points.title: The test device can distract from the design
Key points.detail: In India, a Google designer showed a prototype to a fruit vendor, who was distracted by the phone's bright screen because he had used a second-hand phone with a broken screen for years. Context changes responses. Start with paper, or test on the kind of phone people actually use.

Key points.title: Test copy on paper
Key points.detail: People with digital prototypes tend to press buttons instead of reading. Paper slows them down "long enough to read the text", so it is best for testing UI copy. Paper may also reduce polite, positive feedback, and cutting it to phone size helps.

Key points.title: A scroll walks people through a journey
Key points.detail: Print one page per step, number them, tape them end to end and roll them up. The participant unrolls it at their own pace and narrates what they think is happening. It is cheap feedback on several concepts before building any of them.

Key points.title: Swipe-throughs work offline on common phones
Key points.detail: Load screenshots onto a real phone or SD card and let people swipe through as if tapping. It works with weak internet and before the backend exists. Test on the phones common in that community, and always bring a paper backup.

Key points.title: Static prototypes can fail where motion succeeds
Key points.detail: In one study, a static stack of cards confused most people, who didn't know to swipe. A high-fidelity version with motion got most people swiping straight away. The confusion came from the prototype, not the design.

Title: Simulating Intelligence
Creator: Google Design (Mike Dory, Mindy DelliCarpini)
Bottom line: Before building an AI feature, fake it: match prototype fidelity to the question, use humans behind the curtain (Wizard of Oz), and later test how the real model fails.
What they did: Google UX engineers describe how they prototype machine learning features. Early on they answer "Should we do this?" with simulated, low-fidelity prototypes, often with humans standing in for the model. Later they answer "Could we do this?" with prototypes close to production, to find errors, bias and recovery needs, as with the AIY Vision Kit's odd guesses.
Takeaways: Match prototype fidelity to the problem; Fake the AI with a human (Wizard of Oz); Only build the part you are testing; Later, test how the real model fails
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: Wizard-of-Oz test an AI "explain my mistake" feature, with a doctor on the team writing replies live while 5 aspirants use the prototype. Today's plan: hand-build personalised plans for a few students from their mock test scores before building any algorithm, and see if they follow them. Practice: design a clear "This explanation seems wrong" path for any AI answer, since the model will sometimes be wrong.

Key points.title: Match prototype fidelity to the problem
Key points.detail: First name the question, from "Does anyone find this useful?" to a tactical one. If a feature takes six months to build, that's "five-and-a-half months too late" to learn it was flawed. Broad questions get wireframes or paper; fidelity rises as ideas firm up.

Key points.title: Fake the AI with a human (Wizard of Oz)
Key points.detail: Build a real-looking experience and have people play the system. In personalisation studies, participants share preferences, then assistants quickly customise the screens in real time while participants do scripted tasks. You get feedback on "personalized" results without building the model.

Key points.title: Only build the part you are testing
Key points.detail: Simulate or skip parts of the UI that aren't being tested. Use ready-made design systems like Material and simple storage like Firebase or a spreadsheet. Spend nothing on things unrelated to the one workflow under test.

Key points.title: Later, test how the real model fails
Key points.detail: Later prototypes use real models to check accuracy, bias in training data, and typical errors. The Vision Kit classifier listed things users didn't mean and things that weren't there, like "a bobsled in a meeting room". The team had to guide users through these errors in the documentation. Design ways to recover when the AI is wrong.

Title: Creating the Airbnb Design System
Creator: Airbnb Design (Karri Saarinen)
Bottom line: A small team printed every screen to find where the app broke, set a loose foundation, then built a component library that let them make about 50 screens in a few hours.
What they did: A small group of Airbnb designers and engineers cleared their calendars and worked from a studio outside HQ to build the Design Language System, starting with iOS and Android. They printed old and new flows side by side to audit them, set four principles, and reviewed work daily to spot patterns. Components were defined with required and optional elements in both Sketch and code, and kept in one master library.
Results: With the library, the team "was able to create nearly 50 screens within just a few hours" for a last-minute prototype. Features can now ship "on all native platforms at roughly the same time".
Takeaways: Print every screen to see where things break; A loose foundation keeps everyone aligned; Components are organisms, not loose atoms; A library makes high-fidelity prototyping cheap; Get rows right and document as you go
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: lay out every OnCourse screen side by side (Home, Today's plan, Practice, Lessons, Flashcards, Paywall) and mark each place where headers, cards or rows don't match. Practice: give the row components (question row, lesson row, flashcard deck row) a strict set of required and optional elements, since rows repeat most.

Key points.title: Print every screen to see where things break
Key points.detail: The team audited by printing many designs, old and new, and laying the flows side by side on a board. That showed "where and how the experiences were breaking". Each person then took a screen or area to redesign.

Key points.title: A loose foundation keeps everyone aligned
Key points.detail: A basic style guide covered typography, colours, icons, spacing and information architecture. It guided everyone in one direction while leaving room to explore. Reviewing the day's work together each evening revealed patterns that became standard components.

Key points.title: Components are organisms, not loose atoms
Key points.detail: Reusable atoms tend to be combined in endless ways, which leads to disjointed experiences. Airbnb defined each component by required and optional elements. For example, every component has a built-in divider that view logic shows or hides, instead of designers adding loose divider lines.

Key points.title: A library makes high-fidelity prototyping cheap
Key points.detail: After a week or two, using the master library brought "huge leaps in productivity", including nearly 50 screens in a few hours. Product reviews could then focus on concepts instead of "padding, colors and type choices".

Key points.title: Get rows right and document as you go
Key points.detail: Saarinen wishes they had spent more time on rows, the most repeated component, because they ended up with many inconsistent kinds. A tight timeline also meant skipped documentation, which caused confusion. Document while you build, just like code.

Title: Running productive design critiques
Creator: Intercom (Gustavs Cirulis)
Bottom line: Before showing any design, name the problem in one plain paragraph, then show several named, separate options and say which one you'd pick.
What they did: Intercom's design team runs crits with 1-5 people from different roles. The designer defines the goal and the problem, shows several clearly named options (often printed on the wall), and diagrams how each works as a system before showing UI. Notes and next steps go to a #design-notes Slack channel.
Takeaways: Invite 1-5 people with different views; Name the problem in one plain paragraph; Keep options separate and named; Diagram the system before the UI; Open the discussion with your own pick
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: start every OnCourse crit doc with a one-paragraph problem that includes a PostHog number, such as the share of new users who finish their first Today's plan. Design process: present 2-3 named options (for example "Plan-first Home" vs "Streak-first Home") separately, then state which one you'd pick and why.

Key points.title: Invite 1-5 people with different views
Key points.detail: Bring designers, engineers, support reps and others. The designer leading the crit defines the goal, the problem, the possible solutions and the kind of feedback needed. Printing posters of the problem and options avoids "Can you scroll back to that design?"

Key points.title: Name the problem in one plain paragraph
Key points.detail: Give the problem a simple name and describe it in plain English, for example: "Only 5% of new sign ups invite their colleagues in the first 7 days." Show it with a diagram or screenshots, and include Job Stories for motivation. Without this, people can't judge the designs.

Key points.title: Keep options separate and named
Key points.detail: Show several radically different options, each with a name and a one-paragraph description. Don't mix ideas, "Otherwise you might dismiss a good solution just because it was coupled with a bad one." Be brutally honest about the good and bad in each.

Key points.title: Diagram the system before the UI
Key points.detail: For connected products, draw a high-level map of how the design behaves as a system before diving into interface detail. If people focus on interaction details while the system is still open, say it is too early and steer them back.

Key points.title: Open the discussion with your own pick
Key points.detail: Start by saying which option you think works best and why. Others will quickly push back, improve it or argue for options you didn't show. If someone asks why you're solving this at all, treat it as a useful sanity check.

Title: Intercom's product principles: How connected, modular systems help us to focus on important decisions
Creator: Intercom (Gustavs Cirulis)
Bottom line: Design the system first (objects and how data flows between them), then interaction, then visuals, so feedback lands on the most important decisions first.
What they did: Intercom designer Gustavs Cirulis used to share high-fidelity mockups and get stuck on small interaction debates while people had different mental models of the product. He now starts with a system design diagram. Intercom also merged separate message types into one modular system, and connected Product Tours to its support tools so one feature served many uses.
Takeaways: Hi-fi mockups hide different mental models; Draw the system before any screen; Layer feedback: system, interaction, then visual; Build once, reuse everywhere; Connected systems create unique value
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: before mockups for Streaks or Today's plan, draw a system diagram of the objects (plan, session, streak, reminder) and how data flows between them, and crit that first. Notifications: design one modular reminder system (timing, copy slot, deep link, quiet hours) that streak, plan and renewal reminders all reuse.

Key points.title: Hi-fi mockups hide different mental models
Key points.detail: When Cirulis shared polished mockups, the team argued about small interaction details when "we just had different mental models of how the system should work." Months after shipping they'd find a fundamental mistake. The problem was designing at the UI level, not the system level.

Key points.title: Draw the system before any screen
Key points.detail: A system design shows the objects in your solution and how data flows between them. For the Articles product, a diagram showed how teammates manage content, how users read it, how it gets sent in replies, and how feedback improves it. They aligned without a screen to distract them.

Key points.title: Layer feedback: system, interaction, then visual
Key points.detail: The same system can be built many ways in interaction and visual design. Working through the layers in order means "the right feedback is given at the right time." There is no use sweating visual details before the system is agreed.

Key points.title: Build once, reuse everywhere
Key points.detail: In-app messages, email, SMS, Product Tours and Banners each had slightly different targeting, A/B testing and goals. That made every improvement a separate job. Intercom merged them into one modular system so improvements reach all message types at once.

Key points.title: Connected systems create unique value
Key points.detail: Product Tours were built for onboarding but connected to bots, the support inbox, banners, help articles and email. Building them only for support wouldn't have been worth it, but connecting them made it cheap and different from competitors.
