Title: Stardust Increases Revenue by 4x in Just Six Weeks
Creator: Superwall (Nick Godwin)
Bottom line: Fix the price and how it is shown first, run tests in overlapping layers, and test the paywall's look only after that.
What they did: Stardust, a cycle and pregnancy tracking app with 1.5M+ downloads, had not changed its paywall in over a year. In about six weeks it ran four layered A/B tests: free trial and price, price presentation (a discount badge and weekly equivalent price), a combined-winners test that included a video background, and a trial timeline design. Each winner became the control for the next test.
Results: Adding a free trial to the $24.99 yearly price gave "a stunning 131% increase in paywall conversion rate"; once trials ended, the trial "increased average proceeds per user by 78% and 45% more paying subscribers." Showing a discount percentage and weekly equivalent price "increased the conversion rate by 50%" and proceeds per user "increased by 62.5% due to a 30% increase in the share of new yearly subscriptions." The combined winners with a video background gave "a 67% paywall conversion increase and a 12.5% proceeds per user increase." The trial timeline added a "13.6% conversion rate increase" without hurting trial-to-paid. In total, conversion rate "had grown by 465%", install-to-paying subscriber rate "increased by 252%" and average proceeds per user "increased by 408%."
Takeaways: Start with price and packaging, not visuals; Wait for trials to end before calling a price test; Show the saving and a per-week price; Run tests in layers to learn faster; Combine winners, then test the design; A trial timeline lifts trial starts without hurting retention
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: show the annual plan's saving as a percentage badge and its per-week price in rupees next to it. Paywall: test a free trial on the annual plan and only read the result after every trial in the test has ended. Design process: start a paywall design test while a price test's trials are still maturing, so two questions get answered at once

Key points.title: Start with price and packaging, not visuals
Key points.detail: Stardust had never tested prices, and its two plans showed only price and duration, with no saving or equivalent price. Superwall says value perception depends "as much to do with price presentation design as the actual prices." So the first two tests were about the offer and how it was shown, not colours or images. For OnCourse, the first paywall tests should be about plans, trial and price display.

Key points.title: Wait for trials to end before calling a price test
Key points.detail: The first test compared a control and five price variants, with and without free trials. Every trial variant raised conversion, but the team paused the test until all trials ended so trial-to-paid data could mature. Only then could they confirm the trial raised proceeds per user by 78% and paying subscribers by 45%. Higher prices without a trial converted worse and earned about the same per user.

Key points.title: Show the saving and a per-week price
Key points.detail: Keeping the same prices ($24.99 a year, $2.99 a week), the team tested three layouts. Adding a discount percentage on the yearly plan plus a weekly equivalent price won, with 50% more conversions and 62.5% more proceeds per user. Leading with yearly behind a 'More Pricing' drawer, and showing only the yearly plan, both lost on conversion and proceeds. OnCourse could show the annual plan as a per-week or per-day amount.

Key points.title: Run tests in layers to learn faster
Key points.detail: The second test started while the first test's trials were still running. Superwall calls this experimentation layering: start a new test while the last one waits for trial or retention data. The key is that the second test must answer a question that does not depend on the first test's result. This doubled how fast a lean team could learn.

Key points.title: Combine winners, then test the design
Key points.detail: Test three combined the trial pricing and the new price layout, and added variants like a monthly plan and a video background. The combined winners beat the new control by 55.7%, but the version with a video background won outright with 67% more conversions. Only then did the team test a trial timeline, which added 13.6% more trial starts without lowering trial-to-paid. Design changes paid off once the offer was right.

Title: Multi-page onboarding paywalls convert 37% better than single-page. Here's why.
Creator: Superwall (Michal Parizek)
Bottom line: At the end of onboarding, a short paywall flow of two or three focused screens converts better than one screen that tries to do everything.
What they did: Superwall looked at just over 40 million onboarding paywall opens from February to May 2026. It compared single-page paywalls with multi-page flows of two or more screens, after removing paywalls with zero transactions and requiring at least 50 opens. It then explained why splitting the job across screens helps.
Results: "Single-page paywalls achieved a 9.07% conversion rate, while multi-page paywalls converted at 12.41% — a 37% improvement." Multi-page paywalls accounted "for just 24% of onboarding paywall opens." Conversion is trial starts or direct purchases divided by users who viewed the paywall at onboarding placements.
Takeaways: Multi-page paywalls converted 37% better; One screen has too many jobs; Give each screen one purpose; Start with two or three screens; This is a benchmark, not a controlled test
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: at the end of onboarding, split the paywall into three screens: what OnCourse will do for the aspirant's exam, how the trial and reminder work, then plans and price. Onboarding: make the paywall screens look like the onboarding screens before them, so the extra steps feel like part of setup

Key points.title: Multi-page paywalls converted 37% better
Key points.detail: Across 40M+ onboarding paywall opens, multi-page flows converted at 12.41% against 9.07% for single-page. Multi-page was still the rarer format, at just 24% of opens. Superwall says that if you only run a single-page onboarding paywall, multi-page is "the test to run next."

Key points.title: One screen has too many jobs
Key points.detail: A single-page paywall must show value, answer worries, show prices and ask for payment all at once. Superwall says this "creates an overwhelming experience on one screen." Onboarding is the peak of motivation, so it is a waste to overload the user right then.

Key points.title: Give each screen one purpose
Key points.detail: A multi-page flow spreads the work: first the value, then what to expect, then pricing once the user knows why it matters, then payment. Because users are already moving through setup screens, extra screens feel natural rather than like friction. For OnCourse, each paywall screen should have one clear message.

Key points.title: Start with two or three screens
Key points.detail: The advice is not to add screens for the sake of it. Start with "two to three screens that establish value before requesting payment" and let real data guide the next change. Superwall links templates such as a 'Design your trial' flow and a flow with a carousel page.

Key points.title: This is a benchmark, not a controlled test
Key points.detail: The numbers compare different apps' paywalls, not the same app's users split at random. Apps that bother to build multi-page flows may also be better at other things. Treat 37% as a reason to run your own test, not as the lift you will get.

Title: How many products should you offer on your paywall?
Creator: Superwall (Jake Mor)
Bottom line: Paywalls that offer two or three plans convert more than one-plan paywalls, as long as each plan is worth about the same over a user's lifetime.
What they did: Superwall pulled conversion data from 32M+ paywall opens and grouped it by how many products each paywall showed. It only used apps that had run at least two tests with a different number of products, and took the 15 largest apps, each with more than 10,000 views. The post is from November 2022.
Results: "Conversions: 383,889"; "Paywall Opens: 32,303,995"; "Conversion Rate: 3.77%". 2 products beat 1 product by a "61%" lift; 3 products beat 2 products by a "44%" lift.
Takeaways: Two plans beat one by 61%; Three plans beat two by 44%; One annual plan only if you need cash now; Keep lifetime value equal across plans; The data leaves out price, default and trial
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: if the paywall shows a single plan, test two or three plans (for example monthly, 6-month and till-exam) with one pre-selected. Paywall: check that each plan earns about the same per user over its life, so a cheaper short plan does not drain long-term revenue

Key points.title: Two plans beat one by 61%
Key points.detail: Across 32,303,995 paywall opens and 383,889 conversions, paywalls with two products converted 61% better than paywalls with one. The average conversion rate across the set was 3.77%. Giving people a choice seems to turn 'buy or not' into 'which one'.

Key points.title: Three plans beat two by 44%
Key points.detail: Adding a third product lifted conversion a further 44% over two. Superwall says "in most cases, offering more than two products will result in a higher conversion rate than offering just two." A third option can also act as an anchor that makes the main plan look better.

Key points.title: One annual plan only if you need cash now
Key points.detail: If you need money up front to fund ads or running costs, Superwall says to "stick to one annual product to get money up front." If deferring some revenue will not hurt you, offer more options. This is a cash-flow choice, not just a design choice.

Key points.title: Keep lifetime value equal across plans
Key points.detail: The main warning is to make sure "your LTV for all three products is the same." Otherwise a cheap short plan can win conversions while losing long-term revenue. For OnCourse, compare what a monthly user pays over their whole stay with a till-exam plan.

Key points.title: The data leaves out price, default and trial
Key points.detail: Superwall notes the numbers do not account for how visible the extra plans were (some hide them behind 'More Pricing'), each plan's price and duration, which plan was selected by default, or whether a trial was attached. Those can change results a lot. Use it as a reason to test, not as a rule.

Title: How to know if your free tier is generous enough
Creator: RevenueCat Sub Club (David Barnard)
Bottom line: A free tier only works if non-paying users would recommend the app, so size it by watching install LTV and overall retention together, not paid conversion alone.
What they did: Opal, a screen-time app, moved from a hard paywall to a generous free tier. It tested how many 'blocks' (scheduled app restrictions) free users get, from one up to several, and watched LTV of installs and retention across free and paid users at each step. Its CEO Kenneth Schlenker uses one question as a compass: would a non-paying user recommend the app?
Results: Three blocks was the point where both metrics improved: "Turns out that three [blocks] is enough for free users to get a great experience." After the switch, pay penetration "dropped from 20% to 9%." High school and college students "now make up two-thirds of Opal's DAUs", students led to a B2B line, Opal for Schools, and the shift "pushed Opal past one million daily active users."
Takeaways: Ask if a free user would recommend the app; Paid metrics say nothing about free users; Track install LTV and overall retention together; Opal found the line at three blocks; A lower pay rate can still mean a bigger business
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: test different free daily MCQ limits and pick the one where install LTV and overall retention both rise, not the one with the highest paid conversion. Paywall: make sure the free tier lets an aspirant build a real daily habit, and keep the upgrade for heavy users who want more. Design process: ask free users in a survey if they would recommend OnCourse to a batchmate

Key points.title: Ask if a free user would recommend the app
Key points.detail: Kenneth's test is simple: would a non-paying user recommend the app to a friend? "If you want the freemium dynamic to really pay out, you need to make sure that the free users are recommending the app." If the answer is no, give more away. A free tier that only demos the product is "a trial in disguise."

Key points.title: Paid metrics say nothing about free users
Key points.detail: Conversion rate, paid penetration and LTV all measure what paying users do. None of them tell you whether non-payers are an asset or dead weight. A free tier that is too tight leads to churn before a habit forms and no word of mouth.

Key points.title: Track install LTV and overall retention together
Key points.detail: The recommendation question is a heuristic, so Opal watched two numbers in parallel: LTV of installs and retention across free and paid users. The goal was the point where both rise. If only one improves, you are helping one group at the other's expense.

Key points.title: Opal found the line at three blocks
Key points.detail: Opal tested free allowances from one block up to several. Three blocks let free users "really use the app, try out a few different things", while power users still paid for more. For OnCourse, the same idea applies to a daily free question limit or free flashcard decks.

Key points.title: A lower pay rate can still mean a bigger business
Key points.detail: Pay penetration fell from 20% to 9%, which looked scary. But students, now two-thirds of daily users, told classmates and then their schools, which created Opal for Schools. Kenneth says it is "a short-term, scary drop" that "pays back tenfold."

Title: How a switch from hard paywall to freemium led to a 75% LTV lift and a 50% conversion drop
Creator: RevenueCat Sub Club (David Barnard)
Bottom line: Hard paywalls convert about five times better than freemium, so only move to freemium with strong retention and the runway to absorb a dip, and frame the free version carefully.
What they did: Growth advisor Phil Carter made the same hard-paywall-to-freemium move for two apps. One used a multistep paywall that said the product is free forever but invited users to try the best version for seven days; the other saw conversion collapse and pulled back within weeks. The post sets this against RevenueCat's benchmark data and gives a checklist for when to switch.
Results: Hard paywalls "convert downloads to paid at a median of 10.7% — five times better than the 2.1% median for freemium apps." The hard paywall floor (4.2%) "is actually double the median for freemium." The win: "We saw a 75% increase in LTV per user through the implementation of this multistep paywall along with some other pricing and packaging optimizations." The fail: "more than a 50% reduction in subscriber conversion." Also: "55% of all 3-day trial cancellations happen on Day 0."
Takeaways: Hard paywalls convert five times better; Frame free as forever, with a 7-day taste of the best version; The same move halved conversion elsewhere; Free must be useful but not enough; Freemium is a product strategy, not a paywall style
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: if OnCourse keeps a free tier, end onboarding with a multistep paywall that says 'OnCourse is free, try Pro free for 7 days' instead of a gate. Paywall: before loosening any gate, check retention of core users and plan for a few weeks of lower conversion. Design process: treat a free-tier change as a test with a clear stop rule, like Phil's team pulling back after a couple of weeks

Key points.title: Hard paywalls convert five times better
Key points.detail: RevenueCat's State of Subscription Apps data shows hard paywalls convert downloads to paid at a median of 10.7%, against 2.1% for freemium. Even the hard paywall floor of 4.2% is double the freemium median. For bootstrapped teams, Phil calls the hard paywall "a much more reliable and low-risk way" to grow.

Key points.title: Frame free as forever, with a 7-day taste
Key points.detail: The winning app did not just open up. Its multistep paywall said: this product is free and will always be free, but try the best version for seven days, then keep paying for maximum value. Along with pricing and packaging changes, this gave a 75% increase in LTV per user and widened the top of the funnel.

Key points.title: The same move halved conversion elsewhere
Key points.detail: With a different client, the same shift cut subscriber conversion by more than 50%, and the team pulled it after a couple of weeks. Without the paywall's push, conversion depends fully on the product showing ongoing value. Phil compares the move to going "from playing checkers to playing chess."

Key points.title: Free must be useful but not enough
Key points.detail: If the free experience is too generous, nobody upgrades. If it is too tight, people churn before a habit forms. With 55% of 3-day trial cancellations on Day 0, the first session decides a lot either way.

Key points.title: Freemium is a product strategy, not a paywall style
Key points.detail: Stay hard if you are cash-constrained, need cash for paid ads, solve an acute one-off problem, or lack analytics to test gating. Consider freemium if you have strong retention, runway for a dip, network effects, or a ceiling on paid growth. Treating freemium as just a different paywall display risks halving conversion.

Title: The post-purchase screen: how to stop Day 0 cancellations
Creator: RevenueCat Sub Club (Daphne Tideman)
Bottom line: Most trial cancellations happen on Day 0, so the screen right after purchase should confirm, celebrate, remind users what they got and give one clear next step.
What they did: Daphne Tideman starts from RevenueCat's data on how early trials are cancelled, then reviews post-purchase screens from many apps (mostly via Mobbin). She ranks them in six levels, from dropping users straight into the app to giving one clear next step. She also covers two alternatives, asking for an account and offering an upsell, and how to measure a new screen.
Results: "A staggering 55.4% of 3-day trials are cancelled on Day 0." "Combine Day 0 and Day 1, and you're looking at 84% of 3-day trial cancellations happening in that first 24 hours. For 7-day trials, it's still 64%." Even with a 30-day trial "nearly a third of users cancel on the very first day", and annual subscriptions see "almost 35% of cancellations within the first month." The screens themselves are not A/B tested in the post.
Takeaways: Over half of 3-day trials die on Day 0; A confirmation screen should be the minimum; Remind users what they now have; Ask for notifications with the trial reminder reason; Give one clear first step, not a menu; Upsell only after the basics
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: after purchase, show a 'Welcome to OnCourse Pro' screen that restates what is now unlocked and the exam goal the user gave in onboarding. Notifications: on that screen ask for notification permission with the reason 'We'll remind you before your trial ends'. Today's plan: end the post-purchase flow with one button that starts the first question of today's plan

Key points.title: Over half of 3-day trials die on Day 0
Key points.detail: 55.4% of 3-day trials are cancelled on Day 0, and 84% of cancellations happen within the first 24 hours; for 7-day trials it is 64%. People hand over payment details and then something goes wrong right after. Daphne argues the missing piece is 'aftercare': what users see the moment after they convert.

Key points.title: A confirmation screen should be the minimum
Key points.detail: Many apps rely on Apple's 'You're all set' sheet and drop users into the app (Zero, MasterClass). Level 2 adds your own screen that confirms the purchase and warmly points ahead, like Pillow Talk or Lifesum's "Your journey has begun". It is one screen and a sprint of work, and it also catches users who tapped past Apple's pop-up. Reminding them of their original reason for signing up makes it stronger.

Key points.title: Remind users what they now have
Key points.detail: Users forget what is in the plan, especially if they came through a feature-specific paywall. AllTrails welcomes Peak users with an animation, then lists everything included. Beside and Headway go further and restate the outcome: Headway says "Now you are a member of Headway Premium, together with 1.7 million learners" and "It's Day 1 of your self-growth journey".

Key points.title: Ask for notifications with the trial reminder reason
Key points.detail: AllTrails asks for push permission with "We'll remind you before your trial ends." That gets permission and calms the fear of forgetting to cancel, which drives pre-emptive cancellations. Daphne notes a reminder promise does not land if notifications are off, so the post-purchase screen is the right moment to ask.

Key points.title: Give one clear first step, not a menu
Key points.detail: For content-heavy apps, the barrier after paying is often paralysis, not doubt. Greg gives one job: add your plants with a photo. Picnic drops users straight into swiping through their 2017 photos, so they feel progress before thinking about price. Duolingo shows a short set of steps after the celebratory owl.

Key points.title: Upsell only after the basics
Key points.detail: Flo offers a 'gift' of 44% off annual right after a trial starts, and Headway offers a discounted ebook. These can work in a 'yes' mindset, but sequencing matters: make users feel good about their choice first. Track Day 0 and Day 1 cancellations before and after any change, and judge upsells on realised LTV and retention.

Title: Curse of the first renewal: how to cure churn for each subscription duration
Creator: RevenueCat Sub Club (Daphne Tideman)
Bottom line: Most subscribers are lost at the first renewal, and that is decided in a short activation window early on, so fix activation rather than the renewal moment.
What they did: Using RevenueCat's State of Subscription Apps 2026 data, Daphne Tideman shows first-renewal drop-off for weekly, monthly and annual plans. She proposes an activation window for each (five days, two weeks, one month) and lays out what to do day by day or month by month. She ends with how to find a 'First Renewal Predictor' behaviour from your own data.
Results: First-renewal drop-off: "Weekly subscriptions: 42–65%", "Monthly subscriptions: 39–58%", "Annual subscriptions: 60–77%". For weekly subscribers who reach the second renewal, "74–91% will still be paying by their third." "23–50% of annual subscribers who cancel do so in the first month." By price, "low-priced annual plans see first renewal rates around 36%, while high-priced ones manage just 23%." Annual reactivation is "averaging around 5%." Duolingo found emails "23.5 hours after a user's last lesson worked best." Airship: relevant pushes in the first 90 days give retention "around 3x higher". Greg's monthly retention "sits at 21% after 12 months", then it loses "just 3% more" over nine months.
Takeaways: The first renewal is where most subscribers leave; Each plan length has its own activation window; Weekly plans need a win on Day 0; Do not go quiet in weeks two and three; Annual plans are decided in the first 90 days; Find the one early behaviour that predicts renewal
Ideas for OnCourse: Renewal: before a plan renews, show a progress summary (questions solved, accuracy gains, topics covered) so the renew decision already feels good. Notifications: keep value messages going in weeks 2–3 and months 2–3 of a plan, tapering but never stopping. Design process: compare the first 30 days of aspirants who renewed with those who did not and pick one quality behaviour (for example a 7-day practice streak) as the activation target

Key points.title: The first renewal is where most subscribers leave
Key points.detail: Retention falls 42–65% at the first weekly renewal, 39–58% for monthly and 60–77% for annual. After that, drop-off slows a lot: 74–91% of weekly subscribers who reach the second renewal are still paying at the third. Daphne calls the first renewal "the ultimate test of survival."

Key points.title: Each plan length has its own activation window
Key points.detail: Daphne's windows are the first five days for weekly, the first two weeks for monthly and the first month for annual. For short plans the window closes when users start worrying about the next charge. Users who do not reach value in that window rarely renew, whatever the paywall says.

Key points.title: Weekly plans need a win on Day 0
Key points.detail: With 84% of 3-day trial cancellations on Day 0 or 1, the first session must give a win and the post-purchase screen must push one small action. Days 1–3 deepen value, and Days 4–7 build the first signs of a habit. Messages should celebrate progress and show what is next, not say "Don't forget today's session."

Key points.title: Do not go quiet in weeks two and three
Key points.detail: Most apps "love bomb" for seven days, then go silent. For monthly plans, Daphne says Days 8–21 are for habit reinforcement, with flows that move users from their first session to their second and then to consistency. Days 22–30 should reinforce the decision with progress reports, like Loom showing hours saved, never by hiding the charge.

Key points.title: Annual plans are decided in the first 90 days
Key points.detail: About 30% of annual subscribers cancel in the first month, and starting a save effort in month 11 is too late. Expectations rise with price: cheap annual plans renew around 36%, expensive ones 23%. After 90 days, keep lower-frequency, high-quality check-ins so the product does not feel stale, as Ladder did with new travel workouts.

Key points.title: Find the one early behaviour that predicts renewal
Key points.detail: Map where the renewal curve flattens, compare early behaviour of survivors and churners, and pick what separates them. Good predictors are quality signals, like a core action done X times or coming back on Day 3 and Day 7. Session counts, onboarding completion and trial starts are not. For Duolingo it is a 7-day streak.

Title: ‘Not enough usage’: your biggest churn reason is a broken habit loop
Creator: RevenueCat Sub Club (Daphne Tideman)
Bottom line: 'Not enough usage' churn is a broken habit loop, not a price problem, so find where the loop broke and fix that instead of offering a discount.
What they did: Daphne Tideman shows how to tell usage churn from price churn using pre-cancellation usage, churner segments and price tiers. She maps usage churn to four breaks in Nir Eyal's habit loop: the trigger never fired, the action never stuck, the reward went flat, or the value never landed. Each break gets its own fix and its own shape on the usage curve.
Results: "‘not enough usage’ is the number one reason people cancel subscription apps, accounting for 37% of cancellations — ahead of 'price' at 35%" (2025); in 2026 it ranges "from 26%–40%, depending on the category." A SaaS study found stated exit reasons "matched the actual churn driver only 27.4% of the time"; price was given by 34.2% but was the real driver "in just 11.7% of those cases." A client cohort on a 50% discount "had a £50 lower lifetime value (LTV) and higher churn." Targeted emails to users inactive for five days "drove a 100%+ lift in people completing a workout within three days, versus the control group who received no emails."
Takeaways: Cancel surveys often hide the real reason; Define what enough usage means for your app; Discounts do not fix usage churn; A trigger that never fired needs timely nudges; An action that never stuck needs a quicker win and an anchor; A flat reward needs variety and visible progress
Ideas for OnCourse: Notifications: for aspirants who have not practised in a few days, send a small number of targeted messages that pick up their plan where they left off, tested against a no-message control. Renewal: when a cancel reason is 'not using it enough', offer a short catch-up plan instead of a discount. Design process: before acting on cancel reasons, check each churner's practice in the 30 days before cancelling and plot where activity stopped

Key points.title: Cancel surveys often hide the real reason
Key points.detail: In a SaaS study of 723 people, stated exit reasons matched the real cause only 27.4% of the time, and 'price' was the true driver in just 11.7% of cases where it was given. "Too expensive" can mean "I wasn't getting enough value." So check usage in the 30 days before cancelling, and see whether price complaints come from light or heavy users.

Key points.title: Define what enough usage means for your app
Key points.detail: Enough is set by how often the user meets the problem, not by daily active use. One meditation app had users who opened it once every month or two and happily paid annually. Look at what long-term subscribers repeat in their first billing cycle; that is your 'enough'. For exam prep, daily practice may fit, but the right cadence should come from OnCourse's renewing users.

Key points.title: Discounts do not fix usage churn
Key points.detail: If someone is not using the app, the price is not what is wrong. A client's 50%-off cohort had £50 lower LTV and higher churn than full-price sign-ups. A discount does not create a trigger, make an action stick or refresh a reward.

Key points.title: A trigger that never fired needs timely nudges
Key points.detail: Users who barely used the app and vanished after a session or two never built a reason to return. The fix is a well-timed, relevant re-engagement sequence where usage usually drops. For users with no workout in five days, a few targeted emails gave a 100%+ lift in workouts within three days versus no emails.

Key points.title: An action that never stuck needs a quicker win and an anchor
Key points.detail: Users who tried a few times then tailed off found the effort high and results unseen. Get them to the core action faster, and tie it to an existing routine, like 'after your morning coffee' or 'before you sleep'. Daphne's sister keeps her French going because it is welded to bedtime.

Key points.title: A flat reward needs variety and visible progress
Key points.detail: Users who were steady and then slowly faded once the novelty wore off had a reward that stopped surprising them. Vary rewards, show progress and build investment early, like Finch's rotating shop or the history users build up in Granola. If users kept showing up but nothing changed, surface outcomes, like Loom's monthly recap.

Title: How to build a reactivation strategy that actually works
Creator: RevenueCat Sub Club (Alice Muir Kocourková)
Bottom line: Win-back starts at the cancel screen: tag why people leave, time messages to plan type and reason, use offers that fit that reason, and let people pick up where they left off.
What they did: Alice Muir Kocourková lays out a six-part reactivation system for subscription apps. It begins with a one-question cancel survey whose answers map to follow-up paths, then covers post-churn messages, timing by plan type and churn reason, offers other than discounts, an easy return, and why product quality sets the ceiling.
Results: From the State of Subscription Apps 2026: "Monthly subscribers come back at ~18–24% within a year", "Even weekly plans see ~7–10% reactivation", and "Only annual plans behave like “true churn” (~4–6%)." Suggested (not tested) timing: about 7, 21 and 45 days after churn for monthly users; about 30 days, 90 days and 6 months for annual users.
Takeaways: The cancel flow is step zero of win-back; Map each churn reason to its own path; Time outreach to plan type and reason; Lead with value, not discounts; Make returning feel like continuing; Product quality sets the ceiling
Ideas for OnCourse: Renewal: add a one-question cancel survey with options like 'My exam is done or not needed right now', 'Too expensive', 'Didn't get value' and 'Technical issues', each leading to its own path (pause, cheaper plan, guided restart, support). Home: when a lapsed subscriber returns, keep their progress and plan, show what changed, and offer one quick-win practice set instead of onboarding again. Notifications: for users who left after an exam, time the win-back to the next exam cycle rather than a fixed 30 days

Key points.title: The cancel flow is step zero of win-back
Key points.detail: Instead of 'Sorry to see you go', ask one clear question about why they are leaving, with an 'other' box for bugs you do not know about. Capture churn reason, plan type, tenure, usage before churn and last meaningful action. Without this data, every later message is generic.

Key points.title: Map each churn reason to its own path
Key points.detail: "Not needed right now" leads to a pause instead of a cancel. "Too expensive" leads to a lower tier or an annual reframing. "Didn't get value" leads to guided setup, and "Technical issues" to support. Alice says most apps throw discounts here, which trains users to churn for a deal.

Key points.title: Time outreach to plan type and reason
Key points.detail: Monthly users forget fast, so test touches around 7, 21 and 45 days. Annual users get around 30 days, 90 days and 6 months. Reason matters too: wait until the need returns for 'not needed now', move fast for 'didn't get value', and say nothing about bugs until they are fixed.

Key points.title: Lead with value, not discounts
Key points.detail: Use messages like "Here's what's new since you left" or "Quick win you can get in 2 minutes", matched to the churn reason. Better offers tie to the reason ("You canceled because X. Here's a solution"), give small unlocks or credits, or use time framing like "Restart when you need it." Space messages across email, push and retargeting so it never feels like a chase.

Key points.title: Make returning feel like continuing
Key points.detail: Many teams win the click, then lose the user by treating them like a new one. Skip re-onboarding, keep preferences, history and progress, default to their previous plan, and show what changed. Pause, easy plan switching and grace periods lower the barrier to coming back.

Key points.title: Product quality sets the ceiling
Key points.detail: If users left because they never understood the product or never got value, no win-back message will fix it. Reactivation only works when onboarding, activation and value delivery are solid. Apple's Retention Messaging API is a new place to show a pause or value reminder inside the App Store cancel flow.

Title: How Philips’ Pregnancy+ grew weekly subscription revenue by 300%
Creator: Adapty
Bottom line: A freemium content app grew revenue by testing much more often, and found that a free trial beat an intro discount, a trial timeline helped, and a day-5 offer beat a day-1 offer.
What they did: Pregnancy+, a freemium app with 80 million downloads, used to run about one paywall test per quarter because each needed engineering and an app release. After moving to Adapty in November 2024, one person owned each test end to end, with a written hypothesis and success criteria. Over 12 months the team tested 42 paywall variants; four tests gave the clearest signal.
Results: "The free trial variant generated 140% more revenue than the discounted control." A trial timeline (today, day 3, charge after day 3, when to cancel) raised "Revenue increased 27% against the control." Showing the offer on day five: "Revenue was 17% higher than showing the same offer on day one." Seasonal campaigns: "Black Friday / Cyber Monday (+113% vs prior period), New Year (+53.5%), and Mother's Day UK (+52%)." Overall: "Weekly subscription revenue grew 300% over the 12 months", "Premium conversion grew from 0.4% to approximately 2% in top-performing markets", and "Monthly retention reached 65% at the second renewal." Test cadence went from "1 test per quarter to 3+ per month."
Takeaways: A free trial beat an intro discount by 140%; A trial timeline added 27% revenue; An offer on day 5 beat day 1 by 17%; Match seasonal offers to the moment; More tests, faster, drove most of the growth
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: test a free trial against an intro discount and judge it on revenue and second-renewal retention, not first conversion. Paywall: add a trial timeline that shows what you get today, when the reminder comes, when you are charged and when you can cancel. Notifications: test showing the main upgrade offer on day five, after the aspirant has done some practice, instead of only on day one

Key points.title: A free trial beat an intro discount by 140%
Key points.detail: The team expected a lower intro price to win, but the free trial variant made 140% more revenue. Users who tried the product at full value converted and stayed at higher rates than users won by discounting. The team links this to the 65% monthly retention at second renewal.

Key points.title: A trial timeline added 27% revenue
Key points.detail: The paywall gained a visual breakdown: what you get today, what happens on day 3, what you are charged after day 3, and when you can cancel. Revenue rose 27%. Adapty's point is that unsure users leave before converting, so remove the doubt on the paywall itself, not in later emails.

Key points.title: An offer on day 5 beat day 1 by 17%
Key points.detail: Instead of a promo right at install, the team showed it on day five, after users had explored and used core content. Revenue was 17% higher. On day one users are still deciding if the app is worth their time; by day five the offer "confirms a decision they are already moving toward."

Key points.title: Match seasonal offers to the moment
Key points.detail: Time-limited campaigns ran at Black Friday/Cyber Monday (+113%), New Year (+53.5%) and Mother's Day UK (+52%) without cannibalising baseline conversion. Core messaging stayed the same, but the frame matched each moment's emotion. For OnCourse, the moments might be result day, a new exam date or the start of a prep season.

Key points.title: More tests, faster, drove most of the growth
Key points.detail: Test cadence went from one every two to three months to three or more a month. Each test started with a written hypothesis and success criteria, simple tests first. The PM says the growth "was not one big win. It was dozens of small ones compounding."

Title: What State of Paywalls taught me about the tests subscription apps skip
Creator: Adapty (Victoria Kharlan)
Bottom line: Paywall offer, timing and personalization tests win far more often than visual or copy tests, so spend most of your tests there and only one on looks.
What they did: Adapty's Victoria Kharlan went through State of Paywalls 2026 data (78,000+ paywalls from 30,000+ App Store apps) plus 100 top-app paywalls taken apart via Mobbin. She describes the default paywall, compares win rates by test type, and lists five tests few apps run, each with live examples. She ends with how many tests to run a year.
Results: "35% of visual or copy tests increased LTV", while "62% of localization tests increased LTV, followed by trial tests at 60% and plan-duration tests at 59%." "93% of first purchases happen on the day of install"; onboarding paywalls convert "0.85% of views against 0.23%." Pre-selecting annual with the trial on it "raised ARPU by 25–40%" in winning tests; personalized onboarding "raised ARPU by 13–35%"; explaining the trial "raised ARPU by 12–36%." Only "2% of paywall headlines" use onboarding answers and "24% of trial paywalls show a timeline." A second offer after close converts "at 0.88× the rate of the main paywall" and beats it in 45% of the apps using it. "32% of trials are canceled within an hour and 44% within 24 hours." Education ranks "#3 in the US at 3.28% and drops to #7 in APAC (0.89%)."
Takeaways: Most top paywalls look the same; Visual and copy tests win least often; Test timing and the offer first; Pre-select annual and put the trial on it; Put the onboarding answer in the headline; Show the trial as a timeline; A second offer after close often pays
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: put the onboarding answers in the headline, for example the target exam and date ('Your plan for NEET-PG, starting today'). Paywall: test a one-time second offer after the paywall is closed, keeping the discount at or under 30% so those subscribers stay valuable. Design process: plan the year's paywall tests so most go to timing, plans, trial and personalization, and only one goes to visuals

Key points.title: Most top paywalls look the same
Key points.detail: In 100 top iOS paywalls, 62% show two plans, 73% use cards, 67% pre-select annual, and 36% say "Start free trial" word for word. Only 27% show social proof, 54% have no image, and 2% personalize the headline. That is the market default, a starting line for tests rather than proof of what converts.

Key points.title: Visual and copy tests win least often
Key points.detail: Only 35% of visual or copy tests raised LTV, the lowest of any test type, against 59–62% for localization, trial and plan-duration tests. A redesign changes how the offer looks, but the user still decides on the same price, plan and trial. When visual tests do win, the lift is real: animation and stronger visuals raised ARPU 16–34%.

Key points.title: Test timing and the offer first
Key points.detail: 93% of first purchases happen on install day and 60% of buyers subscribe on the first paywall view. Onboarding paywalls convert almost 4× better than later ones ($170 vs $40 per 1,000 views). Later paywalls still bring 38% of revenue. Education and Health & Fitness are the only categories where most trials run 4–7 days, with the fewest early cancellations.

Key points.title: Pre-select annual and put the trial on it
Key points.detail: This layout change gave the biggest lift in winning tests: 25–40% more ARPU. Cal AI pre-selects annual under a '3 DAYS FREE' banner while monthly has no trial. Buyers mostly keep the default: 90% keep weekly when it is pre-selected, 46% keep annual. Judge price tests on LTV, since 46% of them raise LTV but only 28% raise conversion.

Key points.title: Put the onboarding answer in the headline
Key points.detail: Yazio opens with "We'll help you lose weight to hit 70.0 kg by April 7!" using the goal and date from onboarding; Runna greets the runner by name. Only 2% of headlines do this, yet personalized onboarding raised ARPU 13–35% in winning tests. For OnCourse, the exam, attempt year and weak subjects from onboarding can go straight into the paywall.

Key points.title: Show the trial as a timeline
Key points.detail: Vocabulary gives the trial its own screen: trial starts today, a reminder on March 26, membership on March 27, with a reminder toggle above the button. Only 24% of trial paywalls do this, yet trial explainers raised ARPU 12–36%. It targets the first hour, when 32% of trials are cancelled.

Title: How Quiet scales new apps faster with built-in analytics and A/B testing
Creator: Adapty
Bottom line: Judge a paywall design test by the cost of each paying user against their lifetime value, because a small conversion gap can decide whether an app makes or loses money.
What they did: Quiet, a Paris app studio, keeps or kills each new app within weeks based on whether a cohort pays back its install cost. It runs paywall tests and reads LTV, churn and cohort revenue in one dashboard. In one test it split traffic evenly between a white and a purple main paywall button and turned the result into cost per paying subscriber.
Results: "The white button won, lifting trial conversion from 19% to 23.64%" (purple at 19.05%). At a $2 install cost, trials cost "$8.46 each" for white and "$10.49" for purple; per paying subscriber, "white came out at $25.38 and purple at $31.47." With an app "worth roughly $28 per subscriber", white makes a profit on each and purple loses money. Portfolio: "99 A/B tests", "$16.4M in ARR, from 8M installs and 71k+ subscribers."
Takeaways: A button colour test lifted trials from 19% to 23.64%; Turn conversion into cost per paying user; Compare that cost with lifetime value; Read tests past the first conversion; Same-day tests make small checks cheap
Ideas for OnCourse: Design process: report every paywall test result as cost per paying user and compare it with that user's expected lifetime value, not just conversion percentage. Paywall: test the main button's colour and contrast against the background as a cheap first visual test. Design process: keep a shared readout that follows each test's cohort through renewals, not just first purchase

Key points.title: A button colour test lifted trials from 19% to 23.64%
Key points.detail: Quiet split traffic evenly between a white and a purple main paywall button on an app it was scaling. White won, with trial conversion of 23.64% against 19.05%. The case study does not say why white won or show the paywall's other colours, so treat it as one app's result.

Key points.title: Turn conversion into cost per paying user
Key points.detail: At a $2 install cost, $200 buys 100 users. White turned them into trials at $8.46 each and purple at $10.49. Carried through to paying subscribers, white cost $25.38 and purple $31.47 each.

Key points.title: Compare that cost with lifetime value
Key points.detail: The app earns roughly $28 per subscriber over its life. At $25.38, the white button makes money on each subscriber; at $31.47, purple loses money. A gap that looks minor as a conversion rate is the difference between profit and loss, and Quiet "might have scaled the losing version by default."

Key points.title: Read tests past the first conversion
Key points.detail: Quiet's CEO says they read "LTV, churn, expired users, and cohort revenue in one place." The team follows a paywall test's cohort months later, after renewals and churn. Installs and trials come earlier but do not show whether an app makes money.

Key points.title: Same-day tests make small checks cheap
Key points.detail: Tests launch from a dashboard without an app release, so an idea can go live the day it comes up. That is why a small team ran 99 tests across its apps on iOS and Android. This is a vendor case study, so the tool claims are promotional, but the unit-economics reading applies anywhere.

Title: The Subscription Value Loop: A framework for growing consumer subscription businesses
Creator: Lenny's Newsletter (Phil Carter)
Bottom line: Consumer subscription apps grow by pulling ten levers across the loop of creating value and capturing it, from fast onboarding and a visible paywall to fixing failed payments and smart discounts.
What they did: Phil Carter, a former Quizlet growth leader, describes a loop where users get value, convert, renew and refer others. He lists 10 levers with tactics, target metrics and an app example for each. Examples include Headway's onboarding, Calm's paywall, Duolingo's streaks, Quizlet's study streaks and back-to-school word of mouth, and Flo's trial toggle with a discount for users who decline.
Results: Top-quartile apps "only convert roughly 1 in 20 installs into a paid subscription" and "lose more than half of their annual subscribers after the first year". Pricing and packaging changes "consistently generate 5% to 15% lift on subscription revenue"; at AllTrails a higher price "drove an ~8.3% lift in ARPU" in an A/B test. "More than 75% of trial starts occur on the same day a user installs an app." Blinkist's timeline paywall "boosted Blinkist's trial start rate by 23%, cut cancellations by 4%, and increased subscriber conversion by 9%." "20% to 40% (or more)" of churn can be involuntary.
Takeaways: Most trials start on install day; Show the paywall to almost everyone on day one; Price changes are an underused lever; Fix churn people don't choose; Streaks and badges tap real motivations; Discounts should match low intent
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: ask 2–3 quick questions (exam, attempt date, weak subjects), then show a personal study plan before the paywall so the payoff comes first. Paywall: make sure most new users see it on day 1, and add a timeline that says when the trial ends and when they will be charged. Renewal: retry failed payments and remind users before the card fails, since 20% to 40% of churn can be involuntary.

Key points.title: Most trials start on install day
Key points.detail: The article cites a report that "more than 75% of trial starts occur on the same day a user installs an app (often in the first few minutes)." So onboarding must be built for speed to value. Headway does this with a clear promise, SSO, short questions that build intent, and a personal reading plan. OnCourse onboarding should end with a plan, not a form.

Key points.title: Show the paywall to almost everyone on day one
Key points.detail: Carter says "you want Day 1 Paywall View Rate to be at or above 80%." Blinkist's timeline paywall raised trial starts by 23% and cut cancellations by 4%. Calm keeps its paywall simple, with an emotional headline, a short feature list and a "Most Popular" tag on the annual plan. A clear, honest paywall seen early beats a hidden one.

Key points.title: Price changes are an underused lever
Key points.detail: Carter has seen pricing and packaging changes "consistently generate 5% to 15% lift on subscription revenue." AllTrails raised its price from $29.99 to $35.99 and an A/B test showed an "~8.3% lift in ARPU." Many teams set a price once and never test it. Plans and durations deserve their own tests.

Key points.title: Fix churn people don't choose
Key points.detail: Sources cited say "20% to 40% (or more)" of churn is involuntary, from failed payments. Fixes include payment retries, card updaters and grace periods. Web checkout also helps, because web subscribers have lower involuntary churn. This is a cheap renewal win before any redesign.

Key points.title: Streaks and badges tap real motivations
Key points.detail: Quizlet's survey found "Ownership, Accomplishment, and Scarcity" were its users' main drives. That led to study streaks and accomplishments. Duolingo also uses loss avoidance through streak freezes and repairs. Notifications remind users about these features.

Key points.title: Discounts should match low intent
Key points.detail: Flo shows a toggle for a free 14-day trial. Users who reject the trial see a big lifetime discount as an expiring one-time offer. Another tactic is an email with "a one-time 15%-to-30% discount" to users who don't subscribe within 24 to 48 hours. Seasonal and student discounts also work for study apps.

Title: How to develop product sense
Creator: Lenny's Newsletter (Jules Walter)
Bottom line: Product sense is a skill you build by watching real people use products, taking apart good products, and learning how strong product thinkers reason.
What they did: Jules Walter, a product leader who worked at Slack, defines product sense as the skill of predicting what will help users. He gives four practices: observe users, deconstruct everyday products, learn from great product thinkers, and stay curious about technology. He uses Slack research on mobile churn and Slack experiments as examples.
Results: Slack saw "increases in purchases when we moved some of the information on the various purchase options behind a dropdown list." An early mobile experiment "increased user retention just by telling new users what Slack is and linking to a video". No percentages are given.
Takeaways: Watch real users two to four times a month; Slack users were lost, distracted and wary; People are time-crunched and easily scared off; Less information can sell more; Deconstruct one product a month
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: add one plain line on what OnCourse does and how a day of study works, since telling new Slack users what Slack is raised retention. Paywall: move secondary plan details behind a "See details" toggle so the main choice is easy to scan. Practice: watch 2–4 users a month solve a question set, and note where they hesitate or look nervous.

Key points.title: Watch real users two to four times a month
Key points.detail: Walter recommends observing people "two to four times a month for your product." He says to attend research sessions, not just read reports. Watching builds empathy and shows you the gap between your intent and real behaviour. Notes from each session add up over time.

Key points.title: Slack users were lost, distracted and wary
Key points.detail: Slack's mobile churn research found the homepage was "too abstract", users met "competing calls to action", and they did not want to share their address book. Each finding led to an experiment. Telling new users what Slack is and linking a video increased retention. The lesson is to explain the product before asking for anything.

Key points.title: People are time-crunched and easily scared off
Key points.detail: Walter lists patterns he saw across hundreds of users. People are "time-crunched and distracted", so pick good defaults and make the main action obvious. They "drop out of a product flow as soon as they feel confused or nervous." Small worries end sessions.

Key points.title: Less information can sell more
Key points.detail: On Slack's pricing page, moving some plan details "behind a dropdown list" increased purchases. Too much information at once overwhelms people. Show the key choice first and let curious users expand the rest. This applies directly to paywalls.

Key points.title: Deconstruct one product a month
Key points.detail: Walter spends "one or two hours a month trying out new products and deconstructing them." He uses critique questions to ask why each choice was made. One example is Slack's quiet-hours detail, built "to prevent anxiety", not to move metrics. "The details are not the details."

Title: The PM 🤝 Design Partnership
Creator: Lenny's Newsletter (Katie Dill)
Bottom line: PMs and designers work best when the PM trusts the designer's craft, brings them in early, and both share goals and a north-star vision.
What they did: Katie Dill, then head of design at Lyft, answers a reader who struggles to work with designers. She gives five tips: trust the designer's expertise, be the conductor, include designers early, invest in even small north stars, and create shared goals. She uses Lyft examples to size vision work.
Results: Lyft's high-fidelity rider-app vision "took ~6 months with bi-weekly exec reviews", while a sketch vision for the sign-up flow "took less than a week." No experiment results.
Takeaways: North stars can be small and fast; Without a vision products become Frankensteins; Link design goals to business goals; Bring designers in at the start
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: before redesigning screen by screen, sketch a one-week north star for the whole first-day flow and agree on it with the PM. Home: tie design goals like consistency to a product goal, since "consistency of the system is a sub-goal of usability which is a sub-goal of conversion."

Key points.title: North stars can be small and fast
Key points.detail: Dill says a vision does not have to be huge. Lyft's high-fidelity rider-app vision took "~6 months with bi-weekly exec reviews." A sketch vision of the sign-up flow "took less than a week." Pick the size by scope, fidelity, time horizon and the buy-in you need.

Key points.title: Without a vision products become Frankensteins
Key points.detail: Without a north star, teams "miss the opportunity to innovate" and neglect the long term. The product turns into "a disjointed Frankenstein lacking consistency." A shared picture keeps small changes pointing the same way. Even one screen can be envisioned in a day.

Key points.title: Link design goals to business goals
Key points.detail: Design goals like consistency, usability, accessibility and delight can look indirect. Dill explains "consistency of the system is a sub-goal of usability which is a sub-goal of conversion." Mapping these links helps the team rank and sequence work. Ignoring indirect work "is not an option."

Key points.title: Bring designers in at the start
Key points.detail: Designers add the most when they help frame the problem, not just style the answer. The PM should act as a conductor who brings in the right people at the right time. Trust the designer's expertise rather than dictating solutions. Saying "my design partner" instead of "my designer" signals this.

Title: What working at Figma taught me about customer obsession
Creator: Lenny's Newsletter (Sho Kuwamoto)
Bottom line: Figma stayed close to customers by making support everyone's job and by treating the feel of the product, like speed and consistency, as a core feature.
What they did: Sho Kuwamoto, a former Figma product leader, shares three lessons. Engineers and designers answered support tickets directly. Figma treated software as a service that keeps improving, and it launched without some big features to keep the core feeling good. The team held a bar for feel, such as 60 frames per second.
Results: Support took "sometimes 20% of an engineer's time or more", yet the team found it made product development faster, not slower. Multiplayer shipped "nine months after our initial preview release." No measured experiment.
Takeaways: Support is everyone's job; Ship a core that feels good, not every feature; Feel matters more the more often people use it; Hold a hard bar for speed; Think like a host
Ideas for OnCourse: Practice: set a feel bar for answer feedback (instant tap response, smooth transitions), because daily-use products live or die on feel. Lessons: rotate designers through a weekly hour of reading support chats and app reviews to find friction.

Key points.title: Support is everyone's job
Key points.detail: At Figma, engineers and designers answered customers directly. It took "sometimes 20% of an engineer's time or more." The team found this made development go faster, not slower. They heard problems first-hand and fixed them quickly.

Key points.title: Ship a core that feels good, not every feature
Key points.detail: Figma's first release had no "components, styles, or even multiplayer." Cutting multiplayer was hard, but starting with something that "felt bad" would create a credibility problem. Multiplayer came "nine months after our initial preview release." Quality of the core came before breadth.

Key points.title: Feel matters more the more often people use it
Key points.detail: Kuwamoto writes "the more frequently a piece of software is used, the more important 'feel' is." Daily tools like messaging and spreadsheets win or lose on feel. Feel includes performance, familiarity and consistency. OnCourse is used daily, so this applies strongly.

Key points.title: Hold a hard bar for speed
Key points.detail: Figma tries "to hold ourselves to a bar of 60 frames per second whenever we can." Speed is part of feel, not a separate engineering concern. Slow screens make users trust the product less. Designers should name performance in their specs.

Key points.title: Think like a host
Key points.detail: Kuwamoto imagines himself as "just like a host, inviting my user into my application". He wants them to have a wonderful time. This framing keeps attention on how each moment feels. It suits a study app where users spend long sessions.

Title: Strategy and tactics for improving conversion
Creator: Lenny's Newsletter (Lenny Rachitsky)
Bottom line: Raise conversion by keeping users focused, keeping them motivated and removing friction, then bring bounced users back with a reminder, news that something changed, or more information.
What they did: Lenny shares the biggest conversion wins he saw at Airbnb, grouped into three levers: focus, motivation and friction. Examples include opening listings in a new tab, removing a distracting Neighborhoods section, scarcity messages, Instant Book and smart defaults. He then covers what to say to bounced users and the channels to reach them.
Results: Opening listings in a new tab "turned out to be one of the biggest conversion wins". When the team removed Neighborhoods from the home page, "bookings went up." With Instant Book, "guest conversion significantly increased." No percentages are given.
Takeaways: Three levers: focus, motivation, friction; Interesting content can hurt conversion; Smart defaults beat extra questions; Remind users why to come back
Ideas for OnCourse: Home: remove content that distracts from starting today's plan, since Airbnb's bookings rose when it removed interesting but distracting content. Onboarding: prefill smart defaults (exam, daily target) instead of asking open questions. Notifications: send users who left a set midway a reminder that they are a few questions from finishing.

Key points.title: Three levers: focus, motivation, friction
Key points.detail: Lenny frames every funnel idea as keeping user focus, keeping motivation, or reducing friction. Teams should brainstorm ideas within each lever and test many of them. He advises testing "as many ideas as you can, vs. betting on just a few amazing ideas." Where tests are not possible, do the research and trust your best guess.

Key points.title: Interesting content can hurt conversion
Key points.detail: Airbnb's Neighborhoods content was loved by visitors, "almost too much." It distracted them from booking. "When the team removed it from the home page, bookings went up." Good content in the wrong place is a distraction.

Key points.title: Smart defaults beat extra questions
Key points.detail: New Airbnb hosts faced dozens of questions about price and availability. The team found "a lot of success in setting smart default answers". When you can't remove a step, prefill it. Performance also mattered, especially on mobile.

Key points.title: Remind users why to come back
Key points.detail: Bounced users need a reason to return: a reminder, "something has changed", or more information. Airbnb's best messages included telling new hosts they were "only X steps away". Channels are email or push, retargeting and calls. Push is "simple, effective, but easy to abuse."

Title: How to consistently go viral: Nikita Bier’s playbook for winning at consumer apps (co-founder of TBH, Gas, advisor, investor)
Creator: Lenny's Newsletter (Nikita Bier)
Bottom line: Consumer apps win by showing value in the first seconds, treating every tap as costly, and testing one idea cleanly while sweating the pixels.
What they did: Nikita Bier built TBH and Gas, two teen apps that went viral, and sold them to Facebook and Discord. He explains how he tested ideas by launching in one school at a time to remove confounding variables. He also covers positive-only polls, 24-hour live chat support, contact permissions and why time to value must be seconds.
Results: On day one, "you're lucky if people send three or four" messages, "but we were sending 60". A week after launch, "40% of the high school down your street in Los Angeles has downloaded it". Contact permission screens average "about 65% approval rate across all apps." These are his reported figures, not controlled tests.
Takeaways: Every tap is a miracle; Remove confounding variables when testing; Live chat is the best research tool; Positive mechanics drove huge engagement; Products live and die in the pixels; Show value in three seconds
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: cut every screen that doesn't lead to the first question, because "every tap on a mobile app is a miracle". Practice: show value in the first three seconds by opening the app to a ready question, not a menu. Notifications: keep messages positive and earned (progress, praise) rather than guilt-based.

Key points.title: Every tap is a miracle
Key points.detail: Bier says "every tap on a mobile app is a miracle" because users "bounce to their next app very quickly." Each extra step loses people. He designs flows to get users to value with as few taps as possible. Onboarding length is a real cost.

Key points.title: Remove confounding variables when testing
Key points.detail: Bier tested by launching in a single school so many people adopted at once. This let him "eliminate all those potentially confounding variables so you can know immediately whether something's working." He tests the ideal version of one idea, fully executed. Weak tests give unclear answers.

Key points.title: Live chat is the best research tool
Key points.detail: He recommends "live chat customer support in your app 24 hours a day." It gives users a white-glove experience. It is also "the best vehicle for getting feedback and doing user research" because users tell you their problem directly. Small teams can learn fast this way.

Key points.title: Positive mechanics drove huge engagement
Key points.detail: TBH allowed only positive things through polls, like "who has the best smile". On day one users sent 60 messages, when "you're lucky if people send three or four." People "want to know good things about themselves." Positive feedback loops kept teens coming back.

Key points.title: Products live and die in the pixels
Key points.detail: Bier argues that for consumer products, "products live and die in the pixels." He gets into the pixels and designs flows himself. Details of screens decide whether an app spreads. Process documents matter less than the actual flow.

Key points.title: Show value in three seconds
Key points.detail: Bier says "if you can't demonstrate value in the first three seconds, it's over." Attention is spread thin across notifications and apps. Lenny sums it up as "get to three seconds time to value." The first screen must deliver, not explain.

Title: The hierarchy of engagement | Sarah Tavel (Benchmark, Greylock, Pinterest)
Creator: Lenny's Newsletter (Sarah Tavel)
Bottom line: Products build lasting engagement in three levels: get users to the core action, make the product better the more they use it, then create loops that bring them back on their own.
What they did: Sarah Tavel, a Benchmark partner and early Pinterest PM, explains her Hierarchy of Engagement. Level 1 is growing users who complete the core action. Level 2 is retention, where the product improves with use and users have more to lose by leaving. Level 3 is self-perpetuating loops, like Pinterest's repin notifications. The second half of the episode covers marketplaces.
Results: At Pinterest, "if someone's pinning something, they're coming back to Pinterest the next week with a super high, more than 90% probability at the time." No experiment numbers.
Takeaways: Find the one core action; Rank actions by return rate; Make the product better with use; Notifications can create or break loops; Too much at the start kills activation; Watch for the smile graph
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: define one core action (finishing a first question set) and make the first session lead straight to it. Progress & streaks: show what the user has built (questions solved, weak topics fixed) so leaving feels like a loss. Notifications: track weekly cohorts on the core action and look for a smile-shaped curve, not just daily opens.

Key points.title: Find the one core action
Key points.detail: Tavel says social products have "the core action of that product that forms the foundation". At Pinterest it was pinning. The new user experience must help users understand the product "well enough that they start completing the core action." Everything in onboarding should point there.

Key points.title: Rank actions by return rate
Key points.detail: Pinterest found its core action by looking at which actions predicted return. Users who pinned came back the next week with "more than 90% probability." YouTube first thought watching was core, but found "subscribing was the core action." Data can overturn your assumption.

Key points.title: Make the product better with use
Key points.detail: Level 2 is about accruing benefit. "When they complete that core action, the product gets more retentive for them." A feed picked for you or saved notes give users more to lose by leaving. "If you want to increase retention, get people to do the core action more often."

Key points.title: Notifications can create or break loops
Key points.detail: Level 3 is self-perpetuating loops. Pinterest's repin notification brought people back to pin again. Tavel warns that Houseparty and Clubhouse overused push and broke the loop. Notifications must carry real value.

Key points.title: Too much at the start kills activation
Key points.detail: A common mistake is that "there's too much in the beginning to take in and understand." Then the product doesn't get users "to the thing that you most want them to do." Founders often miss the activation moment. Focus beats features early on.

Key points.title: Watch for the smile graph
Key points.detail: Tavel tracks weekly active users completing the core action by cohort. The hope is "the classic smile graph", where cohorts use the product more over time. The opposite is a leaky bucket where cohorts keep falling. This is a better health signal than raw opens.

Title: Identify your bullseye customer in one day | Michael Margolis (UX Research Partner at Google Ventures)
Creator: Lenny's Newsletter (Michael Margolis)
Bottom line: Learn fast by interviewing five carefully chosen customers in one day, showing them three prototypes, and having the whole team watch together.
What they did: Michael Margolis runs research sprints for Google Ventures startups. His formula is "five and three in one": five bullseye customers, three prototypes, one day. He explains how to define the customer with inclusion and exclusion criteria, recruit and pay them, build simple prototypes, write a two-part interview, and run a team watch party with no report.
Results: He pays participants about "125 bucks an hour" for typical consumer studies. In one sprint, a pharmacy found "a predictable, narrow window of when this was going to arrive was much, much important than ASAP" for refrigerated medicines. No experiment numbers.
Takeaways: Five customers, three prototypes, one day; Define a narrow bullseye customer; Learn what no looks like; Watch together instead of writing a report; Write predictions first to beat hindsight bias; Weight past behaviour over predictions
Ideas for OnCourse: Onboarding: test three onboarding prototypes with five NEET-PG aspirants in one day, and have the PM and engineers watch live. Paywall: write team predictions before the sessions, then compare after, to avoid "we knew that already".

Key points.title: Five customers, three prototypes, one day
Key points.detail: Margolis's "basic formula" is "five and three in one." Five interviews in a single day show patterns fast. Users compare three prototypes like shopping, which gives richer reactions than one. The team gets answers in a week.

Key points.title: Define a narrow bullseye customer
Key points.detail: He defines the target with inclusion criteria, exclusion criteria and triggers. A pharmacy sprint found the bullseye was patients with refrigerated medicines. For them, "a predictable, narrow window" mattered more than ASAP delivery. A narrow target makes the signal clear.

Key points.title: Learn what no looks like
Key points.detail: Seeing customers reject an idea is valuable. One founder said "Now I know what no looks like." Clear rejection saves months of building the wrong thing. It also sharpens what yes looks like.

Key points.title: Watch together instead of writing a report
Key points.detail: The whole team joins a "working watch party". "I'm not doing a report," he says, because everyone sees it first-hand. Watchers take notes in a shared sheet and agree takeaways at the end. This speeds up decisions.

Key points.title: Write predictions first to beat hindsight bias
Key points.detail: Before the watch party, everyone predicts what they will learn. "It's very difficult to remember that you didn't already know this" afterwards. Comparing predictions with results shows real learning. It also reveals the team's blind spots.

Key points.title: Weight past behaviour over predictions
Key points.detail: Margolis advises "put more weight on past experiences than on people's predictions of what they would do." People are poor at forecasting their own behaviour. Ask what they did last time. This is key for pricing and study-habit questions.

Title: The ultimate guide to JTBD | Bob Moesta (co-creator of the framework)
Creator: Lenny's Newsletter (Bob Moesta)
Bottom line: People switch products because of a struggling moment, so design for their context and progress, and reduce the anxiety and habit that hold them back.
What they did: Bob Moesta, co-creator of Jobs To Be Done, explains that demand comes from struggling moments. He describes the four forces of switching (push, pull, anxiety, habit) and six buying phases. He shares how to interview recent switchers without a script, and examples from a condo developer and Autobooks.
Results: Including moving and two years of storage with a condo "increased sales over 30%." Meeting Autobooks buyers by phase made "the sales process almost half and at 4x basically conversion." Giving up a second bedroom suite for dining room table space "increased sales 22%." These are his reported results.
Takeaways: Struggling moments create demand; Reduce anxiety and habit, not just add pull; Meet people where they are in buying; Interview recent switchers, not a script; Complaints are not switching; Choose what to suck at
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: address anxiety directly ("Cancel anytime", "Will this cover my exam?") rather than only adding features. Onboarding: ask what made the user start preparing now, and use that struggling moment to pick their first plan. Renewal: interview users who churned and those who just renewed, about what happened, not what they think.

Key points.title: Struggling moments create demand
Key points.detail: Moesta says people don't buy because of features but because of a struggle in their life. Context and outcome matter more than pain and gain. "A kick-ass half is better than a half-ass whole." Build for the moment of struggle.

Key points.title: Reduce anxiety and habit, not just add pull
Key points.detail: Four forces drive switching: push, pull, anxiety and habit. A condo developer added moving and two years of storage because buyers feared getting rid of their stuff. It "increased sales over 30%" even at a higher price. Removing friction beat adding features.

Key points.title: Meet people where they are in buying
Key points.detail: There are "six phases" from first thought to ongoing use. Autobooks split its demos by phase. It cut the sales cycle "almost half" with "4x basically conversion." Messages should match the phase the user is in.

Key points.title: Interview recent switchers, not a script
Key points.detail: Talk to people who just switched or churned, about what actually happened. About 10–12 interviews show repeating patterns. Moesta uses no discussion guide and plays answers back wrong on purpose. People correct you and reveal more.

Key points.title: Complaints are not switching
Key points.detail: "Bitchin' ain't switchin'," says Moesta. Users who complain often still stay. What matters is what makes them actually move. Basecamp learned this when users asked for Gantt charts.

Key points.title: Choose what to suck at
Key points.detail: Moesta advises: "choose what to suck at and figure out the trade-offs." Your trade-offs should match the customer's. Giving up a second bedroom suite for dining table space "increased sales 22%." Not every feature deserves equal effort.

Title: The UX research reckoning is here | Judd Antin (Airbnb, Meta)
Creator: Lenny's Newsletter (Judd Antin)
Bottom line: Research pays off when it is fast, pointed at business problems and built into the team from the start, not used at the end to validate decisions already made.
What they did: Judd Antin, former head of research at Airbnb, splits research into macro, middle-range and micro. He argues teams do too much vague middle-range research and too little fast micro work like usability. He names "user-centered performance", research done for show. He shares Airbnb's button-copy fix and Facebook's "super hider" interview, and argues for CSAT over NPS.
Results: At Airbnb, research found a CTA felt scary; the team "changed seven characters and made Airbnb millions of dollars", which "added like 1%" to conversion. The insight came "in like 48 hours". No other numbers.
Takeaways: Middle-range research is interesting but weak; Seven characters made millions; Don't validate, falsify; One user can burst a bubble; A/B tests say what, research says why; Use CSAT instead of NPS
Ideas for OnCourse: Paywall: check whether the main button feels like it charges money now; reword it (e.g. "See plans") and test it. Practice: run quick usability checks on new screens within 48 hours rather than broad studies. Renewal: ask a short satisfaction (CSAT) question instead of NPS.

Key points.title: Middle-range research is interesting but weak
Key points.detail: Antin splits research into macro, middle-range and micro. Middle-range work asks broad questions like how hosts feel about payments. It is "really interesting" but "not impactful enough for the business." Point research at a funnel step or goal.

Key points.title: Seven characters made millions
Key points.detail: Airbnb research found buyers were afraid the button would charge them. "The CTA on the button feels scary." The team "changed seven characters and made Airbnb millions of dollars", adding about 1% to conversion. The insight took about 48 hours.

Key points.title: Don't validate, falsify
Key points.detail: Antin's mantra is "We don't validate, we falsify. We are looking to be wrong." Asking for a study at the end "just to validate our assumptions" is user-centered performance. It is too late to change anything. Bring research in early.

Key points.title: One user can burst a bubble
Key points.detail: At Facebook, engineers wanted to use hidden posts as a quality signal. A "super hider" hid every post because she had seen it, aiming for inbox zero. Watching her changed the team's mind. One session can show a wrong assumption.

Key points.title: A/B tests say what, research says why
Key points.detail: A/B tests are "as close as we can get to making causal claims". But they "rarely tell you how and why". Without the why, teams guess and run endless tests. Pair experiments with quick research.

Key points.title: Use CSAT instead of NPS
Key points.detail: Antin calls NPS "the best example of the marketing industry marketing itself." Its 11-point scale is imprecise, and on mobile options fall below the fold. A simple satisfaction question "has better data properties" and is more tied to business outcomes. Airbnb confirmed this in its own data.
